los.lo: Describe the vertical division of the atmosphere up to flight level (FL) 650, based on the temperature variations with height.
los.title: Vertical division of the atmosphere up to FL 650
los.html:
Theory & physics

The atmosphere is divided by the sign of the temperature lapse rate, not by composition. Troposphere: temperature falls with height (ISA 1.98 °C/1000 ft) because the air is heated from below by the ground. Tropopause: the level where the lapse rate drops to ≤ 2 °C/km (WMO definition). Stratosphere: isothermal in its lower part (ISA −56.5 °C from 11 to 20 km), then warming with height because ozone absorbs UV. FL 650 ≈ 20 km, so the syllabus stops at the top of the isothermal layer.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Distractor: "the layers are defined by gas composition" or "by pressure". Correct: by temperature behaviour.
  • Distractor: "temperature rises throughout the stratosphere". ISA: constant to 20 km, rising above.
  • Nearly all weather (cloud, icing, convection) is tropospheric; jet cruise sits near the tropopause, where temperature trend, wind and CAT change.

los.lo: List the different layers and their main qualitative characteristics up to FL 650.
los.title: Layers and their main characteristics up to FL 650
los.html:
Theory & physics

Troposphere: contains almost all water vapour, strong vertical mixing, weather. Tropopause: thin transition layer, often with breaks and jet streams. Stratosphere: very dry, very stable (temperature constant or rising = inversion-like), little vertical motion, horizontal winds decrease above the jet level.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stratospheric cruise is normally smooth and cloud-free; exceptions are overshooting Cb tops, CAT near the tropopause and breaking mountain waves.
  • Question pattern: "which layer contains most of the water vapour?" → troposphere.

los.lo: Describe the troposphere.
los.title: The troposphere
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lowest layer, from the surface to the tropopause: \~8 km (\~FL 250–300) at the poles, \~11 km (36 090 ft) in ISA mid-latitudes, \~16–18 km (\~FL 550) at the equator. Holds about 75–80 % of the mass of the atmosphere and nearly all water vapour. Mean lapse rate 0.65 °C/100 m. Thicker over warm air because warm air columns expand.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "troposphere is thickest at the poles". It is thickest at the equator and in summer.
  • Trap: confusing "mass" percentages: \~75–80 % of mass in the troposphere, \~50 % below 18 000 ft.
  • Icing, turbulence, convection and precipitation are tropospheric hazards.

los.lo: Describe the main characteristics of the tropopause.
los.title: Main characteristics of the tropopause
los.html:
Theory & physics

Boundary where the lapse rate becomes ≤ 2 °C/km and stays so for at least 2 km above. It acts as a lid on convection because the stratosphere above is very stable. It is not continuous: it shows breaks (steps) at the polar front and subtropical boundaries, where jet streams lie. Its height and temperature are plotted on SWC charts (FL in boxes, "H"/"L" for highs/lows of the tropopause).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cb tops flatten into anvils at the tropopause; overshooting tops mean very strong updrafts.
  • Maximum wind and CAT concentrate near tropopause breaks; max wind usually just below the tropopause.
  • Reading SWC: tropopause FL box values are FL (e.g. 340 = FL 340).

los.lo: Describe the proportions of the most important gases in the air in the troposphere.
los.title: Proportions of the main gases in the troposphere
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dry air by volume: N₂ 78 %, O₂ 21 %, Ar 0.93 %, CO₂ \~0.04 %, traces. Water vapour 0–4 % by volume, highly variable (max in warm tropical air). The dry-air proportions stay constant up to \~80 km (homosphere).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "oxygen percentage decreases with height". The percentage is constant; the partial pressure falls → hypoxia.
  • Water vapour, though small, carries latent heat that powers Cb and TRS and is the source of all icing.

los.lo: Describe the variations of the FL and temperature of the tropopause from the poles to the equator.
los.title: Tropopause height and temperature from pole to equator
los.html:
Theory & physics

Height rises from ≈ FL 250–300 at the poles to ≈ FL 550 at the equator. Because the troposphere is deeper and cools further, the equatorial tropopause is colder (≈ −75 to −80 °C) than the polar one (≈ −45 to −55 °C). Rule: high tropopause = cold tropopause.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Classic question: "where is the tropopause coldest?" → over the equator. Not the poles.
  • Lowest SAT on long-haul flights is found at high FL in the tropics (fuel-freezing considerations).
  • Tropical Cb tops reach FL 500+, so you cannot overfly them as in mid-latitudes.

los.lo: Describe the breaks in the tropopause along the boundaries of the main air masses.
los.title: Breaks in the tropopause along air-mass boundaries
los.html:
Theory & physics

The tropopause descends in steps at the boundaries of the main air masses: at the subtropical boundary (\~30°) and at the polar front (\~40–60°). Strong horizontal temperature gradients there create, through the thermal wind, the subtropical jet and polar front jet, located in the breaks just below the higher (warm-side) tropopause.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Crossing a break: sudden temperature change at cruise, strong vertical wind shear, probable CAT.
  • See the jet cross-section under 050.02.07.03.02.

los.lo: Indicate the variations of the FL of the tropopause with the seasons and the variations of atmospheric pressure.
los.title: Tropopause height with season and pressure
los.html:
Theory & physics

Warm air columns are deeper, so the tropopause is higher in summer and over warm highs; lower in winter and over cold lows (cold upper troughs). Over a deep cold low the tropopause can drop to \~FL 250 or below.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "tropopause higher over a low". It is lower over cold lows.
  • At a constant cruise FL over a cold low you may be in the stratosphere (warmer, drier, possibly ozone).

los.lo: Describe the stratosphere up to FL 650.
los.title: The stratosphere up to FL 650
los.html:
Theory & physics

From the tropopause upward. ISA: isothermal −56.5 °C from 11 km (36 090 ft) to 20 km (65 617 ft), then +1 °C/km to 32 km. Real values vary, often warmer in the polar winter stratosphere breakdowns. Very low humidity, very stable, mainly horizontal flow; winds generally decrease above the jet core.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "ISA temperature at FL 450 is −75 °C" (extrapolating the troposphere lapse rate). Correct: −56.5 °C.
  • Smooth, cloud-free flight; watch Mach/buffet margins (coffin corner) due to low density.

los.lo: Describe that ozone can occur at jet cruise altitudes and that it constitutes a hazard.
los.title: Ozone at jet cruise altitudes is a hazard
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ozone (O₃) concentration increases above the tropopause, peaking \~20–25 km. At cruise FLs it is highest when the tropopause is low: high latitudes, winter/spring, and behind cold lows where stratospheric air descends (tropopause folds).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Effects: irritation of eyes, nose, throat, chest pain, coughing, headache, fatigue.
  • Mitigation: catalytic ozone converters, flight planning to avoid high FL in high-latitude spring, descending.
  • Trap: ozone is not a hazard "at the surface only"; the syllabus point is cruise altitude exposure.

los.lo: Define ‘air temperature’.
los.title: Define air temperature
los.html:
Theory & physics

Air temperature is a measure of the mean kinetic energy of the air molecules. Surface temperature is measured in the shade, in a ventilated Stevenson screen (or equivalent) at 1.25–2 m above short grass, so that direct radiation and ground heating do not falsify it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "measured at 10 m" (that is the wind) or "on the runway surface".
  • METAR temperature is screen temperature, not runway-surface temperature: a runway can be icy with a positive METAR temperature after a clear night.
  • OAT/SAT drives density altitude, TAS, icing risk and engine thrust.

los.lo: List the units of measurement of air temperature used in aviation meteorology (Celsius, Fahrenheit, Kelvin). (Refer to Subject 050 10 01 01)
los.title: Units: Celsius, Fahrenheit, Kelvin
los.html:
Theory & physics

°F = 9/5 × °C + 32; °C = 5/9 × (°F − 32); K = °C + 273.15. A temperature difference of 1 °C = 1 K = 1.8 °F.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • −40 °C = −40 °F (common check question).
  • ISA MSL 15 °C = 288.15 K = 59 °F.
  • METAR/TAF in °C (M = minus, e.g. M05); US products may use °F.

los.lo: Describe the mean vertical distribution of temperature up to FL 650.
los.title: Mean vertical distribution of temperature up to FL 650
los.html:
Theory & physics

ISA: +15 °C at MSL, decreasing 0.65 °C/100 m (1.98 °C/1000 ft) to −56.5 °C at 11 km (36 090 ft), then constant to 20 km (≈ FL 650), then increasing. Real atmosphere: same shape on average, but with inversions, isothermal layers and a tropopause height varying with latitude and season.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • See the ISA diagram under 050.01.05.01.02.
  • Trap: assuming the lapse rate continues above the tropopause.

los.lo: Mention the general causes of the cooling of the air in the troposphere with increasing altitude.
los.title: Why the troposphere cools with increasing altitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

The atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming solar radiation, so the ground is heated first and heats the air from below (conduction, convection, turbulence, latent heat, long-wave radiation). Additionally, rising air expands and cools adiabatically because pressure falls with height. Distance from the heat source plus adiabatic expansion gives the negative lapse rate.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "because air is further from the sun" or "because air absorbs sunlight directly".
  • This is why the freezing level, cloud bases and icing layers exist.

los.lo: Calculate the temperature and temperature deviations (in relation to International Standard Atmosphere (ISA)) at specified levels.
los.title: Calculate temperature and ISA deviation at specified levels
los.html:
Theory & physics

ISA temperature below the tropopause: T(ISA) = 15 − 2 × (altitude in thousands of ft) (exact 1.98). Above 36 090 ft: −56.5 °C. ISA deviation = actual temperature − ISA temperature at that pressure level (FL).

Worked: FL 180, OAT −31 °C → ISA = 15 − 36 = −21 °C → ISA −10. FL 390, OAT −50 °C → ISA −56.5 → ISA +6.5.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use the FL (pressure altitude), not the true altitude, for ISA temperature.
  • Sign trap: actual colder than ISA = negative deviation.
  • Chart questions (upper wind/temperature charts) ask for mean ISA deviation along a route: average the spot values first, then subtract ISA.

los.lo: Explain how local cooling or warming processes result in transfer of heat.
los.title: Local cooling or warming leads to heat transfer
los.html:
Theory & physics

Heat flows from warmer to colder bodies. In the atmosphere this happens by radiation, conduction, convection, advection, turbulence and latent heat. Differential heating (land/sea, day/night, slopes) sets up the local transfers that create thermals, breezes and fog.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Match the process to the phenomenon: radiation → radiation fog; advection → advection fog; convection → Cu/Cb; turbulence → mixing that prevents fog.

los.lo: Describe radiation.
los.title: Radiation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Energy transfer by electromagnetic waves; needs no medium. Every body emits according to its temperature (Stefan–Boltzmann: E ∝ T⁴). Wien's law: the hotter the body, the shorter the wavelength of peak emission. Sun (≈ 6000 K) = short-wave; Earth (≈ 288 K) = long-wave (infrared).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "radiation heats the air directly". Short-wave radiation mostly passes through the air and heats the ground.
  • Clear nights maximise radiative cooling: radiation fog, frost, ground inversion.

los.lo: Describe solar radiation reaching the Earth.
los.title: Solar radiation reaching the Earth
los.html:
Theory & physics

Short-wave (visible, UV, near-IR). Of the incoming energy, roughly 30 % is reflected back to space (albedo: clouds, snow, ice), ≈ 20 % is absorbed in the atmosphere (ozone, water vapour, clouds), ≈ 50 % is absorbed by the surface. Intensity depends on sun elevation (latitude, season, time of day).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • High albedo of fresh snow (≈ 80–90 %) keeps snow-covered ground cold by day.
  • Daytime surface heating drives thermals, afternoon Cu/Cb maximum over land.

los.lo: Describe the filtering effect of the atmosphere on solar radiation.
los.title: Filtering effect of the atmosphere on solar radiation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ozone absorbs UV (warming the stratosphere). Water vapour and CO₂ absorb parts of the near-IR. Clouds, dust and aerosols reflect and scatter (blue sky = Rayleigh scattering). The atmosphere is nearly transparent in the visible band, the "atmospheric window" for sunlight.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Overcast skies reduce daytime heating: weaker convection, smaller diurnal range.
  • Higher UV exposure at altitude (less ozone and air above).

los.lo: Describe terrestrial radiation.
los.title: Terrestrial radiation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Long-wave infrared emitted by the Earth's surface day and night, proportional to T⁴. At night it is not compensated by solar input, so the surface cools. Cooling is strongest with clear skies, dry air, light wind and long nights.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "the Earth only radiates at night". It radiates continuously; at night the balance becomes negative.
  • Minimum temperature occurs around sunrise; fog often thickest just after sunrise.

los.lo: Explain how terrestrial radiation is absorbed by some components of the atmosphere.
los.title: Absorption of terrestrial radiation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Water vapour, CO₂, methane, ozone and especially clouds absorb long-wave radiation and re-emit part of it back down (counter-radiation): the greenhouse effect. An "atmospheric window" around 8–12 µm lets some IR escape in clear dry air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Humid or cloudy nights stay warmer; dry desert nights cool sharply (large diurnal range).
  • Question: "which constituent is most effective in absorbing terrestrial radiation?" → water vapour (and cloud).

los.lo: Explain the effect of absorption and radiation in connection with clouds.
los.title: Absorption and radiation with clouds
los.html:
Theory & physics

By day, cloud tops reflect much of the solar radiation (high albedo), reducing surface heating. By night, cloud bases absorb terrestrial radiation and re-radiate it downward, reducing surface cooling. Cloud tops themselves cool by radiation at night, which can destabilise the cloud layer.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Overcast: lower maximum, higher minimum, small diurnal range.
  • Overcast nights rarely produce radiation fog; clearing skies in the evening raise fog risk.
  • Night-time top cooling explains nocturnal maximum of oceanic thunderstorms.

los.lo: Explain the process of conduction.
los.title: Conduction
los.html:
Theory & physics

Heat transfer by molecular contact without bulk movement. Air is a very poor conductor, so conduction only affects the lowest centimetres to metres of air in contact with the surface.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "conduction heats the troposphere". Conduction starts the process; convection and turbulence spread it.

los.lo: Explain the role of conduction in the cooling and warming of the atmosphere.
los.title: Role of conduction in cooling and warming the atmosphere
los.html:
Theory & physics

The ground warms/cools the thin layer of air in contact; that layer's heat is then distributed upward by turbulence (wind) or convection (unstable air). With calm conditions the effect stays in a shallow layer, creating strong surface inversions at night.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Calm + clear night = shallow, intense cooling = shallow radiation fog, ground frost.
  • Wind of 5–10 kt mixes the cooling through a deeper layer: fog thicker or lifted as low St; stronger wind prevents fog.

los.lo: Explain the process of convection.
los.title: Convection
los.html:
Theory & physics

Vertical transport of heat by bulk motion: air heated from below becomes less dense (warmer than its environment) and rises as thermals; colder air sinks to replace it. Convection is efficient only when the air is unstable.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Convection = Cu, TCU, Cb, showers, thermal turbulence below cloud base, good visibility (pollutants mixed out).
  • "Convection" in meteorology = vertical; "advection" = horizontal (classic definition question).

los.lo: Name the situations in which convection occurs.
los.title: Situations in which convection occurs
los.html:
Theory & physics

Strong surface heating of land by day (summer afternoons); cold air moving over a warmer surface (polar air over warm sea, especially winter and at night); lifting of conditionally unstable air at fronts, convergence lines or mountains (forced convection); cooling of cloud tops at night.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Over land: convective maximum in the afternoon. Over sea: maximum at night/early morning.
  • Winter showers on west/north coasts come from polar air crossing warm sea.

los.lo: Explain the process of advection.
los.title: Advection
los.html:
Theory & physics

Horizontal transport of air properties (heat, moisture) by the wind. Warm advection raises temperature at a place; cold advection lowers it. In the vertical, warm advection makes the wind veer with height (NH) and cold advection makes it back.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Warm moist air advected over cold ground or sea → advection fog (can form in wind, any time of day).
  • Cold advection over warm ground → instability, showers.

los.lo: Name the situations in which advection occurs.
los.title: Situations in which advection occurs
los.html:
Theory & physics

Whenever air masses move: frontal systems, air flowing between land and sea (sea breeze, onshore winds), large-scale flow between source regions (e.g. mT air reaching Europe in winter).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Coastal airports: an onshore wind shift can advect sea fog within minutes.
  • Winter warm-sector mT air over cold continent: widespread advection fog and low St.

los.lo: Describe the transfer of heat by turbulence.
los.title: Heat transfer by turbulence
los.html:
Theory & physics

Mechanical turbulence (wind over rough terrain, wind shear) creates eddies that mix air vertically through the friction layer (≈ 1000–3000 ft). It transports heat, moisture and momentum: it lifts surface cooling to higher levels and brings stronger wind down.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Turbulent mixing in moist air can produce a turbulence inversion at the top of the mixed layer with St/Sc beneath.
  • Wind > ≈ 10–15 kt at night usually prevents radiation fog (forms low St instead).

los.lo: Describe the transfer of latent heat.
los.title: Transfer of latent heat
los.html:
Theory & physics

Evaporation absorbs heat (≈ 2500 J/g) from the surroundings; condensation releases the same amount into the air. Water vapour carries this energy from the warm surface (oceans) to where it condenses aloft. Freezing releases ≈ 334 J/g; sublimation/deposition ≈ 2834 J/g.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Latent heat release is the fuel of Cb and tropical revolving storms and the reason SALR < DALR.
  • Evaporation of rain into dry air cools it → dense air → downbursts, virga-related microbursts.

los.lo: Describe qualitatively and quantitatively the temperature lapse rates of the troposphere (mean value 0.65 degrees C/100 m or 2 degrees C/1 000 ft and actual values).
los.title: Tropospheric lapse rates (qualitative and quantitative)
los.html:
Theory & physics

ELR (environmental lapse rate) = actual temperature decrease with height measured by a sounding. Mean value 0.65 °C/100 m = 1.98 ≈ 2 °C/1000 ft. Actual values vary: steeper (up to > 1 °C/100 m) near a heated surface; zero (isothermal) or negative (inversion) in stable layers. Do not confuse with adiabatic rates: DALR 1 °C/100 m (3 °C/1000 ft), SALR ≈ 0.6 °C/100 m (1.8 °C/1000 ft) at low levels.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Freezing level estimate: surface temperature ÷ 2 × 1000 ft (e.g. +12 °C → FZL ≈ 6000 ft AGL).
  • Trap: confusing ELR (property of the environment) with DALR/SALR (properties of a moving parcel).

topics.title: Development of inversions, types of inversions

los.lo: Describe the development and types of inversions.
los.title: Development and types of inversions
los.html:
Theory & physics

Inversion = temperature increasing with height; isothermal layer = constant temperature. They form by cooling from below (radiation, advection), warming from above (subsidence), or by air masses overlapping (frontal). Types: ground/radiation inversion, advection inversion, subsidence inversion, frontal inversion, turbulence (friction-layer) inversion, valley inversion, tropopause.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Inversions trap haze, smoke and fog → poor visibility below.
  • Wind shear and turbulence at the inversion top on climb or approach.

los.lo: Explain the characteristics of inversions and of an isothermal layer concerning stability and vertical motions.
los.title: Stability of inversions and isothermal layers
los.html:
Theory & physics

Both are absolutely stable: a lifted parcel cools at DALR/SALR while the environment stays warm or gets warmer, so the parcel is always colder and denser and sinks back. Vertical motion is suppressed; convection stops at the inversion base.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stable layer = stratiform cloud, flat cloud tops, smooth air above, haze and poor visibility below.
  • Trap: "an isothermal layer is neutral". It is stable (ELR 0 < SALR).

los.lo: Explain the reasons for the formation of the following inversions: ground inversion (nocturnal radiation/advection), subsidence inversion, frontal inversion, inversion above friction layer, valley inversion.
los.title: Formation of specific inversions
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Ground (nocturnal radiation): the surface cools on clear calm nights, chilling the air above. Shallow, breaks with morning heating.
  • Ground (advection): warm air flowing over a cold surface is cooled from below.
  • Subsidence: air sinking in a high warms adiabatically (DALR) and ends warmer than the air below; typically 3000–6000 ft; persistent.
  • Frontal: warm air overlying the cold wedge of a front; slopes with the frontal surface.
  • Above the friction layer (turbulence): mixing creates a DALR layer below; its top is colder than the undisturbed air above.
  • Valley: cold air drains into valleys at night (katabatic) and pools beneath warmer air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Subsidence inversion caps Sc and haze in anticyclones ("anticyclonic gloom").
  • Frontal inversion with rain falling from warm air into sub-zero air below → FZRA.
  • Valley inversion: fog/pollution in the valley, wind shear at the top.

topics.title: Temperature near the Earth’s surface, insolation, surface effects, effect of clouds, effect of wind

los.lo: Explain the cooling/warming of the surface of the Earth by radiation.
los.title: Cooling and warming of the Earth's surface by radiation
los.html:
Theory & physics

The surface temperature follows the radiation balance: positive by day (absorbed solar > emitted IR), negative by night. Land has low heat capacity and poor conduction into depth, so it heats and cools fast; water has high heat capacity, mixes and evaporates, so sea temperature changes very little (≈ < 1 °C/day).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Maximum air temperature ≈ 1–2 h after local noon (balance stays positive after noon); minimum around sunrise.
  • Land–sea contrast drives sea and land breezes and monsoons.

los.lo: Explain the cooling/warming of the air by molecular or turbulent heat transfer to/from the earth or sea surfaces.
los.title: Air cooled or warmed by molecular or turbulent heat transfer
los.html:
Theory & physics

The air in contact with the surface gains/loses heat by conduction; turbulence then spreads it through the friction layer. Over the sea, air temperature follows sea temperature closely, so the diurnal variation of air temperature over the sea is small.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Diurnal temperature range: largest over dry inland deserts, smallest over oceans.
  • Afternoon mixing brings stronger winds down: gusty surface wind by day, calm nights.

los.lo: Describe qualitatively the influence of the clouds on the cooling and warming of the surface and the air near the surface.
los.title: Influence of clouds on surface cooling and warming
los.html:
Theory & physics

Clouds reflect solar radiation by day (lower maximum) and return long-wave radiation at night (higher minimum). Low, thick, water clouds have the strongest effect; thin high Ci the weakest.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Question pattern: "overcast sky reduces the diurnal variation of temperature" = correct.
  • Fog forecasting: evening clearing + moist air + light wind = high fog risk.

los.lo: Explain the influence of the wind on the cooling and warming of the air near the surfaces.
los.title: Influence of wind on cooling and warming near the surface
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wind generates turbulence that spreads surface heating/cooling through a deeper layer, so the near-surface air changes temperature less. Calm air allows extreme surface temperatures and strong inversions.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Calm + clear night: lowest minima, ground frost, shallow fog.
  • Moderate wind: warmer nights, fog replaced by low St.
  • Strong daytime wind reduces maximum temperature by mixing.

los.lo: Define ‘atmospheric pressure’.
los.title: Define atmospheric pressure
los.html:
Theory & physics

Atmospheric pressure = force per unit area exerted by the weight of the air column above a point (P = F/A). Static pressure acts equally in all directions. ISA MSL value 1013.25 hPa = 29.92 inHg = 760 mmHg.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Pressure always decreases with height (there is less air above); it never "inverts" like temperature.
  • Basis of altimetry, ASI and VSI (pitot-static system).

los.lo: List the units of measurement of the atmospheric pressure used in aviation (hPa, inches of mercury). (Refer to Subject 050 10 01 01)
los.title: Units: hPa and inches of mercury
los.html:
Theory & physics

1 hPa = 1 mbar = 100 Pa. 1013.25 hPa = 29.92 inHg; 1 inHg ≈ 33.86 hPa; 1 hPa ≈ 0.0295 inHg.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Europe: hPa. USA/Canada: inHg. Mis-setting 29.92 as "992" hPa gives a ≈ 640 ft error (21 hPa × 30 ft): read ATIS units carefully.

los.lo: Describe the principle of the barometers (mercury barometer, aneroid barometer).
los.title: Principle of mercury and aneroid barometers
los.html:
Theory & physics

Mercury barometer: air pressure on an open reservoir supports a mercury column in an evacuated tube; column height (≈ 760 mm at 1013 hPa) measures pressure. Needs corrections for temperature, gravity and height. Aneroid barometer: a partly evacuated, sealed metal capsule expands or contracts with pressure changes, moving a pointer via linkage. The aircraft altimeter is an aneroid barometer calibrated in feet using ISA.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Barograph = recording aneroid (shows pressure tendency).
  • Because the altimeter is calibrated to ISA, non-standard temperature causes the errors in 050.01.06.

los.lo: Define isobars and identify them on surface weather charts.
los.title: Isobars on surface weather charts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Isobars join points of equal QFF (pressure reduced to MSL). Usually drawn every 4 hPa (or 5 hPa, sometimes 2 hPa) on surface analyses and forecasts. Spacing shows the pressure gradient: close isobars = strong gradient = strong wind.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: isobars use QNH. They use QFF.
  • Chart questions: derive wind direction (parallel, low on the left in NH, then friction correction) and relative strength from spacing and latitude.

los.lo: Define ‘high’, ‘low’, ‘trough’, ‘ridge’, ‘col’.
los.title: High, low, trough, ridge, col
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • High (anticyclone): closed isobars, highest pressure at centre; NH circulation clockwise; divergence and subsidence.
  • Low (depression, cyclone): closed isobars, lowest pressure at centre; NH anticlockwise; convergence and ascent.
  • Trough: elongated extension of low pressure; V-shaped isobars; convergence, often showers/fronts.
  • Ridge: elongated extension of high pressure; U-shaped isobars; fair weather.
  • Col: saddle between two highs and two lows; slack gradient, light variable winds.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Col weather: fog in autumn/winter, thunderstorms in summer (light winds, moist unstable air).
  • Wind veers at trough passage (NH).

los.lo: Explain the pressure variation with height.
los.title: Pressure variation with height
los.html:
Theory & physics

Hydrostatic equation: dP = −ρ g dh. Pressure decreases roughly exponentially with height. Because density falls with height, each hPa represents more height aloft. In cold (dense) air pressure falls faster with height; in warm air more slowly. Thickness between two pressure levels ∝ mean temperature of the layer.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Same pressure level is lower in cold air: root cause of "cold = lower than indicated".
  • Isohypses (contours) on upper charts show the height of a pressure surface: low heights = cold air/low pressure aloft.

los.lo: Describe quantitatively the variation of the barometric lapse rate. Remark: An approximation of the average value for the barometric lapse rate near mean sea level (MSL) is 30 ft (9 m) per 1 hPa.
los.title: Barometric lapse rate
los.html:
Theory & physics

Height change per hPa. Exam value near MSL: 27–30 ft (≈ 8–9 m) per hPa. It increases with height (≈ 50 ft/hPa at 18 000 ft, ≈ 70 ft/hPa at FL 300, ≈ 100+ ft/hPa at FL 400) and with temperature (warmer air: more ft per hPa).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • QNH/QFE conversion: QNH = QFE + elevation/30 (elevation in ft, hPa answer).
  • Trap: using 30 ft/hPa at high altitude (only valid near MSL).

los.lo: State that (under conditions of ISA) pressure is approximately 50 per cent of MSL at 18 000 ft and density is approximately 50 per cent of MSL at 22 000 ft and 25 per cent of MSL at 40 000 ft.
los.title: ISA: 50 % pressure at 18 000 ft, 50 % density at 22 000 ft, 25 % density at 40 000 ft
los.html:
Theory & physics

ISA: P ≈ 500 hPa at 18 000 ft (FL 180). Density falls more slowly than pressure because temperature also falls (ρ = P/RT), so half density is reached higher, at ≈ 22 000 ft; one quarter at ≈ 40 000 ft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Distractors swap the pressure and density figures; memorise 18 / 22 / 40.
  • Lower density: TAS > IAS (TAS ≈ IAS × 1/√σ), reduced thrust/power, hypoxia risk.

los.lo: Define ‘QFF’.
los.title: Define QFF
los.html:
Theory & physics

QFF = station pressure (QFE) reduced to MSL using the actual temperature (and humidity) at the station, assumed to exist in the fictitious air column between station and MSL. Used for synoptic charts.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • QFF ≠ QNH: QNH is reduced using ISA conditions; QFF uses actual temperature.

los.lo: Explain the reduction of measured pressure (QFE) to QFF (MSL).
los.title: Reduction of QFE to QFF
los.html:
Theory & physics

Add the weight of an imaginary column of air from station level down to MSL, calculated with the actual station temperature. Cold column is denser and heavier → larger correction.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Station above MSL, air colder than ISA: QFF > QNH. Air warmer than ISA: QFF < QNH. ISA: QFF = QNH.
  • Station at MSL: QFE = QNH = QFF.
  • Classic question: "Aerodrome at 1000 ft, temperature ISA −15, QNH 1010; QFF is…" → greater than 1010.

los.lo: Mention the use of QFF for surface weather charts.
los.title: Use of QFF for surface charts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Reducing every station to MSL removes the elevation effect so that pressure patterns between stations at different heights can be compared and isobars drawn.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Surface analyses = QFF isobars. Pilots set QNH, not QFF, on altimeters.

topics.title: Relationship between surface pressure centres and pressure centres aloft

los.lo: Illustrate with a vertical cross section of isobaric surfaces the relationship between surface pressure systems and upper-air pressure systems.
los.title: Surface pressure systems vs upper-air systems (cross-section)
los.html:
Theory & physics

The vertical structure depends on the temperature of the column (hypsometric equation: thickness ∝ mean temperature).

  • Cold low (cold-core, e.g. mature depression, upper trough): isobaric surfaces sag more and more with height → low intensifies aloft.
  • Warm high (warm-core, subtropical/blocking): surfaces bulge more with height → high intensifies aloft.
  • Warm (thermal) low: low at the surface but the warm column lifts the upper surfaces → weakens and becomes a high aloft. Shallow.
  • Cold high (cold continental winter high, e.g. Siberia): high at the surface, low aloft. Shallow.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Question: "which pressure systems extend to great heights?" → cold lows and warm highs.
  • Thermal lows (Iberia in summer) and the Siberian high are shallow and do not appear on 300 hPa charts.
  • Upper systems steer surface systems; always check upper-air charts as well as the surface chart.

topics.title: Relationship between pressure, temperature and density

los.lo: Describe the relationship between pressure, temperature and density.
los.title: Relationship between pressure, temperature and density
los.html:
Theory & physics

Equation of state (ideal gas): P = ρ R T (R = 287 J/kg·K for dry air, T in kelvin). At constant pressure, density is inversely proportional to absolute temperature; at constant temperature, density is proportional to pressure. Humidity lowers density (H₂O lighter than N₂/O₂).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Lowest density: high, hot, humid and low pressure → high density altitude → longer take-off run, reduced climb gradient and engine output.
  • Trap: forgetting to use kelvin in ratio calculations.

los.lo: Describe the vertical variation of the air density in the atmosphere.
los.title: Vertical variation of air density
los.html:
Theory & physics

Density decreases with height, but more slowly than pressure because the temperature fall partly compensates. ISA: ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ at MSL; ≈ 50 % at 22 000 ft; ≈ 25 % at 40 000 ft. Above the tropopause (isothermal) density falls at the same rate as pressure.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Explains TAS increase with altitude for constant IAS, lower engine thrust, narrowing buffet margins at high FL.
  • Warm air at the same pressure altitude = lower density = higher density altitude.

los.lo: Explain the use of standardised values for the atmosphere.
los.title: Use of standardised values for the atmosphere
los.html:
Theory & physics

The ICAO Standard Atmosphere (ISA) is a hypothetical, dry, still atmosphere with fixed MSL values and lapse rates. It gives a common reference for calibrating pressure instruments (altimeter, ASI, VSI), for defining pressure altitude and flight levels, and for presenting aircraft performance data that are then corrected for actual ("ISA ±") conditions.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "ISA is the average atmosphere at any given place". It is a model, roughly a mid-latitude annual mean.
  • All performance charts (AFM) are entered with pressure altitude and ISA deviation or OAT.

los.lo: List the main values of the ISA MSL pressure, MSL temperature, the vertical temperature lapse rate up to FL 650, height and temperature of the tropopause.
los.title: Main ISA values
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • MSL: 1013.25 hPa, +15 °C (288.15 K), density 1.225 kg/m³.
  • Lapse rate 0.65 °C/100 m (1.98 °C/1000 ft) from MSL to 11 km.
  • Tropopause 11 km = 36 090 ft, −56.5 °C.
  • Isothermal −56.5 °C from 11 to 20 km (≈ 65 600 ft); then +1 °C/km to 32 km.
  • Pressure levels: 850 hPa ≈ 4 780 ft, 700 hPa ≈ 9 880 ft, 500 hPa ≈ 18 280 ft, 300 hPa ≈ 30 070 ft, 250 hPa ≈ 34 000 ft, 200 hPa ≈ 38 660 ft.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Formula: ISA temp = 15 − 2 × (altitude in 1000 ft) below 36 090 ft; −56.5 °C above.
  • Trap: "tropopause at 11 000 ft" or "at FL 360 exactly". It is 11 km = 36 090 ft.
  • Trap: ISA lapse rate quoted as 3 °C/1000 ft (that is DALR).
  • Pressure-level heights are needed to read upper-air charts (e.g. 300 hPa chart ≈ FL 300).

los.lo: Define the following terms and explain how they are related to each other: height, altitude, pressure altitude, FL, pressure level, true altitude, true height, elevation, QNH, QFE, and standard altimeter setting.
los.title: Height, altitude, pressure altitude, FL, pressure level, true altitude, true height, elevation, QNH, QFE, standard setting
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Height: vertical distance of a level, point or object above a specified datum (AGL, or above aerodrome with QFE).
  • Altitude: vertical distance above MSL (indicated on QNH).
  • Elevation: vertical distance of a point on the Earth's surface above MSL.
  • Pressure altitude: altitude in ISA corresponding to the pressure at that point = altimeter reading with 1013.25 set.
  • Flight level: surface of constant pressure related to 1013.25 hPa, separated by specific intervals; FL = pressure altitude / 100.
  • Pressure level: surface of constant pressure (e.g. 500 hPa).
  • True altitude / true height: actual geometric distance above MSL / ground.
  • QNH: setting that makes the altimeter read aerodrome elevation on the ground (QFE reduced to MSL using ISA). QFE: pressure at aerodrome (threshold) level; altimeter reads zero on the ground. Standard setting: 1013.25 hPa.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • QNH ≠ QFF (QFF uses actual temperature).
  • Indicated altitude on QNH equals true altitude only in ISA conditions (and on the ground at the aerodrome).
  • Trap: "FL is a height above MSL". FL is a pressure surface; its true height varies with pressure and temperature.

los.lo: Describe the terms ‘transition altitude’, ‘transition level’, ‘transition layer’, ‘terrain clearance’, ‘lowest usable flight level’.
los.title: Transition altitude, transition level, transition layer, terrain clearance, lowest usable FL
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Transition altitude (TA): altitude at or below which vertical position is expressed as altitude (QNH).
  • Transition level (TL): lowest FL available for use above the TA. Varies with QNH (and temperature): low QNH → higher TL.
  • Transition layer: airspace between TA and TL (no level flight).
  • Terrain clearance: true vertical distance between aircraft and terrain.
  • Lowest usable FL: lowest FL that still provides the required terrain clearance in the actual pressure and temperature.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Climbing: switch QNH → 1013 passing the TA. Descending: switch 1013 → QNH passing the TL (once cleared to an altitude).
  • Altitude reports in the transition layer: as FL when climbing, as altitude when descending.
  • Low pressure and cold air raise the lowest usable FL.

los.lo: Name the altimeter settings associated to height, altitude, pressure altitude and FL.
los.title: Settings associated with height, altitude, pressure altitude and FL
los.html:
Theory & physics

QFE → height (above aerodrome/threshold). QNH → altitude. 1013.25 → pressure altitude → FL. (Regional QNH/lowest forecast QNH → safe altitude en route in some states.)

Exam traps & operational impact

  • DA/MDA are published on QNH; DH/MDH relate to QFE/radio altimeter.
  • Matching question format: always map the setting to its reference datum.

los.lo: Describe the altimeter-setting procedures.
los.title: Altimeter-setting procedures
los.html:
Theory & physics

Below TA: QNH of the nearest aerodrome (or regional QNH). At or above TL: standard 1013.25. During approach: QNH (or QFE where used) once cleared to descend to an altitude below the TL. Before take-off: check altimeter against known elevation (QNH).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • An error of 1 hPa ≈ 30 ft. Setting a QNH that is too high makes the altimeter over-read → aircraft lower than indicated → CFIT risk.
  • Mnemonic: subscale up = reading up.

los.lo: Calculate the different readings on the altimeter when the pilot uses different settings (QNH, 1013.25, QFE).
los.title: Altimeter readings with different settings
los.html:
Theory & physics

The reading changes by ≈ 30 ft per hPa difference in setting (near MSL). Increasing the subscale by x hPa increases the reading by ≈ 30x ft.

Worked: aircraft at 3000 ft on QNH 1003. With 1013 set: 3000 + (1013 − 1003) × 30 = 3300 ft (FL 033). Aerodrome elevation 600 ft, QFE = 1003 − 600/30 = 983 hPa; on QFE the altimeter reads 3000 − 600 = 2400 ft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Sign errors are the most common mistake: low QNH → pressure altitude is higher than altitude.
  • QFE < QNH for any aerodrome above MSL.

los.lo: Illustrate with a numbered example the changes of altimeter setting and the associated changes in reading when the pilot climbs through the transition altitude or descends through the transition level.
los.title: Setting changes through TA and TL (numbered example)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Worked: TA 5000 ft, QNH 993 hPa. Climbing through 5000 ft on QNH, set 1013: reading jumps to 5000 + 20 × 30 = 5600 ft (FL 056); the aircraft has not moved. Descending: TL e.g. FL 070; at FL 070 set QNH 993, the reading drops to 7000 − 600 = 6400 ft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • With QNH < 1013 the reading increases when 1013 is set; with QNH > 1013 it decreases.
  • TL must keep a buffer above TA: low QNH → higher TL.

los.lo: Derive the reading of the altimeter of an aircraft on the ground when the pilot uses the different settings.
los.title: Altimeter reading on the ground with different settings
los.html:
Theory & physics

On the aerodrome: QFE → 0 ft; QNH → elevation; 1013.25 → pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft.

Worked: elevation 1500 ft, QNH 1023 → 1013 set reads 1500 − 300 = 1200 ft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Pre-flight check: QNH set, reading within tolerance of elevation (typically ± 60 ft or per AFM).
  • High QNH: pressure altitude lower than elevation (better performance).

los.lo: Explain the influence of the air temperature on the distance between the ground and the level read on the altimeter and between two FLs.
los.title: Effect of air temperature on altimeter indications and FL spacing
los.html:
Theory & physics

The altimeter assumes ISA temperature. In cold air the column is denser, pressure falls faster with height, and pressure levels are closer together and lower: true altitude < indicated, and the true vertical spacing between two FLs is less than nominal. Warm air does the opposite. Error ≈ 4 % of the height above the setting datum per 10 °C ISA deviation (exam rule).

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • "From high to low (temperature or pressure), look out below."
  • The error is measured from the pressure datum (aerodrome level on QNH ≈ elevation), not from MSL, when the question gives terrain height.
  • Cold-temperature corrections are added to minimum altitudes (DA, MDA, step-downs) in very cold weather.
  • Two aircraft 1000 ft apart by FL in cold air are actually less than 1000 ft apart.

los.lo: Explain the influence of pressure areas on true altitude.
los.title: Influence of pressure areas on true altitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

Flying at constant indicated altitude without updating QNH means following a constant pressure surface. Towards a low that surface descends, so true altitude decreases (≈ 30 ft per hPa). Towards a high, true altitude increases.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Classic: flying at FL from A (1030 hPa) to B (990 hPa) at constant FL → true altitude ≈ 1200 ft lower at B.
  • Drift to the right (NH, wind from the left) means flying towards lower pressure → lower than indicated.

los.lo: Determine the true altitude/height for a given altitude/height and a given ISA temperature deviation.
los.title: True altitude for a given ISA deviation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Correction ≈ 4 ft per 1000 ft per °C ISA deviation, applied to the height above the setting datum. True = indicated + (ISA dev × 4 × height/1000).

Worked: indicated 9000 ft on QNH at an aerodrome at 1000 ft, ISA −15 °C: height above datum ≈ 8000 ft → correction = −15 × 4 × 8 = −480 ft → true ≈ 8520 ft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use the ISA deviation of the mean column temperature where given.
  • Always check whether the question wants the correction from MSL or from station level.

los.lo: Calculate the terrain clearance and the lowest usable FL for given atmospheric temperature and pressure conditions.
los.title: Terrain clearance and lowest usable FL
los.html:
Theory & physics

Step 1, pressure: true height of FL above MSL in ISA temperature = FL × 100 − (1013 − QNH) × 30. Step 2, temperature: apply 4 %/10 °C. Step 3: subtract terrain elevation.

Worked: FL 080, QNH 998, ISA −10, terrain 5000 ft. Pressure: 8000 − 15 × 30 = 7550 ft. Temperature: − 4 % of 7550 ≈ − 300 → ≈ 7250 ft. Clearance ≈ 2250 ft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Low QNH and cold air both reduce clearance; combine them.
  • Lowest usable FL rises when QNH falls below 1013.

los.lo: State that the 4 per cent-rule can be used to calculate true altitude from indicated altitude, and also indicated altitude from true altitude (not precise but sufficient due to the approximation of the 4 per cent-rule.)
los.title: The 4 % rule
los.html:
Theory & physics

True altitude differs from indicated by ≈ 4 % for every 10 °C ISA deviation (warmer = higher, colder = lower). It can be used in both directions (true from indicated, or indicated from true); the small error introduced is acceptable for exam purposes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Same as 4 ft / 1000 ft / °C.
  • Apply it to the height above the setting datum, then add the datum elevation.

topics.title: Effect of accelerated airflow due to topography

los.lo: Describe qualitatively how the effect of accelerated airflow due to topography (the Bernoulli effect) affects altimetry.
los.title: Accelerated airflow due to topography (Bernoulli effect) and altimetry
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wind accelerated over ridges or through gaps (Venturi) has lower static pressure (Bernoulli: p + ½ρv² = constant). The altimeter senses lower pressure and over-reads: the aircraft is lower than indicated, close to the terrain causing the effect. Combined with cold air and mountain-wave downdrafts the error can reach several hundred to 1000+ ft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Strong wind across mountains: add margin to MSA; cross ridges well above.
  • Trap: "altimeter under-reads in accelerated flow". It over-reads.

los.lo: Define ‘wind’ and ‘surface wind’.
los.title: Define wind and surface wind
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wind = horizontal movement of air relative to the Earth's surface, described by the direction it blows from and its speed. Surface wind = wind measured at 10 m above ground over open, level terrain. Vertical motions are called up/downdrafts, not wind.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Direction is always "from": 270/20 = from the west.
  • Surface wind drives runway choice, crosswind/tailwind limits and take-off/landing distances.

los.lo: State the units of wind directions (degrees true in reports; degrees magnetic from tower) and speed (kt, m/s).
los.title: Units of wind direction and speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

Direction: degrees true in METAR, TAF, SIGMET, upper-wind charts and written reports; degrees magnetic in wind given by ATC/tower and ATIS (for runway use). Speed: kt (KT) or m/s (MPS); 1 m/s ≈ 2 kt; km/h on some charts.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Crosswind from a METAR: convert true to magnetic with local variation before comparing with the runway QDM.
  • Trap: assuming ATIS wind is true.

los.lo: Describe that the reported wind is an average wind derived from measurements with an anemometer at a height of 10 m over 2 min for local routine and special reports and ATS units, and over 10 min for aerodrome routine meteorological reports (METARs) and aerodrome special meteorological reports (SPECIs).
los.title: Averaging of reported wind
los.html:
Theory & physics

Anemometer and vane at 10 m. Averaging: 2 minutes for local routine/special reports and ATS units (tower wind); 10 minutes for METAR/SPECI (except where a marked discontinuity occurs, then the period after it). Gusts: maximum 3-s mean wind, reported when it exceeds the mean by ≥ 10 kt. Variable direction (VRB) when mean ≤ 3 kt or with large variation; "dddVddd" when variation ≥ 60° with mean ≥ 3 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Tower wind (2-min) is more representative for landing than the 10-min METAR wind.
  • Trap: swapping 2 min and 10 min.

topics.title: Primary cause of wind, pressure gradient, Coriolis force, gradient wind

los.lo: Define the term ‘horizontal pressure gradient’.
los.title: Horizontal pressure gradient
los.html:
Theory & physics

Rate of change of pressure with horizontal distance, measured perpendicular to the isobars from high to low (e.g. hPa per 100 km). Closely spaced isobars = strong gradient.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • On a chart, compare spacing at the same latitude: equal spacing gives stronger wind at lower latitudes.

los.lo: Explain how the pressure gradient force acts in relation to the pressure gradient.
los.title: Pressure gradient force (PGF)
los.html:
Theory & physics

PGF per unit mass = (1/ρ) × ΔP/Δn. It acts from high to low pressure, at right angles to the isobars, and is the force that starts the air moving. For the same ΔP, PGF is larger where density is lower (aloft).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "PGF acts parallel to the isobars". It is perpendicular.
  • Same isobar spacing gives stronger wind at altitude than at the surface (lower density, less friction).

los.lo: Explain how the Coriolis force acts in relation to the wind.
los.title: Coriolis force
los.html:
Theory & physics

Apparent (deflecting) force due to Earth's rotation: CF = 2 Ω V sin φ (Ω = Earth's angular velocity, V = wind speed, φ = latitude). Acts at 90° to the motion: to the right in the NH, left in the SH. Zero at the equator, maximum at the poles, proportional to wind speed; it changes direction, not speed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "Coriolis is maximum at the equator". It is zero there.
  • No wind → no Coriolis. Coriolis cannot start motion.

los.lo: Explain the development of the geostrophic wind.
los.title: Development of the geostrophic wind
los.html:
Theory & physics

Air at rest accelerates towards low pressure under PGF; as speed builds, Coriolis deflects it (right in NH) until Coriolis exactly balances PGF. Result: unaccelerated flow parallel to straight isobars. Formula: Vg = ΔP/Δn ÷ (ρ · 2Ω sin φ). Valid above the friction layer, with straight isobars, outside ≈ 15° of the equator.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Conditions for geostrophic wind: straight parallel isobars, no friction, steady flow, not near the equator.

los.lo: Indicate how the geostrophic wind flows in relation to the isobars/isohypses in the northern and in the southern hemisphere.
los.title: Geostrophic flow and isobars in NH and SH
los.html:
Theory & physics

Flow parallel to isobars (or contours on upper charts). Buys Ballot's law: in the NH, with your back to the wind, low pressure is on your left; in the SH, on your right. NH: anticlockwise round lows, clockwise round highs (SH reversed).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • In NH, a drift to the right (wind from the left) means flying towards lower pressure: altimeter over-reads.
  • Chart question: wind direction at a point = tangent to the isobar with low on the left (NH).

los.lo: Analyse the effect of changing latitude on the geostrophic wind speed.
los.title: Effect of latitude on geostrophic wind speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

The geostrophic wind is the speed at which the Coriolis force has grown just big enough to balance the pressure gradient force (PGF). Compare the two forces:

  • PGF depends only on the isobar spacing (and air density). Latitude does not change it.
  • Coriolis = 2Ω · V · sin φ. It grows with wind speed V, but each knot of wind produces less Coriolis force the closer you are to the equator, because sin φ gets smaller.

So with the same isobar spacing, the air at low latitude must blow faster before its (weaker per-knot) Coriolis force can match the same PGF. At high latitude a modest speed is already enough. Rearranged: Vg = PGF ÷ (ρ · 2Ω · sin φ), so Vg ∝ 1 / sin φ.

Latitudesin φSame spacing gives
90°1.0017 kt
60°0.8720 kt (reference)
45°0.7124 kt
30°0.5035 kt (≈ 1.7×)
15°0.2667 kt on paper

Near the equator (within about 15°) sin φ is so small that the Coriolis force can never balance the PGF at a realistic speed. The balance never forms, the air flows straight across the isobars from high to low and fills the pressure difference. That is why tropical pressure gradients are weak and why tropical charts use streamlines instead of isobars.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "same spacing = same wind at all latitudes". False: lower latitude, stronger wind.
  • Turned round: to give the same wind speed, isobars at low latitude must be further apart.
  • The geostrophic wind scale printed on a chart only works at the latitude it is drawn for; compare spacing only at similar latitudes.
  • Tropical charts use streamlines rather than isobars.

los.lo: Explain the gradient wind effect and indicate how the gradient wind differs from the geostrophic wind in cyclonic and anticyclonic circulation.
los.title: Gradient wind vs geostrophic wind
los.html:
Theory & physics

With curved isobars a net centripetal force is needed. Round a low: PGF (inward) = Coriolis (outward) + centrifugal (outward) → Coriolis smaller than PGF → gradient wind < geostrophic (sub-geostrophic). Round a high: Coriolis (inward) = PGF (outward) + centrifugal → gradient wind > geostrophic (super-geostrophic).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • For identical isobar spacing and latitude: wind round a high > straight isobars > wind round a low.
  • In practice highs have weak gradients, so winds in highs are usually lighter anyway.

topics.title: Variation of wind in the friction layer

los.lo: Describe why and how the wind changes direction and speed with height in the friction layer in the northern and in the southern hemisphere (rule of thumb).
los.title: Wind change with height in the friction layer (rule of thumb)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Surface friction reduces wind speed; Coriolis (∝ speed) weakens, so PGF dominates and the wind crosses the isobars towards low pressure. With height friction decreases: speed increases and direction veers (NH; backs in SH) until it becomes geostrophic at the top of the friction layer (≈ 2000–3000 ft).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • NH: climbing out, the wind veers and increases; descending, it backs and decreases (expect a headwind/crosswind change on final).
  • SH: reversed (backs with height).

los.lo: State the surface and air-mass conditions that influence the wind in the friction layer (diurnal variation).
los.title: Surface and air-mass conditions: diurnal variation
los.html:
Theory & physics

By day, heating creates turbulence that mixes faster, veered upper air down: surface wind stronger and veered, gusty, max in early afternoon. By night, a surface inversion decouples the surface layer: surface wind lighter and backed; the wind above the inversion may strengthen (low-level jet).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Calm night at surface + strong wind at 1000–2000 ft = low-level wind shear on approach.
  • Over the sea the diurnal variation is small.

los.lo: Name terrain, wind speed and stability as the main factors that influence the vertical extent of the friction layer.
los.title: Factors affecting the depth of the friction layer
los.html:
Theory & physics

Deeper with rough terrain, strong wind and unstable air (turbulence and convection mix momentum higher). Shallower with smooth surfaces (sea), light wind and stable air (night inversions). Typical ≈ 1000 ft (sea, stable) to 3000+ ft (rough, unstable).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Exam: "which three factors" → terrain roughness, wind speed, stability.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between isobars and wind (direction and speed). Remark: Approximate value for variation of wind in the friction layer (values to be used in examinations): Type of landscape: Wind speed in friction layer in per cent of the geostrophic wind: over water: ca. 70 per cent; over land: ca. 50 per cent; The wind in the friction layer blows across the isobars towards the low pressure. Angle between wind direction and isobars. Over water: ca. 10 degrees; over land: ca. 30 degrees. WMO - No. 266.
los.title: Isobars and wind: exam values
los.html:
Theory & physics

Surface wind relative to geostrophic: over water ≈ 70 % speed, ≈ 10° across isobars; over land ≈ 50 % speed, ≈ 30° across isobars, always towards low pressure. NH: surface wind is backed compared with the 2000 ft wind; SH: veered.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Worked: 2000 ft wind 270/40 over land (NH) → surface ≈ 240/20. Over sea → ≈ 260/28.
  • Trap: veering instead of backing for the surface (NH).
  • SH: Coriolis to the left, circulation reversed; surface wind veered from the gradient wind.

los.lo: Describe atmospheric convergence and divergence.
los.title: Convergence and divergence
los.html:
Theory & physics

Convergence = net horizontal inflow into a region (air piles up); divergence = net outflow. By continuity, low-level convergence must be balanced by rising air (and divergence aloft); low-level divergence by sinking air (and convergence aloft).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Low-level convergence (troughs, ITCZ, sea-breeze fronts) = ascent, cloud, showers.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between convergence and divergence on the following: pressure systems at the surface and aloft; wind speed; vertical motion and cloud formation (relationship between upper-air conditions and surface pressure systems).
los.title: Convergence/divergence: pressure systems, wind speed, vertical motion, cloud
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Surface low: friction-induced convergence at the surface, ascent, divergence aloft. If upper divergence > surface convergence, the low deepens.
  • Surface high: divergence at the surface, subsidence, convergence aloft. Upper convergence > surface divergence → high builds.
  • Wind speed changes along the flow (jet entrances/exits) create divergence/convergence aloft that develop surface systems.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Lows/troughs = cloud and precipitation; highs = subsidence, clear or stratiform under an inversion, haze/fog.
  • Question: "what causes a surface low to deepen?" → upper-level divergence exceeding low-level convergence.

los.lo: Describe the general global circulation. (Refer to Subject 050 08 01 01)
los.title: General global circulation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Uneven heating (surplus at the equator, deficit at the poles) drives a poleward heat transport. Earth's rotation breaks the single convection cell into three cells per hemisphere:

  • Hadley cell (0–30°): air rises at the equator (ITCZ), flows poleward aloft, sinks at ≈ 30° (subtropical highs), returns as the trade winds. Thermally direct.
  • Ferrel cell (30–60°): surface flow poleward (westerlies), rising at ≈ 60° (subpolar lows, polar front). Thermally indirect.
  • Polar cell (60–90°): sinking at the pole (polar high), surface polar easterlies, rising at 60°.

Aloft: predominantly westerly from ≈ 20° poleward, with the subtropical and polar front jets.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: the Ferrel cell is thermally indirect (rising over colder air, sinking over warmer air).
  • Surface pressure belts: equatorial low, subtropical highs (horse latitudes), subpolar lows, polar highs.

los.lo: Name and sketch or indicate on a map the global distribution of the surface pressure and the resulting wind pattern for all latitudes at low level in January and July.
los.title: Surface pressure and winds in January and July
los.html:
Theory & physics

Pattern: equatorial trough/ITCZ → NE trades (NH) / SE trades (SH) → subtropical highs (Azores, Pacific, St Helena, Mascarene, S Pacific) → westerlies → subpolar lows (Icelandic, Aleutian) → polar easterlies. January: belts shifted south; strong continental highs (Siberian, N American); Icelandic/Aleutian lows deep; NE monsoon over S Asia. July: belts shifted north; Asian (Pakistan) thermal low; SW monsoon; Azores high extends towards Europe.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Map questions: identify the Siberian high only in winter, the Asian low only in summer.
  • Long-haul planning: monsoon and ITCZ positions change seasonal weather on routes.

los.lo: Sketch or indicate on a map the westerly and easterly tropospheric winds at high level in January and July.
los.title: Upper westerlies and easterlies in January and July
los.html:
Theory & physics

Upper troposphere: westerlies from ≈ 20–30° poleward in both hemispheres, strongest in winter (bigger pole–equator temperature contrast). Easterlies aloft over the tropics, extending further in the summer hemisphere; Tropical Easterly Jet (≈ FL 450–500) over S Asia/Africa in NH summer.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Eastbound N Atlantic flights benefit from strong westerly tailwinds, especially in winter; westbound tracks avoid the jet core.
  • Trap: "upper easterlies dominate mid-latitudes in summer". Westerlies persist, just weaker.

topics.title: Anabatic and katabatic winds, mountain and valley winds, Venturi effects, land and sea breezes

los.lo: Describe and explain anabatic and katabatic winds.
los.title: Anabatic and katabatic winds
los.html:
Theory & physics

Anabatic: by day, slopes heated by the sun warm the air in contact; it becomes less dense than air at the same level over the valley and flows upslope. Weak (≈ 5–10 kt), may form Cu over ridges. Katabatic: at night, slopes cool by radiation, the air in contact becomes denser and drains downslope under gravity. Can be strong where large cold plateaux or ice sheets feed it (Greenland, Antarctica, Bora is partly katabatic).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: anabatic = downslope. Remember "ana = up".
  • Katabatic flow fills valleys with cold air: valley fog, frost, inversion, wind shear at the valley rim.

los.lo: Describe mountain and valley winds.
los.title: Mountain and valley winds
los.html:
Theory & physics

Valley-scale version of the slope winds: valley wind (day) blows up the valley towards the mountains; mountain wind (night) blows down the valley. Stronger in summer with clear skies and weak synoptic gradient.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Valley aerodromes: runway in use may change between morning and afternoon.

los.lo: Describe the Venturi effect, convergence in valleys and mountain areas.
los.title: Venturi effect and convergence in valleys and mountain areas
los.html:
Theory & physics

Air forced through a gap or narrowing valley accelerates (continuity) and its static pressure falls (Bernoulli). Examples: Mistral (Rhône valley), Tramontane, winds through straits (Gibraltar Levante).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Expect much stronger local wind and turbulence in passes than the gradient suggests; altimeter over-reads (050.01.06.04.01).

los.lo: Describe land and sea breezes, and sea-breeze front.
los.title: Land and sea breezes, sea-breeze front
los.html:
Theory & physics

Sea breeze (day): land heats faster than sea → rising air over land, thermal low at the surface, air flows onshore at low level with a return flow aloft. Typically 10–15 kt, ≈ 1000–3000 ft deep, penetrating 10–30 nm inland (more in the tropics); starts mid-morning, peaks mid-afternoon, veers during the day in NH under Coriolis. Land breeze (night): weaker (≈ 5 kt), offshore. Sea-breeze front: leading edge of the cool marine air; convergence line with Cu, possibly showers/TS, wind shear and turbulence; haze/smoke drop in visibility.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Conditions: strong heating, weak synoptic gradient (often under a high).
  • Coastal runway wind can reverse in the late morning; sea fog may be advected inland.

los.lo: Describe that local, low-level jet streams can develop in the evening.
los.title: Evening low-level jet
los.html:
Theory & physics

After sunset a surface radiation inversion decouples the air above from surface friction. Freed from friction, the wind just above the inversion accelerates and can become super-geostrophic (inertial oscillation), peaking around midnight to early morning at a few hundred to ≈ 2000 ft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Night/early-morning approaches with calm surface wind: strong shear at 300–1500 ft; be ready for airspeed fluctuations.

los.lo: Explain the origin and formation of mountain waves.
los.title: Origin and formation of mountain waves
los.html:
Theory & physics

Stable air forced up a ridge is displaced from its equilibrium level; on the lee side it sinks below that level, becomes warmer than its surroundings, rebounds, and keeps oscillating downstream. The oscillation is held in place by the wind, forming standing (lee) waves. Energy can also propagate vertically to great heights.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Needs stable air; in unstable air you get convection instead of waves.

los.lo: State the conditions necessary for the formation of mountain waves.
los.title: Conditions for mountain waves
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Wind direction within ≈ 30° of perpendicular to the ridge.
  • Wind speed at ridge top ≥ ≈ 15 kt (small ridges) to ≥ 25 kt (big ranges), increasing with height with little change of direction.
  • A stable layer near ridge-top level, with less stable air above and below.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Classic question lists these three; distractors include "unstable air at ridge level" or "wind decreasing with height".

los.lo: Describe the structure and properties of mountain waves.
los.title: Structure and properties of mountain waves
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wavelength ≈ 2–30 km (longer with stronger wind and weaker stability); amplitude can reach several thousand ft; vertical speeds up to ≈ 2000 ft/min or more. Strong downdraft on the immediate lee slope. Rotor zones form beneath the wave crests near or below ridge-top height, with severe turbulence. Waves may extend into the stratosphere. Laminar (smooth) flow in the wave above the rotor.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most severe turbulence: in the rotor, below the crests, on the lee side, roughly at ridge height.
  • Smooth flight in the wave itself can still involve large altitude deviations (± several thousand ft) when holding attitude.

los.lo: Explain how mountain waves may be identified by their associated meteorological phenomena.
los.title: Identification by associated phenomena
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Lenticular clouds (ACSL, CCSL, SCSL): smooth lens shapes, stationary, at the wave crests, sometimes stacked ("pile of plates").
  • Rotor (roll) clouds: ragged Cu/Sc lines parallel to the ridge, under the crests at low level.
  • Cap cloud / Föhn wall: cloud draped over the ridge on the windward side, with a clear Föhn gap in the lee.
  • Without moisture the waves are invisible.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Lenticulars do not move with the wind: they form and dissolve in place.
  • Absence of cloud does not mean absence of waves.

los.lo: Describe that mountain wave effects can exceed the performance or structural capability of aircraft.
los.title: Mountain wave effects can exceed aircraft capability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Downdrafts of 2000+ ft/min can exceed the climb performance of light and even heavy aircraft at high altitude; rotor turbulence can exceed structural limits; altimeter over-reading (accelerated flow, lower pressure) adds to the danger near terrain.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cross ridges with a margin of at least 50 % of the ridge height (rule of thumb in strong wind) and at a 45° angle so you can turn away.
  • Fly turbulence penetration speed; avoid the lee side at low level.

los.lo: Describe that mountain wave effects can propagate from low to high level, e.g. over Greenland and elsewhere.
los.title: Waves propagating from low to high level
los.html:
Theory & physics

With favourable wind and stability profiles, wave energy propagates up to the tropopause and into the stratosphere; waves may break at high level, producing CAT at cruise FLs. Known hot spots: Greenland, Rockies, Andes, Alps, Himalaya, Norway.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • SWC charts mark severe mountain wave (SEV MTW) areas; SIGMET for SEV MTW.
  • Mountain-wave turbulence at FL 300+ is often reported as CAT over Greenland on N Atlantic tracks.

los.lo: Describe turbulence and gustiness.
los.title: Turbulence and gustiness
los.html:
Theory & physics

Turbulence: irregular, random eddying motion of the air in all directions, causing rapid changes in aircraft attitude, altitude and airspeed (load factor variations). Gustiness: rapid fluctuations of surface wind speed and direction about the mean, caused by turbulent eddies; reported as gusts (G) when the peak exceeds the mean by ≥ 10 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Intensity terms (ICAO): light, moderate, severe; see 050.09.02.01.01.
  • Gusty surface wind: add gust factor to approach speed per SOP.

los.lo: List the common types of turbulence (convective, mechanical, orographic, frontal, clear-air turbulence).
los.title: Common types of turbulence
los.html:
Theory & physics

Convective (thermal), mechanical (friction with surface/obstacles), orographic (mountains, waves, rotors), frontal (shear and lifting at fronts), clear-air turbulence (high-level shear). Plus wake turbulence (aircraft-generated, not meteorological).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Match type to forecast product: convective → CB areas on SWC; CAT → CAT areas on SWC; orographic → MTW.

los.lo: Explain the formation of convective turbulence, mechanical and orographic turbulence, and frontal turbulence.
los.title: Formation of convective, mechanical/orographic and frontal turbulence
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Convective: uneven surface heating creates thermals and compensating downdrafts; strongest on sunny afternoons over land, in and below Cu/Cb. Above cloud tops/inversion the air is smoother.
  • Mechanical: wind over rough terrain, buildings, trees creates eddies; increases with wind speed, roughness and instability; confined to the friction layer.
  • Orographic: flow over/around mountains; lee eddies, waves, rotors.
  • Frontal: vertical shear and lifting across the frontal surface; strongest with fast-moving, active cold fronts and squall lines.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Convective turbulence below Cu bases on summer afternoons: expect a bumpy approach; smoother above cloud tops.
  • Mechanical turbulence downwind of hangars/buildings on short final.

los.lo: State where turbulence will normally be found (rough-ground surfaces, relief, inversion layers, cumulonimbus (CB), thunderstorm (TS) zones, unstable layers).
los.title: Where turbulence will normally be found
los.html:
Theory & physics

Near rough surfaces and relief (friction layer, lee of hills); at inversion layers (shear between air layers); in and near Cb/TS (up to 20 nm and above the tops); in unstable layers (convection); near jet streams and tropopause breaks (CAT).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Avoid Cb by ≥ 10 nm (20 nm for severe or at high level); never fly under the anvil.
  • Expect shear crossing a low inversion on climb/descent, especially at night.

topics.title: Clear-air turbulence (CAT) - description, cause and location

los.lo: Describe CAT.
los.title: Describe CAT
los.html:
Theory & physics

Clear-air turbulence: high-level turbulence (usually above FL 200) in cloud-free air, not associated with convection, caused by strong wind shear. Patchy: typically 50–100 nm long, 10–20 nm wide, 2000–5000 ft deep; often in bands parallel to the jet.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No visual cue and no radar return: keep seat belts fastened while seated.

los.lo: Describe the formation of CAT.
los.title: Formation of CAT
los.html:
Theory & physics

Strong vertical wind shear (and horizontal shear) in a stable layer causes Kelvin–Helmholtz instability: waves on the interface grow and break into turbulent eddies. Probability rises with shear: rule of thumb, vertical shear ≥ 5 kt/1000 ft or horizontal shear ≥ 20 kt/100 nm (typical forecaster thresholds; > 6 kt/1000 ft often severe).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Richardson number concept: turbulence when shear overcomes stability.
  • Temperature gradients drive shear (thermal wind), so strong isotherm packing on charts flags CAT.

los.lo: State where CAT is found in association with jet streams, in high-level troughs and in other disturbed high-level air flows. (Refer to Subject 050 09 02 02)
los.title: CAT locations: jets, upper troughs, disturbed flow
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Near jet streams: mainly on the cold (polar) side, just below the core, and above the core near the tropopause break.
  • In sharply curved upper troughs and ridges, and where the jet curves.
  • At jet exit and entrance regions and confluence/diffluence zones.
  • Near tropopause breaks and in breaking mountain waves.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "CAT is worst on the warm side of the jet". Usual answer: cold (low-pressure) side.
  • See the jet cross-section under 050.02.07.03.02.

los.lo: State that remote sensing of CAT from satellites is not possible and that forecasting is limited.
los.title: CAT cannot be sensed by satellite; forecasting is limited
los.html:
Theory & physics

CAT occurs in clear air with no moisture or particles: invisible to satellites and to weather radar. Forecasts use diagnostic indices (shear, deformation, Ellrod index) from NWP and are probabilistic.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Forecast CAT areas mean "possible"; turbulence may also occur outside them.

los.lo: State that pilot reports of turbulence are a very valuable source of information as remote measurements are not available.
los.title: Pilot reports are very valuable
los.html:
Theory & physics

Because CAT cannot be observed remotely, AIREPs/special air-reports (and automated EDR reports) are the only direct observations; they feed SIGMETs and help other crews.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Report MOD/SEV TURB promptly with position, FL, time and aircraft type.

los.lo: Describe jet streams.
los.title: Describe jet streams
los.html:
Theory & physics

A jet stream is a strong, narrow, quasi-horizontal current of air with its axis near the tropopause, characterised by strong vertical and lateral wind shear and one or more velocity maxima. Formed by strong horizontal temperature gradients (thermal wind): the wind increases with height through a layer with a strong temperature contrast. Mostly westerly.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Jets bring tailwind/headwind of 100–200 kt and CAT; flight planning uses them (eastbound) or avoids them (westbound).

los.lo: State the defined minimum speed of a jet stream (60 kt).
los.title: Defined minimum speed: 60 kt
los.html:
Theory & physics

WMO: a jet stream has a core speed of at least 60 kt. SWC charts plot jets of ≥ 80 kt (WAFS convention), with arrows, wind barbs and FL of the core, and the 80 kt isotach depth boundaries in some formats.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Exam distractors: 50, 80 or 100 kt. Definition: 60 kt; SWC depiction threshold: 80 kt.

los.lo: State the typical figures for the dimensions of jet streams.
los.title: Typical dimensions of jet streams
los.html:
Theory & physics

Length: thousands of nm (often 1000–3000 nm segments). Width: ≈ 100–300 nm (≈ 200–500 km). Depth: ≈ 10 000–15 000 ft (3–5 km). Core speed: typically 100–200 kt, up to 250–300 kt over Japan in winter. Typical shear: vertical 5–10 kt/1000 ft, horizontal ≈ 20–50 kt/100 nm on the cold side.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Jets are much wider than they are deep: a small FL change can leave the core faster than a lateral diversion.

topics.title: Formation and properties of jet streams

los.lo: Explain the formation and state the heights, the speeds, the seasonal variations of speeds, the geographical positions, the seasonal occurrence and the seasonal movements of the arctic (front) jet stream, the polar (front) jet stream, the subtropical jet stream, and the tropical (easterly/equatorial) jet stream.
los.title: Arctic, polar front, subtropical and tropical easterly jets
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Arctic (front) jet: ≈ FL 200–250, ≈ 60–70°; mainly winter; along the arctic front.
  • Polar front jet: ≈ FL 300–350, ≈ 40–65°; follows the polar front: further south and stronger in winter (≈ 40°, 150+ kt), further north and weaker in summer; variable position, meanders with Rossby waves.
  • Subtropical jet: ≈ FL 400 (≈ 200 hPa), ≈ 25–30° (winter) moving to ≈ 40° in summer; persistent, at the poleward edge of the Hadley cell; strongest in winter (max over Japan).
  • Tropical easterly jet: ≈ FL 450–500 (≈ 100–150 hPa), ≈ 10–20°N; NH summer only (June–September), over S India, the Arabian Sea and Africa; easterly, ≈ 50–100 kt; linked to the SW monsoon.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: the tropical jet is easterly and only in summer.
  • Subtropical jet is higher and more persistent; polar front jet more variable and associated with fronts and CAT.

topics.title: Location of jet streams and associated CAT areas

los.lo: Sketch or describe where polar front and arctic jet streams are found in the troposphere in relation to the tropopause and to fronts.
los.title: Polar front and arctic jets relative to tropopause and fronts
los.html:
Theory & physics

The polar front jet lies in the warm air, just below the higher (warm-side) tropopause, at the tropopause break, and roughly 300–600 km poleward of the surface front (above the cold air at the surface, because the frontal surface slopes poleward with height). The arctic jet lies similarly relative to the arctic front, at lower level. On satellite images the jet axis often coincides with the sharp poleward edge of the frontal cirrus shield.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact
