  • Trap: "jet core above the surface front" or "in the cold air". It is in the warm air, displaced poleward of the surface front.
  • Max wind level is below the tropopause, near FL 300–350 for the polar front jet.

los.lo: Describe and indicate the areas of worst wind shear and CAT.
los.title: Areas of worst wind shear and CAT
los.html:
Theory & physics

Worst CAT: on the cold (polar/low-pressure) side of the jet, just below the core, and in the stable layer above the core near the tropopause break; also where the jet curves sharply (upper troughs), and at jet exits. Maximum vertical shear lies above and below the core; maximum horizontal shear on the cold side.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Escape strategy in jet CAT: change FL (often descend on the cold side or climb above the core) or move laterally towards the warm side.
  • Rapid OAT change at constant FL suggests crossing the frontal zone near the jet: anticipate CAT.

los.lo: State that the density of moist air is less than the density of dry air.
los.title: Moist air is less dense than dry air
los.html:
Theory & physics

At the same pressure and temperature, a given volume contains the same number of molecules (Avogadro). Water vapour (molar mass 18) replaces N₂ (28) and O₂ (32), so the mixture is lighter. Meteorologists account for this with virtual temperature (the temperature dry air would need to have the same density).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "humid air is heavier" (intuition from "heavy" humid days).
  • Humidity slightly raises density altitude: longer take-off run in hot, humid conditions.

los.lo: Describe the significance for meteorology of water vapour in the atmosphere.
los.title: Significance of water vapour for meteorology
los.html:
Theory & physics

Water vapour is the source of all cloud, fog and precipitation; it stores and transports latent heat (energy source of Cb and TRS); it is the main greenhouse gas (absorbs long-wave radiation); its content determines the SALR and therefore stability.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • More moisture = more potential energy for convection and more supercooled water for icing.

los.lo: Indicate the sources of atmospheric humidity.
los.title: Sources of atmospheric humidity
los.html:
Theory & physics

Mainly evaporation from oceans; also lakes, rivers, wet ground, snow/ice (sublimation) and transpiration from vegetation (evapotranspiration). Evaporation increases with water temperature, wind and dryness of the air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Maritime air masses are moist; continental air masses dry.

los.lo: Define ‘saturation of air by water vapour’.
los.title: Saturation of air by water vapour
los.html:
Theory & physics

Air is saturated when it holds the maximum water vapour possible at its temperature (equilibrium: evaporation = condensation over a flat water surface); RH = 100 %. Saturation vapour pressure rises roughly exponentially with temperature (doubles every ≈ 10 °C), and is lower over ice than over water at the same sub-zero temperature.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Saturation is reached by cooling (most common) or by adding moisture.
  • Lower saturation pressure over ice drives the WBF precipitation process (050.05).

los.lo: Define ‘dew point’.
los.title: Dew point
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dew point (Td): the temperature to which air must be cooled, at constant pressure and constant water vapour content, to become saturated. It is a direct measure of the absolute moisture content: Td only changes if moisture is added or removed (or pressure changes).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • METAR group 08/06: T 8 °C, Td 6 °C → spread 2 °C → fog/low cloud risk if cooling continues.
  • Frost point: same concept relative to ice.

los.lo: Define ‘relative humidity’.
los.title: Relative humidity
los.html:
Theory & physics

RH = actual vapour pressure (or content) ÷ saturation vapour pressure at that temperature × 100 %. It describes how close air is to saturation, not how much water it contains.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "RH 100 % in the desert at night means more water than tropical air at 80 %". RH says nothing about absolute amount.

los.lo: Explain the factors that influence the relative humidity at constant pressure.
los.title: Factors influencing RH at constant pressure
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Temperature: cooling raises RH (saturation content falls); warming lowers RH.
  • Moisture content: adding water vapour (evaporation, advection of moist air) raises RH.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • With constant moisture, RH and temperature vary inversely.

los.lo: Explain the diurnal variation of the relative humidity.
los.title: Diurnal variation of RH
los.html:
Theory & physics

With roughly constant moisture content over a day, RH follows temperature inversely: maximum around sunrise (minimum temperature), minimum early afternoon (maximum temperature).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Fog/mist and low St most likely around dawn; clear as RH drops with heating.

los.lo: Describe the relationship between temperature and dew point.
los.title: Relationship between temperature and dew point
los.html:
Theory & physics

Td ≤ T always; T = Td at saturation. The spread (T − Td) shrinks as air cools or moistens. In rising unsaturated air, T falls at 1 °C/100 m and Td at ≈ 0.2 °C/100 m, so the spread closes at ≈ 0.8 °C/100 m (≈ 2.5 °C/1000 ft).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Convective cloud base ≈ (T − Td) × 400 ft (or × 125 m).
  • Converging T and Td in successive METARs → deteriorating visibility.

los.lo: Estimate the relative humidity of the air from the difference between dew point and temperature.
los.title: Estimate RH from the spread
los.html:
Theory & physics

Approximate values near 10–20 °C: spread 0 → 100 %; 1 °C → ≈ 94 %; 2 °C → ≈ 88 %; 5 °C → ≈ 70 %; 10 °C → ≈ 50 %; 20 °C → ≈ 25 %. (Roughly RH falls ≈ 5–6 % per °C of spread for small spreads.)

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Small spread (≤ 2–3 °C) + clear calm night = fog forecast.
  • Large spread = high cloud bases, possible virga/dry microbursts under high-based Cb.

topics.title: Condensation, evaporation, sublimation, freezing and melting, latent heat

los.lo: Define ‘condensation’, ‘evaporation’, ‘sublimation’, ‘freezing and melting’ and ‘latent heat’.
los.title: Condensation, evaporation, sublimation, freezing, melting, latent heat
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Condensation: vapour → liquid (releases ≈ 2500 J/g).
  • Evaporation: liquid → vapour (absorbs ≈ 2500 J/g).
  • Freezing: liquid → ice (releases ≈ 334 J/g). Melting: ice → liquid (absorbs ≈ 334 J/g).
  • Sublimation: ice → vapour (absorbs ≈ 2834 J/g); deposition (also called sublimation in many texts): vapour → ice (releases ≈ 2834 J/g).
  • Latent heat: energy absorbed or released during a change of state without a change in temperature.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • EASA texts often use "sublimation" for both directions; read the context.
  • Going "up" in energy (ice → water → vapour) absorbs heat; going "down" releases it.

los.lo: List the conditions for condensation/evaporation.
los.title: Conditions for condensation and evaporation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Condensation: air at or slightly beyond saturation (RH ≥ 100 %) and condensation nuclei. Evaporation: unsaturated air (RH < 100 %), energy supply; faster with higher temperature, wind and larger spread.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Rain falling into dry air evaporates and cools it: virga, downdrafts, microbursts.

los.lo: Explain the condensation process.
los.title: The condensation process
los.html:
Theory & physics

Air is cooled to its dew point by adiabatic expansion (lifting: convection, orographic, frontal, convergence), radiation, advection over a cold surface or mixing of air masses. Water vapour condenses on nuclei forming droplets of ≈ 10–20 µm, visible as cloud or fog.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most clouds form by adiabatic cooling of rising air; fog by surface cooling.

los.lo: Explain the nature of and the need for condensation nuclei.
los.title: Condensation nuclei
los.html:
Theory & physics

Without nuclei, pure air would need supersaturation of several hundred % for droplets to form (surface-tension barrier). Hygroscopic aerosols (sea salt, sulphates, combustion products, dust) attract water and allow condensation at RH ≈ 100 % or even below (haze/mist at 75–95 %). Abundant in the lower atmosphere.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Polluted/industrial areas: fog forms earlier, is thicker and persists longer.

los.lo: Explain the effects of condensation on the weather.
los.title: Effects of condensation on the weather
los.html:
Theory & physics

Produces cloud and fog; releases latent heat into the air, which reduces the cooling rate of rising saturated air (SALR < DALR), warms the cloud relative to its environment and fuels further ascent (instability, Cb, TRS).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Explains why the lee side of a Föhn mountain ends up warmer (050.03.03.01.08).

los.lo: List the conditions for freezing/melting.
los.title: Conditions for freezing and melting
los.html:
Theory & physics

Melting: ice above 0 °C. Freezing: liquid at or below 0 °C and a freezing (ice) nucleus or a surface to freeze on; otherwise water remains supercooled. Pure small droplets freeze spontaneously only at about −40 °C.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Clouds between 0 and −20 °C hold large amounts of supercooled water: airframe icing zone.

los.lo: Explain the process of freezing.
los.title: The freezing process
los.html:
Theory & physics

Water molecules arrange onto an ice lattice starting at a nucleus or surface. Latent heat of fusion is released, warming the remaining water towards 0 °C and slowing further freezing. Large drops therefore freeze slowly and flow before freezing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Slow freezing of large supercooled drops = clear ice with runback (050.09.01.02.03).

los.lo: Explain the nature of and the need for freezing nuclei.
los.title: Freezing nuclei
los.html:
Theory & physics

Particles with a crystal structure similar to ice (some clay minerals, silver iodide, certain bacteria). They are scarce and become effective mostly below ≈ −10 to −15 °C; their number increases as temperature decreases.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Scarcity of freezing nuclei is why supercooled water is common between 0 and −20 °C.

los.lo: Define ‘supercooled water’. (Refer to Subject 050 09 01 01)
los.title: Supercooled water
los.html:
Theory & physics

Liquid water at a temperature below 0 °C. It is in an unstable state and freezes on contact with a nucleus or a surface (e.g. an airframe). Can exist down to ≈ −40 °C (small droplets); large drops usually freeze above ≈ −15/−20 °C.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most dangerous icing temperature band: 0 to −10 °C (most supercooled water, largest drops).
  • Below ≈ −40 °C there is no supercooled water: no airframe icing from droplets.

los.lo: List the conditions for sublimation.
los.title: Conditions for sublimation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Deposition (vapour → ice): air saturated with respect to ice at sub-zero temperature, with deposition nuclei or a sub-zero surface. Sublimation (ice → vapour): ice exposed to air that is unsaturated relative to ice (dry air), energy supplied.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Frost forms when the surface is below the frost point, even if the air at screen level is above 0 °C.

los.lo: Explain the sublimation process.
los.title: The sublimation process
los.html:
Theory & physics

Water vapour deposits directly as ice crystals on a nucleus or surface, without passing through the liquid phase, building feathery/hexagonal crystals; releases ≈ 2834 J/g. Reverse: ice evaporates directly in dry air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Hoar frost on parked aircraft (clear night) or in flight when a cold-soaked aircraft descends into warm moist air.

los.lo: Explain the nature of and the need for sublimation nuclei.
los.title: Sublimation (deposition) nuclei
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ice-forming nuclei that allow vapour to deposit directly as ice; even rarer than freezing nuclei and effective mainly below ≈ −15 to −20 °C (many only below −30 °C).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Explains why pure ice clouds (Ci, Cs, Cc) appear mainly at very low temperatures and high levels.

los.lo: Describe the absorption or release of latent heat in each change of state of water.
los.title: Latent heat absorbed or released in each change of state
los.html:
Theory & physics

Released: condensation (2500 J/g), freezing (334 J/g), deposition (2834 J/g). Absorbed: evaporation, melting, sublimation (same values). Deposition = condensation + freezing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Melting snow cools the air: isothermal 0 °C layer near the freezing level; snow can lower the freezing level in heavy precipitation.
  • Evaporative cooling of precipitation powers downbursts.

los.lo: Illustrate all the changes of state of water with practical examples.
los.title: Practical examples of all changes of state
los.html:
Theory & physics

Condensation: cloud, fog, dew. Evaporation: drying runway, virga, fog dispersal by heating. Freezing: freezing rain glaze, clear ice. Melting: snow turning to rain below the freezing level. Deposition: hoar frost, cirrus, rime-like frost. Sublimation: snow cover shrinking in dry cold wind.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Matching questions pair phenomenon and process; frost is deposition, not freezing of dew (frozen dew is a separate case: dew forming above 0 °C then freezing).

topics.title: Adiabatic processes, stability of the atmosphere

los.lo: Describe the adiabatic process in an unsaturated rising or descending air particle.
los.title: Adiabatic process in an unsaturated air parcel
los.html:
Theory & physics

Adiabatic = temperature change caused by compression or expansion without heat exchange with the surroundings. A rising parcel meets lower pressure, expands, does work against its surroundings and cools; a sinking parcel is compressed and warms. Valid for parcels moving fast relative to heat exchange.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "adiabatic means constant temperature" (that is isothermal).

los.lo: Explain the variation of temperature of an unsaturated rising or descending air particle.
los.title: Temperature of an unsaturated parcel
los.html:
Theory & physics

Changes at the dry adiabatic lapse rate, DALR = 1 °C/100 m = 3 °C/1000 ft (9.8 °C/km), up or down, as long as the parcel remains unsaturated.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Worked: surface 20 °C, parcel lifted dry 3000 ft → 20 − 9 = 11 °C.

los.lo: Explain the variation of humidity of an unsaturated rising or descending air particle.
los.title: Humidity of an unsaturated parcel
los.html:
Theory & physics

The mixing ratio (g of vapour per kg of dry air) stays constant. Rising: T falls fast, Td falls slowly (≈ 0.2 °C/100 m) → RH increases until saturation (cloud base = condensation level). Sinking: RH decreases (subsiding air is dry).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cloud base ≈ (T − Td) × 400 ft / × 125 m.
  • Subsidence in highs dries the air: clear skies, but haze trapped under the inversion.

los.lo: Describe the adiabatic process in a saturated rising or descending air particle.
los.title: Adiabatic process in a saturated parcel
los.html:
Theory & physics

A saturated rising parcel still cools by expansion but condensation releases latent heat, partly offsetting the cooling. Descending saturated air (e.g. in cloud with droplets evaporating) warms at the same reduced rate while evaporation absorbs heat.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Once the moisture has rained out, descending air warms at DALR (Föhn).

los.lo: Explain the variation of temperature of a saturated air particle with changing altitude.
los.title: Temperature of a saturated parcel with altitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

Changes at the saturated adiabatic lapse rate, SALR: exam value 0.6 °C/100 m = 1.8 °C/1000 ft at low levels. SALR is not constant: small (≈ 0.4 °C/100 m) in warm moist air with lots of condensation, approaching DALR in cold air and at high altitude where little vapour is left.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "SALR is constant at 1.8 °C/1000 ft at all levels". It increases with height/cold.

los.lo: Explain the static stability of the atmosphere using the actual temperature curve with reference to the adiabatic lapse rates.
los.title: Static stability from the temperature curve vs adiabatic lapse rates
los.html:
Theory & physics

Compare the ELR (from a sounding) with the parcel's lapse rate. Displace a parcel upward: if it ends up colder (denser) than the environment, it sinks back = stable; if warmer, it keeps rising = unstable; if equal, it stays = neutral. Steeper ELR (faster cooling of the environment) = less stable.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stability is a property of the environment relative to the parcel process, not of the parcel alone.
  • Stable: stratiform cloud, steady precipitation, poor visibility, smooth air. Unstable: Cu/Cb, showers, good visibility, turbulence.

los.lo: Define qualitatively and quantitatively the terms ‘stable’, ‘conditionally unstable’, ‘unstable’ and ‘indifferent’.
los.title: Stable, conditionally unstable, unstable, indifferent
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Absolutely stable: ELR < SALR (including isothermal layers and inversions).
  • Conditionally unstable: SALR < ELR < DALR: stable for dry air, unstable once saturated.
  • Absolutely unstable: ELR > DALR (only near a strongly heated surface).
  • Indifferent (neutral): ELR = DALR (dry air) or ELR = SALR (saturated air).

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Typical question: "ELR 0.8 °C/100 m. The atmosphere is…" → conditionally unstable (between 0.6 and 1.0).
  • ELR 2 °C/1000 ft (ISA) is conditionally unstable.
  • Absolutely unstable ELR is rare above the lowest few hundred metres.

los.lo: Illustrate with a schematic sketch the formation of Foehn.
los.title: Föhn (schematic)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Moist air is forced over a mountain range. Windward: rises dry at DALR to the condensation level, then at SALR in cloud; precipitation removes moisture (and latent heat stays in the air). Lee: descends dry at DALR from the crest. Net result: at the same level the lee air is warmer and drier than on the windward side. Cloud base on the lee side is higher (the dew point has fallen).

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Calculation steps: cloud base from spread (× 400 ft), DALR below base, SALR in cloud to the crest, DALR all the way down the lee.
  • Windward: low cloud, rain, icing, hill fog, obscured terrain. Lee: clear, warm, dry, gusty; mountain waves, rotors, lenticulars; rapid snowmelt.
  • Named examples: Föhn (Alps), Chinook (Rockies), Zonda (Andes).

los.lo: Explain the effect of the advection of air (warm or cold) on the stability of the air. Remark: Dry adiabatic lapse rate = 1 degrees C/100 m or 3 degrees C/1 000 ft; average value at lower levels for saturated adiabatic lapse rate = 0.6 degrees C/100 m or 1.8 degrees C/1 000 ft (values to be used in examinations).
los.title: Effect of warm or cold advection on stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Stability changes when the lapse rate changes:

  • Cold air advected over a warm surface (or warm air at low level, cold air advected aloft): ELR steepens → less stable / unstable (showers, Cb).
  • Warm air advected over a cold surface (or warm air advected aloft): ELR becomes shallower, inversion forms → more stable (St, fog, drizzle).

Exam values: DALR 1 °C/100 m (3 °C/1000 ft), SALR 0.6 °C/100 m (1.8 °C/1000 ft).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Polar maritime air over a warm sea in winter = unstable, showers, good visibility.
  • Tropical maritime air over cold land/sea = stable, St, drizzle, advection fog.

los.lo: Explain cloud formation by adiabatic cooling, conduction, advection and radiation.
los.title: Cloud formation by adiabatic cooling, conduction, advection and radiation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cloud forms when air is cooled to its dew point (or moistened) and condensation occurs on nuclei. Cooling mechanisms:

  • Adiabatic cooling of rising air: by far the main cause of cloud (convection, orographic lift, frontal lift, convergence, turbulence).
  • Conduction: contact with a cold surface (fog, St).
  • Advection: moist air moving over a colder surface (advection fog/St).
  • Radiation: nocturnal surface or cloud-top radiative cooling (radiation fog; St at the top of moist layers).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Question: "most cloud is formed by…" → adiabatic cooling in rising air.
  • Surface-based cooling usually produces fog and low St, not deep cloud.

los.lo: Describe cloud formation based on the following lifting processes: unorganised lifting in thin layers and turbulent mixing; forced lifting at fronts or over mountains; free convection.
los.title: Lifting processes: turbulent mixing, forced lifting, free convection
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Unorganised lifting in thin layers / turbulent mixing: mechanical turbulence lifts moist air in the friction layer; cooling to saturation at the top of the mixed layer gives St/Sc under a turbulence inversion.
  • Forced lifting: at fronts (Ns, As, Cs at warm fronts; Cb at active cold fronts) and over mountains (orographic St/Ns in stable air, Cu/Cb in unstable air, cap cloud).
  • Free convection: surface heating makes parcels buoyant → Cu, TCU, Cb, depending on depth of instability and moisture.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Same lifting mechanism produces stratiform or cumuliform cloud depending on the stability of the lifted air.

los.lo: List cloud types typical for stable and unstable air conditions.
los.title: Cloud types typical for stable and unstable air
los.html:
Theory & physics

Stable: St, Sc (under inversions), As, Ns, Cs, Ci, lenticulars. Unstable: Cu, TCU, Cb, Ac castellanus/floccus, Cc. Stable air gives layered cloud with flat tops; unstable air gives vertical development.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stable: continuous precipitation, poor visibility, smooth air, rime/mixed icing over large areas.
  • Unstable: showers, good visibility outside showers, turbulence, clear icing in short exposures.

los.lo: Summarise the conditions for the dissipation of clouds.
los.title: Conditions for the dissipation of clouds
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cloud dissolves when its air is warmed above the dew point or dried: subsidence (adiabatic warming in highs and behind troughs), mixing with dry air (entrainment at edges), surface heating (morning St/fog), advection over a warmer surface, loss of moisture by precipitation, end of the lifting mechanism.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Morning St/fog lifts and breaks with heating; may first lift to a low ceiling.
  • Lee side of mountains: descending air clears cloud (Föhn gap).

los.lo: Describe the different cloud types and their classification.
los.title: Cloud types and classification
los.html:
Theory & physics

WMO classification: 10 genera grouped by étage (height) and form; each genus divides into species (shape/structure, e.g. castellanus, lenticularis, congestus), varieties (arrangement/transparency) and supplementary features/accessory clouds (virga, mamma, incus/anvil, pileus).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • In METAR/TAF only CB and TCU are named; other cloud is reported by amount and base.

los.lo: Identify by shape cirriform, cumuliform and stratiform clouds.
los.title: Cirriform, cumuliform and stratiform clouds
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Cirriform: fibrous, hair-like, made of ice crystals (Ci, Cc, Cs).
  • Cumuliform: heaped, detached, with vertical development and sharp outlines; convection (Cu, Cb; lumpy elements in Sc, Ac, Cc).
  • Stratiform: uniform sheets or layers; stable lifting (St, As, Ns, Cs).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cs is both cirriform and stratiform (sheet of ice); halo phenomena only in Cs (ice crystals).

los.lo: Identify by shape and typical level the 10 cloud types (general).
los.title: The 10 cloud types: shape and typical level
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • High: Ci (white fibrous filaments/hooks), Cc (small white ripples/grains), Cs (transparent whitish veil, halo).
  • Middle: Ac (white/grey patches, rolls, shading, "mackerel sky"), As (grey/bluish sheet, sun as through ground glass, no halo).
  • Low: Sc (grey/whitish patches with dark parts), St (uniform grey layer, low base, drizzle).
  • Vertical/multi-level: Ns (dark grey thick layer, base low, continuous rain/snow, sun hidden), Cu (detached, sharp-outlined heaps, flat base), Cb (very large, towering, anvil of ice, showers, thunder).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Halo → Cs (thin ice veil); corona → Ac/As (water droplets).
  • Ns is classed as middle-level by WMO but its base is usually low and it extends through several étages.

los.lo: Describe and identify by shape the following species and supplementary features: castellanus, lenticularis, congestus, calvus, capillatus and virga.
los.title: Castellanus, lenticularis, congestus, calvus, capillatus, virga
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Castellanus (cas): turreted tops rising from a common base (Ac, Sc, Cc) → mid-level instability.
  • Lenticularis (lent): smooth lens/almond shapes (Ac, Sc, Cc) → mountain waves.
  • Congestus (con): Cu with strong vertical growth, cauliflower tops → TCU.
  • Calvus (cal): Cb whose top has lost its sharp outline but shows no fibrous ice yet.
  • Capillatus (cap): Cb with fibrous/striated ice top, often an anvil (incus) → mature/dissipating.
  • Virga: precipitation trails that evaporate before reaching the ground.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Ac castellanus in the morning → thunderstorms likely later in the day.
  • Virga below high-based Cb in dry air → dry microburst risk.

los.lo: Distinguish between low-, medium- and high-level clouds according to the World Meteorological Organization’s (WMO) ‘cloud etage’.
los.title: Low, medium and high clouds by WMO étage
los.html:
Theory & physics

Mid-latitude étages: low surface to 6 500 ft (2 km); middle 6 500 to 23 000 ft (2–7 km); high 16 500 to 45 000 ft (5–13 km). Levels overlap and rise towards the tropics (high up to 60 000 ft) and fall towards the poles (high 10 000–25 000 ft).

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: étage heights quoted for the tropics vs mid-latitudes.
  • SWC charts give layer base/top in FL; map them to genus expectations.

los.lo: Distinguish between ice clouds, mixed clouds and pure-water clouds.
los.title: Ice clouds, mixed clouds and pure-water clouds
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Water clouds: temperature above 0 °C, or slightly below with only supercooled droplets (St, Sc, Cu at low levels).
  • Mixed clouds: supercooled droplets and ice crystals together, roughly 0 to −20 °C (−40 °C in strong updrafts): Ns, As, Ac, TCU, Cb middle parts.
  • Ice clouds: below ≈ −20 to −40 °C: Ci, Cc, Cs, Cb anvils.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most icing in water (supercooled) and mixed clouds; ice clouds rarely cause airframe icing (but see ice-crystal engine icing, 050.09.01.04).

topics.title: Influence of inversions on cloud development

los.lo: Explain the influence of inversions on vertical movements in the atmosphere.
los.title: Influence of inversions on vertical movements
los.html:
Theory & physics

An inversion is a very stable layer: rising parcels become colder than the warm air of the inversion and stop. Convection, cloud tops, haze and pollutants are capped at its base.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Flat Cu or Sc tops at a uniform height indicate an inversion; above it, smooth air and better visibility.

los.lo: Explain the influence of an inversion on the formation of stratus clouds.
los.title: Inversions and the formation of stratus
los.html:
Theory & physics

Moisture trapped beneath an inversion (subsidence, turbulence or frontal) accumulates; turbulent mixing cools the top of the moist layer to saturation → extensive St or Sc with flat tops just below the inversion. Night radiative cooling of the cloud top reinforces it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Anticyclonic gloom: persistent Sc sheet under a winter high; poor visibility below, "VFR on top" above.

los.lo: Explain the influence of ground inversion on the formation of fog.
los.title: Ground inversion and fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Radiation cooling creates a surface (ground) inversion; the coldest, moist air near the ground saturates first. The inversion prevents mixing with drier air above, so fog forms and stays confined to the inversion layer (usually a few hundred ft).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Shallow fog: vertical visibility can be good (sky visible) while horizontal and slant visibility are poor; RVR governs.

los.lo: Describe the role of the tropopause inversion with regard to the vertical development of clouds.
los.title: Tropopause inversion and vertical cloud development
los.html:
Theory & physics

The stable stratosphere above the tropopause stops convective updrafts; Cb tops spread horizontally into an anvil (incus) at the tropopause. Very strong updrafts can overshoot a few thousand ft into the stratosphere.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cb tops: ≈ FL 350–450 in mid-latitudes, FL 500–600 in the tropics.
  • Overshooting tops on satellite = intense storm (hail, severe turbulence).

topics.title: Flying conditions in each cloud type

los.lo: Assess the 10 cloud types for icing and turbulence.
los.title: Icing and turbulence in the 10 cloud types
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cloud Icing (if T 0 to −20 °C) Turbulence
Cb Severe, clear (and mixed) Severe to extreme
Cu / TCU Moderate to severe, clear Moderate (TCU: up to severe)
Ns Moderate to severe, mixed/clear Light to moderate
As Light to moderate Nil to light
Ac Light to moderate (cas: more) Light (cas: moderate)
Sc Light to moderate, rime Light
St Light, rime Nil to light
Ci / Cc / Cs Nil (ice crystals) Nil (Cc may mark shear)

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most severe icing and turbulence: Cb; next Cu/TCU and Ns.
  • Question: "in which cloud is moderate icing least likely?" → Ci/Cs.

los.lo: Define ‘fog’, ‘mist’ and ‘haze’ with reference to the WMO standards of visibility range.
los.title: Fog, mist and haze (WMO visibility)
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Fog (FG): visibility < 1000 m caused by water droplets (or ice crystals) suspended in the air.
  • Mist (BR): visibility 1000–5000 m caused by water droplets, high RH (typically ≥ 95 %).
  • Haze (HZ): visibility reduced (reported when ≤ 5000 m) by dry particles (dust, smoke, salt) invisible to the eye; RH lower.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • BR vs HZ distinguished by humidity (wet vs dry), not by visibility.
  • MIFG (shallow fog), BCFG (patches), PRFG (partial), FZFG (freezing fog) are METAR descriptors.

los.lo: Explain briefly the formation of fog, mist and haze.
los.title: Formation of fog, mist and haze
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fog/mist: air in contact with the surface is cooled to its dew point (radiation, advection) or moistened (evaporation from warm water or rain) until saturated; condensation on nuclei. Haze: dry particles accumulate in stable air, especially under inversions, with no precipitation to remove them.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Fog types are named by their cooling/moistening process: radiation, advection, steam (sea smoke), frontal, orographic.

los.lo: Name the factors that generally contribute to the formation of fog and mist.
los.title: Factors that contribute to fog and mist
los.html:
Theory & physics

High relative humidity (small spread), effective cooling (clear sky, long nights), light wind (≈ 2–8 kt) to mix the cooling through a layer, abundant condensation nuclei, moist ground, stable air (inversion).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Calm wind: dew/frost or shallow fog only. Strong wind (> ≈ 10–15 kt): low St instead of fog (for radiation fog).

los.lo: Name the factors that contribute to the formation of haze.
los.title: Factors that contribute to haze
los.html:
Theory & physics

Stable air with a low-level (subsidence) inversion, persistent anticyclone, sources of dust/smoke/pollution, no rain to wash out particles, light winds.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Haze is worst late in a long-lasting summer anticyclone; slant visibility into the sun is especially poor.

los.lo: Describe freezing fog and ice fog.
los.title: Freezing fog and ice fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Freezing fog (FZFG): fog of supercooled droplets at temperatures below 0 °C; deposits rime on surfaces and aircraft. Ice fog: fog of ice crystals, at very low temperatures (typically below ≈ −30 °C), often near settlements/airports in arctic regions where combustion adds moisture.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • FZFG: aircraft must be de-iced/anti-iced; holdover times are short; taxiing aircraft collect rime.
  • METAR: FZFG is reported when fog occurs at temperature below 0 °C.

los.lo: Explain the formation of radiation fog.
los.title: Formation of radiation fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

On clear nights the ground loses heat by long-wave radiation; the air in contact cools by conduction; light turbulence spreads the cooling upward; once the air reaches its dew point, fog forms. Requires: clear sky, light wind (2–8 kt), moist air (small spread), long night, and land surface (sea does not cool enough).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Classic setting: autumn/winter anticyclone or ridge/col, inland, low-lying ground, after rain.
  • Radiation fog never forms over the sea.

los.lo: Describe the significant characteristics of radiation fog, and its vertical extent.
los.title: Characteristics and vertical extent of radiation fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Shallow (a few metres to ≈ 300–500 ft, deeper in long winter nights), often patchy, densest in valleys and hollows (cold air drainage); forms after midnight, thickest around and just after sunrise.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • RVR can fall suddenly; neighbouring aerodromes may be clear.
  • From above, shallow fog may look thin while slant visibility on final is very poor.

los.lo: Summarise the conditions for the dissipation of radiation fog.
los.title: Dissipation of radiation fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Warming by the sun from below (fog burns off from the edges and from the bottom, often lifting into low St first); increase in wind (mixing with drier air); arrival of cloud cover (stops radiative cooling, warms surface); advection of drier air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Typically clears mid-morning; in winter with weak sun and thick fog it may persist all day ("anticyclonic fog").
  • An increase in wind at first may lift fog into low St (ceiling) rather than clear it.

los.lo: Explain the formation of advection fog.
los.title: Formation of advection fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Warm, moist air moves over a surface that is colder than its dew point; the air is cooled from below by conduction, and turbulence (wind) spreads the cooling, producing fog. Can form with wind and at any time of day or night.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Distinguish from radiation fog: advection fog does not need clear skies and can form in winds up to ≈ 15–20 kt (stronger wind lifts it to St).

los.lo: Describe the different possibilities of advection-fog formation (over land, sea and coastal regions).
los.title: Advection fog over land, sea and coastal regions
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Sea: warm air over a cold sea current (Newfoundland, California, North Sea in spring/early summer).
  • Land: mild, moist air (mT) over cold or snow-covered ground in winter (warm sector over a continent).
  • Coastal: sea fog carried inland by onshore wind or sea breeze.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Sea fog season in western Europe: spring/early summer when the sea is still cold.

los.lo: Describe the significant characteristics of advection fog.
los.title: Characteristics of advection fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Extensive (can cover large areas), deeper than radiation fog (hundreds to > 1000 ft), persistent, little diurnal change over the sea, moves with the wind.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Choose alternates outside the affected air mass; a nearby coastal alternate may be equally fogged in.

los.lo: Summarise the conditions for the dissipation of advection fog.
los.title: Dissipation of advection fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Change of air mass or wind direction (e.g. frontal passage, offshore wind), increase of wind lifting it to low St, warming of the underlying surface (over land, strong heating in spring/summer). Over the sea: very little diurnal effect.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Do not count on morning burn-off for sea fog.

los.lo: Explain the formation of sea smoke.
los.title: Formation of sea smoke (steam fog)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Very cold air flows over much warmer water; intense evaporation saturates the lowest layer of cold air and the vapour immediately condenses: fog rising like steam. Also called arctic sea smoke or steam fog.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Moistening, not cooling, is the mechanism: opposite to advection fog (warm air over cold water).

los.lo: Explain the conditions for the development of sea smoke.
los.title: Conditions for sea smoke
los.html:
Theory & physics

Large water–air temperature difference (≈ ≥ 10 °C), cold stable air aloft (inversion) to keep it shallow, light to moderate wind; typical over ice-free water at high latitudes in winter, lakes in autumn, fjords, off ice edges.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • At sub-zero temperatures it can contain supercooled droplets (icing of ships, low-level aircraft, helicopters).

los.lo: Summarise the conditions for the dissipation of sea smoke.
los.title: Dissipation of sea smoke
los.html:
Theory & physics

Decrease of the temperature contrast (air warming or water cooling/freezing), stronger wind mixing it out, change of air mass.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Usually shallow (tens to a few hundred ft); offshore helicopter operations most affected.

los.lo: Explain the formation of frontal fog.
los.title: Formation of frontal fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Rain from the warm air above a frontal surface falls into the cold air below; the drops are warmer than the cold air and evaporate, adding moisture until the cold air saturates. Most common ahead of warm fronts and occlusions.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Mechanism is moistening by evaporating precipitation (plus some cooling), not radiation.

los.lo: Describe the significant characteristics of frontal fog.
los.title: Characteristics of frontal fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wide band parallel to the front (often 100–200 km ahead of the surface warm front), associated with low St, continuous rain/drizzle; may occur with moderate winds; moves with the front.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Large areas below minima at the same time; plan distant alternates and extra fuel.

los.lo: Summarise the conditions for the dissipation of frontal fog.
los.title: Dissipation of frontal fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Passage of the front (the cold air with its fog is replaced by warm-sector air), end of precipitation, increase in wind.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Improvement usually follows warm-front passage, though warm-sector St/drizzle may keep ceilings low.

los.lo: Summarise the features of orographic fog.
los.title: Features of orographic (hill) fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Moist, stable air forced up a slope cools adiabatically to its dew point; the cloud forms on the hillside and covers the high ground. It is effectively low St or cap cloud seen from within.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Mechanism = adiabatic cooling (not radiation or advection).

los.lo: Describe the significant characteristics of orographic fog.
los.title: Characteristics of orographic fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Persists as long as the upslope wind continues; can occur in moderate or strong winds; often accompanied by drizzle; covers ridges and passes while valleys may be clear.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • VFR flights over high ground: terrain hidden in cloud → CFIT risk; passes closed.

los.lo: Summarise the conditions for the dissipation of orographic fog.
los.title: Dissipation of orographic fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Change in wind direction (no more upslope flow), arrival of a drier air mass, or warming.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No diurnal clearance to rely on; wait for a wind shift or air-mass change.

los.lo: Describe the two basic processes of forming precipitation (the Wegener-Bergeron-Findeisen process, Coalescence).
los.title: Two basic processes of precipitation formation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cloud droplets (≈ 10–20 µm) are far too small to fall; a raindrop contains about a million droplets. Two growth processes: the ice-crystal (Wegener–Bergeron–Findeisen) process in mixed (sub-zero) clouds and coalescence (collision–coalescence) in warm clouds.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Mid- and high-latitude precipitation: mainly WBF (rain usually starts as snow). Tropical warm-cloud rain: coalescence.

los.lo: Summarise the outlines of the ice-crystal process (the Wegener-Bergeron-Findeisen process).
los.title: Ice-crystal (Wegener–Bergeron–Findeisen) process
los.html:
Theory & physics

In a mixed cloud below 0 °C, ice crystals and supercooled droplets coexist. The saturation vapour pressure over ice is lower than over water, so air saturated for water is supersaturated for ice: vapour deposits on the crystals while droplets evaporate. Crystals grow rapidly, aggregate into snowflakes and fall; they melt into rain below the freezing level. Most effective around −10 to −20 °C.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Clouds that are too warm (no ice) or too thin cannot use WBF.
  • Mixed-phase clouds are both precipitation producers and icing hazards.

los.lo: Summarise the outlines of the coalescence process.
los.title: Coalescence process
los.html:
Theory & physics

Larger droplets fall faster than small ones, collide and merge (coalesce), growing further. Efficient in deep clouds with strong updrafts, high liquid water content and a broad drop-size spectrum (maritime clouds with large salt nuclei). Works above and below 0 °C.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Coalescence in supercooled clouds produces supercooled large drops (SLD): freezing drizzle/rain without a warm layer aloft.

los.lo: Explain the development of snow, rain, drizzle and hail.
los.title: Development of snow, rain, drizzle and hail
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Snow: ice crystals grow (WBF) and aggregate; reach the ground when temperature stays near or below 0 °C (snow can fall with surface temperature up to ≈ +2/+3 °C in dry air).
  • Rain: melted snow or coalescence drops (≥ 0.5 mm).
  • Drizzle: fine drops (< 0.5 mm) from shallow St/Sc via coalescence; weak updrafts.
  • Hail: ice embryos (graupel/frozen drops) carried repeatedly through regions of supercooled water by strong Cb updrafts; accrete layers of clear and opaque ice; fall when too heavy for the updraft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Hail requires a Cb with strong updrafts and a deep supercooled layer; size ∝ updraft strength.
  • Drizzle indicates St and stable air: low ceilings and poor visibility, potential FZDZ.

topics.title: Types of precipitation, relationship with cloud types

los.lo: List and describe the types of precipitation given in the aerodrome forecast (TAF) and METAR codes (drizzle, rain, snow, snow grains, ice pellets, hail, small hail, snow pellets, ice crystals, freezing drizzle, freezing rain).
los.title: Precipitation types in TAF and METAR
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • DZ drizzle: fine drops < 0.5 mm, close together, from St.
  • RA rain: drops ≥ 0.5 mm, or smaller and widely separated.
  • SN snow: ice crystals, mostly branched (stars), often aggregated into flakes.
  • SG snow grains: very small (< 1 mm) white opaque grains, from St/fog (solid equivalent of drizzle).
  • PL ice pellets: transparent or translucent pellets < 5 mm (frozen raindrops or largely melted then refrozen snow); bounce on hard ground.
  • GR hail: ice balls ≥ 5 mm, from Cb.
  • GS small hail and/or snow pellets (graupel): < 5 mm, opaque/white, soft or with thin ice coat, from convective cloud.
  • IC ice crystals (diamond dust): tiny crystals in very cold, clear air.
  • FZDZ / FZRA: supercooled drizzle/rain that freezes on impact.
  • Qualifiers: SH showers (convective), TS thunderstorm, intensity − / (moderate) / +.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • GR vs GS: 5 mm threshold.
  • PL indicates freezing rain aloft (a warm layer above a cold one): FZRA may be nearby.

los.lo: State the ICAO/WMO approximate diameters for cloud, drizzle and rain drops.
los.title: Approximate diameters of cloud, drizzle and rain drops
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cloud droplets ≈ 0.01–0.02 mm (10–20 µm, up to ≈ 50 µm); drizzle drops < 0.5 mm (≈ 0.2–0.5 mm); raindrops ≥ 0.5 mm, typically 1–2 mm, maximum ≈ 5–6 mm (larger drops break up).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Drop size controls icing: large supercooled drops impinge further aft and freeze more slowly (runback, clear ice beyond protected areas).

los.lo: State that, because of their size, hail stones can cause significant damage to aircraft.
los.title: Hail damage
los.html:
Theory & physics

Hailstones can exceed 5 cm; at aircraft speeds the kinetic energy is very high. Hail can fall from the anvil and outside the visible precipitation core, several nm from the storm, and can occur at high altitude above the freezing level (no melting).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Damage: cracked windscreens, radome, leading edges, engine fan blades and core; possible engine flame-out (water/ice ingestion).
  • Avoid flying under anvils and close to Cb (≥ 10–20 nm).

los.lo: Explain the mechanism for the formation of freezing precipitation.
los.title: Mechanism of freezing precipitation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Classical (melting) mechanism: snow falls into a warm layer (> 0 °C) aloft, melts into rain, then falls into a sub-zero layer near the surface; drops become supercooled and freeze on impact. If the cold layer is deep enough the drops refreeze into ice pellets (PL). Warm-rain (supercooled coalescence) mechanism: in shallow supercooled St/Sc, drops grow by coalescence without ever freezing → FZDZ with no warm layer aloft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Inversion (warm air above cold) is the key signature of FZRA.
  • Climbing into the warm layer can be an escape (if known and permitted); descending into colder air may convert to ice pellets.

los.lo: Describe the weather conditions that give rise to freezing precipitation.
los.title: Weather situations producing freezing precipitation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ahead of warm fronts and warm occlusions in winter, when mild air overruns a shallow layer of sub-zero continental air; also in cold-air pools (valleys, basins) with a warmer layer above; FZDZ in stratiform cloud in stagnant cold anticyclonic air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Winter continental Europe, North America: FZRA ahead of warm fronts; airports may close (de-icing ineffective).

los.lo: Distinguish between the types of precipitation generated in convective and stratiform clouds.
los.title: Convective vs stratiform precipitation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Convective (Cu, TCU, Cb): showers (SH), sudden start and end, rapid intensity changes, large drops, possibly hail/GS, short duration, variable visibility. Stratiform (Ns, As, St, Sc): continuous (or intermittent), uniform intensity, light to moderate, long-lasting, smaller drops/drizzle.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • SHRA → Cu/Cb (convective); RA continuous → Ns/As; DZ → St.

los.lo: Assign typical precipitation types and intensities to different cloud types.
los.title: Typical precipitation and intensity by cloud type
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cloud Typical precipitation Intensity
Cb SHRA, SHSN, GR, GS, TS Moderate to heavy
Cu / TCU SHRA, SHSN, GS Light to moderate
Ns Continuous RA, SN, (PL, FZRA) Moderate to heavy
As Continuous or intermittent RA, SN Light to moderate
Sc Light RA, SN, DZ Light
St DZ, SG, FZDZ Light
Ac, Ci, Cc, Cs Mostly virga None at surface

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Heavy continuous rain → Ns, not Cb (Cb = showers).

los.lo: Explain the relationship between moisture content and visibility during different types of winter precipitation (e.g. large vs small snowflakes).
los.title: Moisture content and visibility in winter precipitation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Visibility depends more on the number and size of falling particles than on water content. Snow reduces visibility far more than rain of the same water content. Large, wet flakes (near 0 °C, high water content) fall in clusters with gaps between them; small dry flakes at low temperature are numerous and can reduce visibility more for the same precipitation rate. Heavy snow can give visibility < 500 m; moderate ≈ 500–1000 m.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Wet snow near 0 °C: heavy accumulation on airframe and runway, poor braking, short holdover times.
  • Blowing snow adds to visibility loss (050.09.09.02.01).

topics.title: Description, classification and source regions of air masses

los.lo: Define the term ‘air mass’.
los.title: Define air mass
los.html:
Theory & physics

An air mass is a large body of air (hundreds to thousands of km across) whose temperature and humidity are nearly uniform horizontally at any given level, having acquired these properties over a source region.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Vertical properties (lapse rate) can vary; uniformity is horizontal.
  • Air-mass weather is the background between fronts.

los.lo: Describe the properties of the source regions.
los.title: Properties of source regions
los.html:
Theory & physics

Extensive, uniform surface (ocean, snow/ice field, desert, large continent); light winds and slow subsidence so the air stays long enough (days–weeks) to reach equilibrium with the surface; typically under semi-permanent anticyclones.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Depressions and mid-latitude westerly belts are not source regions (too mobile, too mixed).

los.lo: Summarise the classification of air masses by source regions.
los.title: Classification by source region
los.html:
Theory & physics

By latitude: Arctic/Antarctic (A), Polar (P), Tropical (T), Equatorial (E). By surface: maritime (m) or continental (c). Examples: mP (N Atlantic), cP (Siberia/Canada in winter), mT (Azores), cT (Sahara), mA/cA (Arctic).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • "Polar" air originates in high-mid latitudes (≈ 50–70°), not at the pole (that is Arctic).

los.lo: State the classifications of air masses by temperature and humidity at source.
los.title: Classification by temperature and humidity at source
los.html:
Theory & physics

Temperature: A/P = cold, T/E = warm. Humidity: m = moist, c = dry. Third letter (exam convention): c (k) = colder than the surface it is over (→ unstable), w = warmer than the surface (→ stable).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • mPc / mPk: polar maritime colder than the surface: showers. mTw: tropical maritime warmer than the surface: fog, St.

los.lo: State the characteristic weather in each of the air masses.
los.title: Characteristic weather of each air mass
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • mP: cool, moist, unstable over warmer sea/land: Cu, Cb, showers (rain, snow, hail), good visibility outside showers, gusty; at night over land may clear.
  • cP: winter: very cold, dry, stable at source, clear skies, frost, haze; picks up moisture over seas (snow showers on windward coasts). Summer: warm, dry, Cu.
  • mT: warm, moist, stable over colder surfaces: St, Sc, drizzle, advection fog, poor visibility, hill fog; in summer over hot land can become unstable (TS).
  • cT: hot, dry, dusty, unstable at low levels in summer (dust, haze, dry convection, high cloud bases).
  • mA/cA: very cold; snow showers over open water; very good visibility otherwise.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Showers and good visibility → mP. Drizzle, fog, poor visibility → mT.

los.lo: Name the three main air masses that affect Europe.
los.title: Three main air masses affecting Europe
los.html:
Theory & physics

Maritime polar (mP) from the N Atlantic (most frequent), maritime tropical (mT) from the Azores region (warm sectors), continental polar (cP) from Russia/Siberia (winter cold spells, easterly winds). Less often: mA, cT (Saharan dust episodes).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Answer pattern: mP, mT, cP.

los.lo: Classify air masses on a surface weather chart. Remark: Names and abbreviations of air masses used in examinations: first letter: humidity continental (c) maritime (m) second letter: type of air mass arctic (A) polar (P) tropical (T) equatorial (E) third letter: temperature cold (c) warm (w)
los.title: Classify air masses on a surface chart
los.html:
Theory & physics

Exam notation: first letter humidity (c continental, m maritime), second letter type (A arctic, P polar, T tropical, E equatorial), third letter temperature relative to the surface (c cold, w warm). Identify from: source direction of isobaric flow, position relative to fronts (warm sector = mT; behind cold front = mP), temperature/dew point at stations.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • On a chart: air in the warm sector is the warm air mass; air behind the cold front is the polar air mass.

los.lo: List the environmental factors that affect the final properties of an air mass.
los.title: Factors that affect the final properties of an air mass
los.html:
Theory & physics

Temperature and moisture of the surface along the track, length of time over each surface (track length/speed), season, terrain (orographic lifting, Föhn), diurnal heating/cooling over land, and vertical motion (subsidence or ascent).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The same source can give very different weather depending on the track.

los.lo: Explain how maritime and continental tracks modify air masses.
los.title: Maritime and continental tracks
los.html:
Theory & physics

A sea track adds moisture (and heat in winter, cooling in summer); a land track dries the air and increases the diurnal temperature range (heating by day, cooling by night). Example: cP crossing the North Sea becomes "cPm", moist and unstable at low levels.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Snow showers on the east coast of Britain in winter easterlies (cP modified over the North Sea).

los.lo: Explain the effect of passage over cold or warm surfaces.
los.title: Passage over cold or warm surfaces
los.html:
Theory & physics

Over a warmer surface: heated from below, ELR steepens, air becomes unstable: convection, Cu/Cb, showers, good visibility (mixing). Over a colder surface: cooled from below, inversion forms, stable: St, fog, drizzle, poor visibility, smooth air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Key rule behind almost every air-mass weather question.

los.lo: Explain how air-mass weather is affected by the season, the air-mass track and by orographic and thermal effects over land.
los.title: Season, track, orographic and thermal effects over land
los.html:
Theory & physics

Summer: land warmer than sea, so maritime air becomes unstable over land by day (afternoon Cu/Cb), stable at night. Winter: land colder than sea, so maritime air is cooled over land (St, fog), especially at night. Mountains force ascent (windward cloud/precipitation, lee clearance and Föhn).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • mT in winter over Europe: fog/St; mT in summer: TS over land in the afternoon.

los.lo: Assess the tendencies of the stability of an air mass and describe the typical resulting air-mass weather including the hazards for aviation.
los.title: Stability tendencies and resulting air-mass weather/hazards
los.html:
Theory & physics

Air mass becoming less stable (cold air over warm surface, or cold air aloft): showers, Cb, turbulence, icing in convective cloud, hail, gusty winds, good visibility. Becoming more stable (warm air over cold surface, subsidence): low St, fog, drizzle, possible FZDZ, poor visibility, inversions with wind shear, smooth air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Plan alternates by air-mass hazard: stable air masses close many aerodromes at once (fog), unstable ones affect aerodromes briefly (showers).

los.lo: Describe the boundaries between air masses (fronts).
los.title: Boundaries between air masses (fronts)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Where two air masses of different temperature (density) meet, they do not mix readily; the colder, denser air forms a wedge under the warmer air. The boundary is a sloping surface along which the warm air rises, producing cloud and precipitation. Fronts lie in troughs of low pressure: isobars kink at the front and the wind changes direction across it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Frontal surfaces always slope with the cold air underneath; wind veers at frontal passage (NH).

los.lo: Define ‘front’ and ‘frontal zone’.
los.title: Front and frontal zone
los.html:
Theory & physics

Frontal zone: the three-dimensional transition layer between the air masses (tens to ≈ 200 km wide, strong temperature gradient). Front: the line of intersection of the frontal zone (frontal surface) with the ground or a given level (e.g. surface front, 500 hPa front).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Weather is spread across the frontal zone, far ahead of warm fronts, mostly near and behind cold fronts.

los.lo: Name the global frontal systems (polar front, arctic front).
los.title: Global frontal systems: polar front, arctic front
los.html:
Theory & physics

Polar front: between polar (mP/cP) and tropical (mT) air in mid-latitudes; birthplace of most mid-latitude depressions. Arctic front: between arctic and polar air at higher latitudes. (The ITCZ is not a front in the classical sense: it is a convergence zone.)

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: calling the ITCZ a front between air masses of different temperature.

los.lo: State the approximate seasonal latitudes and geographic positions of the polar front and the arctic front.
los.title: Seasonal positions of the polar front and arctic front
los.html:
Theory & physics

Polar front over the N Atlantic: ≈ 30–45°N in winter (from Florida towards SW Europe), ≈ 45–60°N in summer (Newfoundland towards the British Isles/Scandinavia). Arctic front: ≈ 60–70°N, further south over the continents in winter. Positions vary day to day.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Spain and the Mediterranean are affected by polar-front depressions mainly in winter.

topics.title: Warm front, associated clouds and weather

los.lo: Define a ‘warm front’.
los.title: Define warm front
los.html:
Theory & physics

A warm front is a front along which warm air advances and replaces cold air, gliding up over the retreating cold wedge (anafront-type ascent). Chart symbol: red line with semicircles pointing in the direction of movement.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The cold air at the surface retreats; surface friction slows it, keeping the slope shallow.

los.lo: Describe the cloud, weather, ground visibility and aviation hazards at a warm front depending on the stability of the warm air.
los.title: Warm-front cloud, weather, visibility and hazards (stable vs unstable warm air)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Stable warm air (typical): cloud sequence ahead of the surface front Ci → Cs (halo) → As → Ns, cloud base lowering steadily; continuous precipitation starting ≈ 300 km ahead (≈ 12 h before passage); St fractus and frontal fog in the cold air; visibility poor in rain and fog. Unstable warm air: Cb and TCU embedded in the Ns/As layers, heavy showers and TS hidden in layer cloud.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Hazards: low ceilings over a wide area, moderate/severe icing in Ns, FZRA in winter ahead of the front, embedded Cb (use radar), mountain obscuration.
  • At passage: rain stops or turns to drizzle, temperature and dew point rise, wind veers, pressure stops falling.

los.lo: Explain the seasonal differences in the weather at warm fronts.
los.title: Seasonal differences at warm fronts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Winter: low freezing level, snow or freezing rain/ice pellets ahead of the front, widespread fog, very low ceilings; continental cold air at the surface makes FZRA common. Summer: higher freezing level, rain; warm air more often unstable, so embedded TS more likely; less fog.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Winter warm front = classic FZRA case on exam questions.

los.lo: Describe the structure, slope and dimensions of a warm front.
los.title: Structure, slope and dimensions of a warm front
los.html:
Theory & physics

Shallow slope ≈ 1:100 to 1:200 (average ≈ 1:150). Cloud extends up to ≈ 800–1000 km ahead of the surface front (Ci at ≈ 25 000–30 000 ft); precipitation belt ≈ 200–300 km wide; speed slower than cold fronts (≈ 2/3 of the geostrophic component across it, typically 10–20 kt).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • With slope 1:150, the frontal surface is ≈ 10 000 ft above a point 450 km ahead of the surface front (450 km ÷ 150 = 3 km).

los.lo: Sketch a cross section of a warm front showing weather, cloud and aviation hazards.
los.title: Cross-section of a warm front
los.html:
Theory & physics

Warm air rises over the cold wedge; cloud forms in the warm air above the frontal surface: Ns near the surface front, As further ahead, Cs and Ci at the leading edge; precipitation falls from Ns/As into the cold air; St and frontal fog form in the cold air.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Where is FZRA? In the cold wedge ahead of the surface front, where rain from the warm air falls into sub-zero air.
  • Distance/time question: Ci first, then cloud lowering over 12–24 h.

topics.title: Cold front, associated clouds and weather

los.lo: Define a ‘cold front’.
los.title: Define cold front
los.html:
Theory & physics

A cold front is a front along which cold air advances and replaces warm air, undercutting it like a wedge and forcing it up. Chart symbol: blue line with triangles pointing in the direction of movement.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cold fronts move faster than warm fronts and catch up with them (occlusion).

los.lo: Describe the cloud, weather, ground visibility and aviation hazards at a cold front depending on the stability of the warm air.
los.title: Cold-front cloud, weather, visibility and hazards (stable vs unstable warm air)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Unstable warm air (active, ana-type): forced lifting at the steep leading edge produces a line of Cb/TCU, heavy showers, hail, TS, squalls, sometimes a pre-frontal squall line. Stable warm air (kata-type, inactive): mainly Ns/As or St/Sc, moderate rain, little convection. Weather band narrow (≈ 50–100 km), passage quick.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Hazards: severe turbulence and icing in Cb, hail, lightning, wind shear and gust fronts at aerodromes, sudden visibility drop in heavy showers.
  • At passage: sharp pressure rise (after a trough), temperature and dew point drop, wind veers sharply (e.g. SW → NW) and gusts, visibility improves behind.

los.lo: Explain the seasonal differences in the weather at cold fronts.
los.title: Seasonal differences at cold fronts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Summer: very active over land, especially in the afternoon: TS, hail, squalls. Winter: less convection over cold land but snow showers, icing, low freezing level; over warm seas still active (Cb).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most violent: summer afternoon cold front over land with unstable mT ahead.

los.lo: Describe the structure, slope and dimensions of a cold front.
los.title: Structure, slope and dimensions of a cold front
los.html:
Theory & physics

Steep slope ≈ 1:50 to 1:100 (average ≈ 1:80), steepened at the surface by friction (nose of cold air). Weather band ≈ 50–100 km (cloud/precipitation mainly at and just behind the surface front for ana-fronts). Speed ≈ the full geostrophic wind component normal to the front (often 20–30 kt).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Steeper slope = more vigorous lifting = convective weather concentrated in a narrow band.

los.lo: Sketch a cross section of a cold front showing weather, cloud and aviation hazards.
los.title: Cross-section of a cold front
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cold air pushes under the warm air; the steep leading edge lifts unstable warm air rapidly into Cb with anvils at the tropopause; heavy showers at and behind the surface front; post-frontal Cu/Cb in the cold air with good visibility.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cb line may be hidden in Ns behind it; airborne radar essential.
  • Behind the front: wind NW (NH), gusty, showers; good VFR between showers.

topics.title: Warm sector, associated clouds and weather

los.lo: Describe fronts and air masses associated with the warm sector.
los.title: Fronts and air masses of the warm sector
los.html:
Theory & physics

The warm sector is the wedge of warm air (usually mT) between the warm front ahead and the cold front behind, south/equatorward of the depression centre; its isobars are straight and parallel, indicating the direction of movement of the depression.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Depression moves parallel to the warm-sector isobars.

los.lo: Describe the cloud, weather, ground visibility and aviation hazards in a warm sector.
los.title: Warm-sector cloud, weather, visibility and hazards
los.html:
Theory & physics

Stable mT cooled from below: extensive St/Sc, drizzle, mist and fog (especially over cold sea/land), hill fog; visibility moderate to poor; temperature steady, wind steady (SW in NH).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Low ceilings and poor visibility can persist for hours between the fronts; high ground obscured.

los.lo: Explain the seasonal differences in the weather in the warm sector.
los.title: Seasonal differences in the warm sector
los.html:
Theory & physics

Winter: low St, drizzle, advection fog over cold land: worst visibility. Summer: over land, daytime heating may lift and break the St into Sc/Cu and give isolated TS; over sea, sea fog.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Winter warm sector: aerodromes below minima for long periods; plan alternates outside the warm sector.

los.lo: Sketch a cross section of a warm sector showing weather, cloud and aviation hazards.
los.title: Cross-section of the warm sector
los.html:
Theory & physics

Between the two frontal surfaces: warm moist air with a low St/Sc layer under an inversion; drizzle; the upper parts may be cloud-free or have Ac/As.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Icing in St/Sc only if temperatures in the layer are sub-zero (often not in the warm sector).

los.lo: Describe the cloud, weather, ground visibility and aviation hazards behind the cold front.
los.title: Cloud, weather, visibility and hazards behind the cold front
los.html:
Theory & physics

Polar (mP) air moving over a warmer surface becomes unstable: Cu and Cb, showers of rain, snow, hail or graupel, very good visibility outside showers, gusty NW winds (NH), temperature low. Often a secondary trough with a further band of showers.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Showery turbulence and icing in Cu/Cb; sudden snow showers with visibility drops at aerodromes.

los.lo: Explain the seasonal differences in the weather behind the cold front.
los.title: Seasonal differences behind the cold front
los.html:
Theory & physics

Winter: over the sea showers continue day and night (sea warmer than air); over land showers die out at night, clear skies, frost and fog possible. Summer: over land showers/TS develop by day, clear nights.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Winter coastal aerodromes: snow showers drifting in from the sea at night.

los.lo: Define the term ‘occlusion’ and ‘occluded front’.
los.title: Occlusion and occluded front
los.html:
Theory & physics

The faster cold front overtakes the warm front, lifting the warm-sector air off the ground. The resulting front, where the two cold air masses meet, is the occluded front (purple, alternating triangles and semicircles). The warm air aloft forms a trough of warm air (trowal).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Occlusion = mature/old depression; it usually fills afterwards.

los.lo: Describe the cloud, weather, ground visibility and aviation hazards in a cold occlusion.
los.title: Cold occlusion
los.html:
Theory & physics

The air behind the cold front is colder than the air ahead of the warm front: the cold front continues to the ground and the warm front is lifted aloft (upper warm front ahead). Weather: warm-front type cloud and precipitation ahead, then cold-front type (possible Cb, heavy showers) at the surface occlusion; clearing behind.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Typical in summer over Europe (cool maritime air behind, warmer continental air ahead).
  • Hazards: embedded Cb, icing, low ceilings.

los.lo: Describe the cloud, weather, ground visibility and aviation hazards in a warm occlusion.
los.title: Warm occlusion
los.html:
Theory & physics

The air ahead of the warm front is colder than the air behind the cold front: the cold front rides up over the cold air ahead (upper cold front). The upper cold front runs ahead of the surface occlusion, so convective weather (Cb) can arrive aloft before the surface front. Weather mostly warm-front type.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Typical in winter over western Europe (very cold continental air ahead).
  • Embedded Cb at height ahead of the surface front; FZRA possible at the surface.

los.lo: Explain the seasonal differences in the weather at occlusions.
los.title: Seasonal differences at occlusions
los.html:
Theory & physics

Winter: warm occlusions dominate over western/central Europe, with extensive layer cloud, snow, FZRA. Summer: cold occlusions dominate, with more convective activity.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Match: winter → warm occlusion; summer → cold occlusion (for W Europe).

los.lo: Sketch a cross section of occlusions showing weather, cloud and aviation hazards.
los.title: Cross-sections of occlusions
los.html:
Theory & physics

In both types the warm air is lifted into an inverted V (trowal) above the two cold air masses; the colder of the two stays at the surface. Cloud: Ns/As around the trowal, Cs/Ci ahead, Cb embedded where the lifted warm air is unstable.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Identify the type from which surface air is colder; the slope of the surface occlusion copies that of the front that stays on the ground.

los.lo: On a sketch illustrate the development of an occlusion and the movement of the occlusion point.
los.title: Development of an occlusion and movement of the occlusion point
los.html:
Theory & physics

Occlusion starts at the depression centre (where the warm sector is narrowest) and spreads outward along the fronts. The occlusion point (triple point), where warm front, cold front and occluded front meet, moves away from the centre, towards the equator/along the warm front, as the occlusion lengthens. The low centre is left behind in cold air and begins to fill.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • New secondary lows often form at the triple point.
  • Weather is often worst near the triple point.

topics.title: Stationary front, associated clouds and weather

los.lo: Define a ‘stationary front’.
los.title: Define stationary front
los.html:
Theory & physics

A front with little or no movement (≤ ≈ 5 kt), because the wind blows almost parallel to it on both sides. Symbol: alternating red semicircles and blue triangles on opposite sides of the line.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Isobars run parallel to a stationary front.

los.lo: Describe the cloud, weather, ground visibility and aviation hazards in a stationary front.
los.title: Weather at a stationary front
los.html:
Theory & physics

Similar to a weak warm front: extensive layer cloud (St, Ns, As), persistent precipitation and low visibility on the cold side, lasting for days; embedded Cb if the warm air is unstable. Frontal waves often form along it and can develop into depressions.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Prolonged bad weather; check for wave development (falling pressure along the front).

topics.title: Movement of fronts and pressure systems, life cycle

los.lo: Describe the movements of fronts and pressure systems and the life cycle of a mid-latitude depression.
los.title: Movement of fronts and pressure systems; life cycle of a mid-latitude depression
los.html:
Theory & physics

Frontal depressions travel generally eastward (NH: E to NE) with the upper westerlies, steered by the 500 hPa flow, at ≈ 15–30 kt, slowing when occluded. Life cycle ≈ 3–7 days: wave → developing (open warm sector, deepening) → mature (occluding, deepest) → dissipating (fully occluded, filling, cold-cored).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Deepest pressure at about the time of occlusion.

los.lo: State the rules for predicting the direction and the speed of movement of fronts.
los.title: Rules for direction and speed of fronts
los.html:
Theory & physics

A front moves with the component of the geostrophic wind perpendicular to it, measured in the air behind it (cold front: from the cold air; warm front: from the warm air). Cold front speed ≈ the full normal component (reduced by friction at the surface); warm front speed ≈ 2/3 of the normal component. Fronts parallel to the isobars hardly move.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Chart exercise: measure isobar spacing behind the front, convert to geostrophic speed, take the normal component.

los.lo: State the difference in the speed of movement between cold and warm fronts.
los.title: Speed of cold vs warm fronts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cold fronts move faster (≈ 1.5 times the speed of warm fronts) because the dense cold air pushes under the warm air, while at warm fronts friction holds the retreating cold air back.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Consequence: occlusion.

los.lo: State the rules for predicting the direction and the speed of movement of frontal depressions.
los.title: Rules for direction and speed of frontal depressions
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Moves parallel to the warm-sector isobars, with cold air on the left (NH).
  • Speed ≈ the geostrophic wind in the warm sector (or ≈ 70–80 % of it).
  • Moves towards the area of greatest pressure fall (isallobaric low).
  • Steered by the upper (500 hPa) flow; slows and turns left (NH) when occluding.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Occluded lows become slow-moving and may stall over the same area for days.

los.lo: Describe, with a sketch if required, the genesis, development and life cycle of a frontal depression with associated cloud and rain belts.
los.title: Genesis, development and life cycle with cloud and rain belts
los.html:
Theory & physics

  1. Stationary polar front with shear between easterly cold air and westerly warm air.
  2. A wave forms (upper divergence ahead of an upper trough); pressure falls at the crest.
  3. Wave amplifies: warm front and cold front with an open warm sector; rain belts ahead of the warm front (wide) and along the cold front (narrow).
  4. Cold front catches up near the centre: occlusion begins; the cloud system takes a comma shape on satellite.
  5. Fully occluded: the low fills, cold-core; showers in the cold air. New waves may form on the trailing cold front (families of depressions).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Satellite: the comma head = occlusion; the tail = cold front.

topics.title: Changes of meteorological elements at a frontal wave

los.lo: Sketch a plan and a cross section of a frontal wave (warm front, warm sector, and cold front) and illustrate the changes of pressure, temperature, surface wind and wind in the vertical axis.
los.title: Plan and cross-section of a frontal wave: changes of pressure, temperature, surface wind and wind with height
los.html:
Theory & physics

As a frontal wave passes a station east of the low (NH): pressure falls ahead of the warm front, steadies in the warm sector, rises behind the cold front. Temperature rises at the warm front, drops at the cold front. Surface wind backs and increases ahead of the warm front, veers at each front. In the vertical: warm advection ahead of the warm front makes the wind veer with height; cold advection behind the cold front makes it back with height.

Exam diagram

Passage of a frontal wave at a fixed station (NH)

Temperature Cold Rises Warm, steady Sharp drop Cold
Dew point Rises in rain Rises High, steady Drops Low

Precipitation Continuous RA/SN, increasing Stops or DZ DZ Heavy SHRA, GR, TS Showers
Visibility Deteriorating, frontal fog Poor Poor (BR, FG) Poor in showers Very good outside showers

Exam traps & operational impact

  • NH: wind veers at each frontal passage; SH: backs.
  • Veering wind with height = warm advection (approaching warm front); backing with height = cold advection.
  • Station north of the low centre sees no fronts: wind backs steadily (e.g. E → N → NW) and pressure falls then rises.

topics.title: Location of the principal pressure areas

los.lo: Identify or indicate on a map the principal global high-pressure and low-pressure areas in January and July.
los.title: Principal global highs and lows in January and July
los.html:
Theory & physics

Permanent (dynamic): subtropical highs, the Azores (Bermuda) high, N Pacific (Hawaiian) high, S Atlantic (St Helena), S Indian (Mascarene) and S Pacific highs; subpolar lows, the Icelandic low and Aleutian low (deepest in winter); equatorial trough.

January (NH winter): Siberian high (strongest, > 1035 hPa), N American (Canadian) high; deep Icelandic and Aleutian lows; thermal lows over S Africa, Australia, S America.

July (NH summer): Asian (Pakistan/Persian Gulf) thermal low, SW US low, Iberian/Saharan thermal lows; Azores and Pacific highs strong and displaced north; Icelandic low weak; Australian high (SH winter).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Map questions: the Siberian high appears only in winter; the Asian low only in summer.
  • Icelandic low is a statistical average of travelling depressions, not a single stationary low.

los.lo: Explain how these pressure areas are formed.
los.title: How these pressure areas are formed
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dynamic: subtropical highs from subsidence of the Hadley cell (upper convergence, ≈ 30°); subpolar lows from convergence/ascent at the polar front (and the frequent passage of depressions). Thermal: continental highs from intense winter radiative cooling of dense air (shallow, cold-core); continental summer lows from strong surface heating (shallow, warm-core). Equatorial trough from heating and trade-wind convergence.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Thermal systems are shallow and reverse aloft (see 050.01.03.04.01); dynamic subtropical highs are deep warm highs.

los.lo: Explain how the pressure areas move with the seasons.
los.title: Seasonal movement of the pressure areas
los.html:
Theory & physics
