The whole system shifts poleward in the summer hemisphere and equatorward in winter, following the sun with a lag of ≈ 1–2 months; the shift is larger over continents than over oceans. Continental thermal highs and lows reverse between seasons.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Spain: summer under the Azores ridge and Iberian thermal low (heat, afternoon TS inland); winter in the path of Atlantic depressions and sometimes cP outbreaks.

topics.title: Anticyclones, types, general properties, cold and warm anticyclones, ridges and subsidence

los.lo: List the different types of anticyclones.
los.title: Types of anticyclones
los.html:
Theory & physics

Warm anticyclones (dynamic, deep, warm-core: subtropical highs, blocking highs), cold anticyclones (thermal, shallow, cold-core: continental winter highs, polar highs), ridges (wedges of high pressure between lows), blocking highs (persistent mid/high-latitude warm highs).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Distinguish by depth: warm highs extend to the tropopause; cold highs disappear aloft.

los.lo: Describe the effect of high-level convergence in producing areas of high pressure at ground level.
los.title: High-level convergence producing surface highs
los.html:
Theory & physics

Where upper-level flow converges (e.g. behind upper troughs, at jet entrance regions on one side, at the descending branch of the Hadley cell), air accumulates in the column; if upper convergence exceeds low-level divergence, surface pressure rises. The excess air sinks (subsides) and diverges at the surface.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Surface highs = low-level divergence + subsidence + upper convergence.

los.lo: Describe air-mass subsidence, its effect on the environmental lapse rate, and the associated weather.
los.title: Subsidence, its effect on the ELR and weather
los.html:
Theory & physics

Sinking air warms adiabatically at DALR and dries; the upper part of a subsiding layer descends further than the lower part, so it warms more: the lapse rate becomes stable and a subsidence inversion forms (typically 3000–6000 ft, lowering over time). Weather: little cloud above the inversion, light winds, but haze, smoke and Sc (or fog/St in winter) trapped beneath.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Subsidence explains clear skies in highs but also persistent poor visibility and anticyclonic gloom.

los.lo: Describe the formation of warm and cold anticyclones.
los.title: Formation of warm and cold anticyclones
los.html:
Theory & physics

Warm: dynamic, from upper convergence and subsidence; the column is warm, so the high intensifies with height (subtropical highs, blocking highs). Cold: thermal, from intense radiative cooling of air over snow-covered continents in winter; the column is cold and dense, so pressure is high at the surface but the system weakens with height and becomes a low aloft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Siberian high: cold, shallow; Azores high: warm, deep.

los.lo: Describe the formation of ridges.
los.title: Formation of ridges
los.html:
Theory & physics

A ridge is an elongated extension of a high, typically between two depressions moving through the westerlies (the cold air behind one low and ahead of the next); associated with subsidence and divergence at the surface; moves with the depression family.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Isobars U-shaped (rounded) around the ridge axis; wind backs at ridge passage (NH) after veering in the preceding trough.

los.lo: Describe the properties of and the weather associated with warm and cold anticyclones.
los.title: Weather in warm and cold anticyclones
los.html:
Theory & physics

Warm high: fine, settled weather, light winds, little cloud or Sc under the inversion; summer: heat, haze, possible isolated TS at the edges; winter over land: fog, St, anticyclonic gloom. Cold high: very cold, dry, clear skies, severe frosts, radiation fog/ice fog, poor visibility in smoke haze; low St under the inversion.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Winter highs: fog/St at dawn closing many aerodromes; good flying conditions above the inversion.

los.lo: Describe the properties of and the weather associated with ridges.
los.title: Weather in ridges
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fair weather interval between fronts: subsidence clears cloud, light winds, good visibility (fresh polar air), radiation fog possible at night in winter; short-lived as the next front approaches (cirrus increasing on the western side).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Good VFR window; plan for the next frontal system arriving within 12–24 h.

los.lo: Describe the blocking anticyclone and its effects.
los.title: Blocking anticyclone and its effects
los.html:
Theory & physics

A persistent warm high at mid/high latitudes (e.g. over Scandinavia or the British Isles) that interrupts the westerly flow (omega block); depressions are deflected north and south of it and become slow-moving. Lasts days to weeks.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Effects: prolonged settled weather (heatwaves in summer, cold spells, fog and smog in winter) under the block; persistent rain where depressions stall at its flanks; unusual easterly winds over Europe.
  • Atlantic routes and tracks shift around the block.

topics.title: Thermal, orographic, polar and secondary depressions; troughs

los.lo: Describe the effect of high-level divergence in producing areas of low pressure at ground level.
los.title: High-level divergence producing surface lows
los.html:
Theory & physics

Where upper-level air diverges (ahead of upper troughs, jet exit/entrance quadrants), mass is removed from the column faster than low-level convergence replaces it, so surface pressure falls and the low deepens; air rises through the column, producing cloud and precipitation.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Deepening lows are found ahead (downstream) of upper troughs, under upper divergence.

los.lo: Describe the formation and properties of thermal, orographic (lee lows), polar and secondary depressions.
los.title: Thermal, orographic (lee), polar and secondary depressions
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Thermal low: strong surface heating over land in summer (Iberia, Sahara, N India); shallow, warm-core, weak circulation, high aloft; afternoon TS if the air is moist enough.
  • Orographic (lee) low: airflow across a mountain range; air descending on the lee side is stretched vertically and pressure falls (e.g. Genoa low south of the Alps with northerly flow, lows in the lee of the Rockies). Can develop into active depressions with severe weather.
  • Polar low: small (≈ 200–500 km), intense low in very cold arctic air over a relatively warm sea in winter; heavy snow showers, gales, Cb; forms and deepens quickly; hard to forecast.
  • Secondary low: forms within the circulation of a primary depression, often on its trailing cold front or at the triple point; may deepen rapidly and become dominant.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Genoa lows bring severe weather to the western Mediterranean, Italy and the Alps; Mistral/Bora often accompany them.
  • Secondary lows can bring worse weather than the primary.

los.lo: Describe the formation, the properties and the associated weather at troughs.
los.title: Troughs: formation, properties, weather
los.html:
Theory & physics

A trough is an elongated area of low pressure (V-shaped isobars) extending from a low, along which convergence and ascent occur. Frontal troughs contain fronts; non-frontal troughs (e.g. post-frontal troughs in polar air, upper troughs) bring bands of showers and TS. Wind veers at trough passage (NH); pressure falls ahead and rises behind.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Behind a cold front, a non-frontal trough may bring a second line of showers.
  • Upper troughs (500 hPa) drive surface development and convection.

los.lo: State the conditions necessary for the formation of tropical revolving storms.
los.title: Conditions for tropical revolving storm formation
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Sea-surface temperature ≥ 26–27 °C over a deep layer (≈ 50 m).
  • Latitude ≥ 5° (Coriolis needed for rotation); hence never on the equator.
  • High humidity through the troposphere, conditionally unstable air.
  • Weak vertical wind shear (otherwise the warm core is torn apart).
  • A pre-existing disturbance (easterly wave, ITCZ disturbance) and upper divergence.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No TRS in the S Atlantic and SE Pacific (cold currents, shear) and none within ≈ 5° of the equator.
  • TRS weaken quickly over land or cold water (energy source = latent heat from warm sea).

los.lo: State how a tropical revolving storm generally moves in its area of occurrence.
los.title: Typical movement of a TRS
los.html:
Theory & physics

Steered by the surrounding flow: in the NH, initially westward to west-north-westward with the trade winds on the equatorward side of the subtropical high (≈ 10–15 kt), then recurving poleward and north-eastward into the westerlies around the western edge of the high, accelerating (20–30+ kt). SH: mirror image (WSW then recurving SE).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • After recurvature the storm often becomes extra-tropical and can still be dangerous at mid-latitudes.

los.lo: Name the stages of the development of tropical revolving storms (tropical disturbance, tropical depression, tropical storm, severe tropical storm, tropical revolving storm).
los.title: Stages of development
los.html:
Theory & physics

  1. Tropical disturbance: organised convection, no closed circulation.
  2. Tropical depression: closed circulation, max sustained wind < 34 kt.
  3. Tropical storm: 34–47 kt (named).
  4. Severe tropical storm: 48–63 kt.
  5. Tropical revolving storm (hurricane/typhoon/cyclone): ≥ 64 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 64 kt = hurricane force (Beaufort 12).

los.lo: Describe the meteorological conditions in and near a tropical revolving storm.
los.title: Conditions in and near a TRS
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Eye: ≈ 10–40 nm diameter, light winds, little cloud, subsiding warm air, lowest pressure (can be < 920 hPa).
  • Eyewall: ring of Cb up to the tropopause around the eye, strongest winds (≥ 64 kt, up to 150+ kt), torrential rain, severe turbulence and icing.
  • Spiral rain bands: Cb/TS bands spiralling inwards, with gusts and squalls.
  • Outflow cirrus shield aloft (anticyclonic outflow); storm surge and flooding at the coast.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Strongest winds and worst weather in the eyewall, often on the right-hand (poleward/forward) side in the NH.
  • Aircraft must be evacuated or secured; aerodromes close.

los.lo: State the approximate dimensions of a tropical revolving storm.
los.title: Approximate dimensions of a TRS
los.html:
Theory & physics

Diameter of the circulation ≈ 200–500 nm (gale-force winds over ≈ 100–300 nm), eye ≈ 10–40 nm, vertical extent to the tropopause (≈ FL 500+).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Avoid by hundreds of nm, not tens.

los.lo: State that the movement of a tropical revolving storm can only rarely be forecast exactly, and that utmost care is necessary near a tropical revolving storm.
los.title: Movement rarely forecast exactly; utmost care required
los.html:
Theory & physics

Tracks can stall, loop or recurve unexpectedly; intensity can change rapidly (rapid intensification). Forecast cones widen with lead time.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use the latest TC advisories (TCAC), SIGMET (TC) and keep generous fuel and alternates.

topics.title: Origin and local names, location and period of occurrence

los.lo: List the areas of origin and occurrence of tropical revolving storms, and their specified names (hurricane, typhoon, tropical cyclone).
los.title: Areas of origin and local names
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Hurricane: North Atlantic, Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, NE Pacific (off Mexico).
  • Typhoon: NW Pacific (Philippines, China, Japan).
  • Cyclone / tropical cyclone: North Indian Ocean (Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea), South Indian Ocean (Madagascar, Mauritius), Australia, SW Pacific. (Australia: also "willy-willy" historically.)

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No TRS in the South Atlantic (rare exceptions) or SE Pacific.

los.lo: State the expected times of occurrence of tropical revolving storms in each of the source areas, and their approximate frequency.
los.title: Times of occurrence and frequency
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • N Atlantic: June–November, peak August–October; ≈ 10–15 named storms per year, ≈ 6 hurricanes.
  • NE Pacific: May/June–November.
  • NW Pacific: all year, peak July–October; most frequent basin (≈ 25–30 storms/year).
  • N Indian Ocean: April–June and October–December (before and after the SW monsoon), ≈ 5 per year.
  • S Indian Ocean, Australia, SW Pacific: November–April, peak January–March.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Bay of Bengal: two seasons (pre- and post-monsoon), little activity during the monsoon itself (strong shear).

topics.title: General circulation in the troposphere and lower stratosphere

los.lo: Describe the general tropospheric and low stratospheric circulation. (Refer to Subject 050 02 03 01)
los.title: General circulation in the troposphere and lower stratosphere
los.html:
Theory & physics

See 050.02.03.01.01 (three-cell model). Summary: Hadley cells with ITCZ ascent and subtropical subsidence; mid-latitude westerlies with travelling depressions and the polar front; polar easterlies. Upper troposphere: westerlies with subtropical and polar front jets; tropical easterlies aloft in summer. Lower stratosphere: winter westerlies (polar night jet at high levels), summer easterlies.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Climatology questions combine the circulation with seasonal shifts: know which belt dominates a region in January and July.

los.lo: Describe the characteristics of the tropical rain climate, the dry climate, the mid-latitude climate (warm temperate rain climate), the subarctic climate (cold snow forest climate) and the snow climate (polar climate).
los.title: Main climate types
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Tropical rain climate (A): warm all year (coldest month > 18 °C), high humidity, heavy convective rain (rainforest) or wet/dry seasons (savanna, monsoon).
  • Dry climate (B): evaporation exceeds precipitation; deserts and steppes; large diurnal temperature range, dust, strong heating.
  • Mid-latitude / warm temperate rain climate (C): mild winters (coldest month −3 to 18 °C), frontal precipitation; includes Mediterranean (dry summer) and maritime west-coast types.
  • Subarctic / cold snow-forest climate (D): cold winters with snow cover (coldest month < −3 °C), warm short summers; continental interiors of N America and Eurasia (taiga).
  • Snow / polar climate (E): warmest month < 10 °C; tundra and ice caps.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Spain: mainly Mediterranean (C, dry summer), with semi-arid (B) zones in the south-east.

los.lo: Explain how the seasonal movement of the sun generates the transitional climate zones.
los.title: Transitional climate zones from the seasonal movement of the sun
los.html:
Theory & physics

As the pressure and wind belts follow the sun, some regions lie in one belt in summer and another in winter: savanna (ITCZ rains in summer, dry trade winds in winter), Mediterranean (subtropical high in summer = dry; westerlies in winter = rain), monsoon regions (wind reversal).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Mediterranean winter rain comes from polar-front depressions; summer drought from the subtropical high.

los.lo: State the typical locations of each major climatic zone.
los.title: Typical locations of each climatic zone
los.html:
Theory & physics

Tropical rain ≈ 0–15° (Amazon, Congo, Indonesia; savanna/monsoon to ≈ 20°). Dry ≈ 15–35° on western sides of continents and interiors (Sahara, Arabia, Kalahari, Atacama, central Australia, SW USA). Mid-latitude ≈ 35–55° (Western Europe, Mediterranean, E USA, E China). Subarctic ≈ 50–70° continental interiors (Siberia, Canada). Polar > ≈ 65–70°, Greenland, Antarctica.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Deserts lie under the subtropical highs and on the cold-current side of continents.

topics.title: Cause and development of tropical showers and thunderstorms: humidity, temperature, tropopause

los.lo: State the conditions necessary for the formation of tropical showers and thunderstorms (mesoscale convective complex, cloud clusters).
los.title: Conditions for tropical showers and thunderstorms (MCC, cloud clusters)
los.html:
Theory & physics

High surface temperature and humidity (high θe), deep conditional instability, a high tropopause (Cb tops FL 500–600), and a lifting mechanism: convergence (ITCZ, easterly waves, sea-breeze fronts), orography, daytime heating. Convection organises into cloud clusters (hundreds of km) and mesoscale convective complexes (MCC): long-lived (> 6 h), large (cold cloud shield > 100 000 km²), often nocturnal.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Over land: afternoon/evening maximum; over sea: night/early morning maximum.
  • Embedded Cb in huge cloud shields: weather radar essential; ice-crystal icing risk.

los.lo: Describe the characteristics of tropical squall lines.
los.title: Tropical squall lines
los.html:
Theory & physics

Organised lines of Cb, several hundred km long, moving (often westward in West Africa, ≈ 20–30 kt) faster than the mean wind, with a leading gust front, sharp wind shift and gusts (40–60+ kt), sudden temperature drop, heavy rain for ≈ 1 h, then lighter stratiform rain behind. West African "line squalls" in the wet season.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Severe turbulence, wind shear, heavy rain/low visibility at aerodromes; cannot be overflown; usually cannot be circumnavigated easily.

los.lo: Explain the formation of convective cloud structures caused by convergence at the boundary of the NE and SE trade winds (Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)).
los.title: Convective structures at the ITCZ
los.html:
Theory & physics

The NE and SE trades converge at the Intertropical Convergence Zone; the converging moist, unstable air is forced to rise, producing bands and clusters of Cu/Cb, not a continuous wall. Activity is strongest over land in summer and where the convergence is strongest; weak or broken over some oceans.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The ITCZ is not a front (no temperature contrast); it is a convergence zone.

los.lo: State the typical figures for tropical surface air temperatures and humidities, and for heights of the zero-degree isotherm.
los.title: Tropical surface temperatures, humidity and freezing level
los.html:
Theory & physics

Surface temperatures ≈ 25–30 °C (higher inland in dry season), dew points ≈ 20–25 °C, RH often > 70–80 %. Freezing level ≈ 15 000–16 000 ft (≈ FL 150–160) all year.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Airframe icing confined to higher levels (above FL 150), but tropical Cb carry supercooled water and ice crystals far above that.
  • Hot, humid surface: high density altitude.

topics.title: Seasonal variations of weather and wind, typical synoptic situations

los.lo: Indicate on a map the trade winds (tropical easterlies) and describe the associated weather.
los.title: Trade winds (tropical easterlies) and weather
los.html:
Theory & physics

Steady NE (NH) and SE (SH) winds blowing from the subtropical highs towards the ITCZ, ≈ 10–20 kt, very constant. A trade-wind inversion (subsidence, ≈ 5000–8000 ft) caps convection: fair-weather Cu with flat tops, good visibility, showers mainly on windward slopes of islands; the inversion rises and weakens towards the ITCZ.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Generally good flying weather below FL 100 except near windward mountains.

los.lo: Indicate on a map the doldrums and describe the associated weather.
los.title: Doldrums
los.html:
Theory & physics

The equatorial belt of low pressure (part of the ITCZ zone, mainly over oceans) with light, variable winds or calms, hot humid air, Cb and heavy showers/TS, especially in the afternoon/night.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Associated with the ITCZ hazards: embedded Cb, heavy rain, turbulence.

los.lo: Indicate on a sketch the latitudes of subtropical high (horse latitudes) and describe the associated weather.
los.title: Subtropical highs (horse latitudes) and weather
los.html:
Theory & physics

At ≈ 25–35°, under the descending branch of the Hadley cell: subsidence, light variable winds, clear skies or low Sc under the inversion (eastern oceans), dry; deserts beneath on land; haze and dust.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Fog/St along cold-current coasts (California, Morocco, Namibia, Peru) under the subtropical highs.

los.lo: Indicate on a map the major monsoon winds.
los.title: Major monsoon winds
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • South Asia: SW monsoon June–September (wet), NE monsoon December–February (dry).
  • West Africa: SW monsoon in summer (wet), NE trade/Harmattan in winter (dry, dusty).
  • East Asia: S/SE summer monsoon (wet), N/NW winter monsoon (cold, dry from the Siberian high).
  • Northern Australia: NW monsoon December–March (wet), SE trades in winter (dry).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Map question: identify SW monsoon over India in July.

topics.title: Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), weather in the ITCZ, general seasonal movement

los.lo: Identify or indicate on a map the positions of the ITCZ in January and July.
los.title: ITCZ positions in January and July
los.html:
Theory & physics

July: furthest north over land: ≈ 15–20°N over West Africa and up to ≈ 25–30°N over India/Pakistan (monsoon trough); over the Atlantic and Pacific ≈ 5–10°N. January: south of the equator over land: ≈ 10–20°S over southern Africa, northern Australia, Brazil; over the oceans close to the equator, remaining slightly north (≈ 0–5°N) in the eastern Atlantic and Pacific.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Over the E Atlantic and E Pacific the ITCZ stays in the NH all year.
  • Largest seasonal swing over Africa and Asia (continents).

los.lo: Explain the seasonal movement of the ITCZ.
los.title: Seasonal movement of the ITCZ
los.html:
Theory & physics

Follows the zone of maximum heating (overhead sun) with a lag of ≈ 1–2 months; moves further over continents (low heat capacity) than over oceans; its position defines wet and dry seasons in the tropics.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • West Africa: ITCZ north in July (wet season, line squalls), south in January (Harmattan).

los.lo: Describe the weather and winds at the ITCZ.
los.title: Weather and winds at the ITCZ
los.html:
Theory & physics

Light, variable winds where the trades meet; Cu/Cb in lines and clusters, heavy showers, TS, tops FL 450–600; activity varies along its length; over land maximum in the afternoon/evening, over sea at night. Width varies from a narrow line to a broad zone hundreds of km wide.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Not continuous: crews choose crossing points with lower activity using satellite and radar.

los.lo: Explain the flight hazards associated with the ITCZ.
los.title: Flight hazards at the ITCZ
los.html:
Theory & physics

Severe turbulence in Cb, icing above the freezing level (≈ FL 150) including high ice water content (ice-crystal icing) in and near Cb anvils, hail, lightning, heavy rain (engine water ingestion, low visibility), wind shear, sand/dust in squalls over Africa.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Indicators of ice-crystal icing: appearance of rain on the windscreen at sub-zero temperatures, TAT anomalies, light weather radar returns in heavy IMC.

los.lo: Define in general the term ‘monsoon’ and give a general overview of regions of occurrence.
los.title: Monsoon definition and regions
los.html:
Theory & physics

A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of the prevailing wind direction (≥ 120° change) caused by the different heating of continents and oceans, with associated wet and dry seasons. Main regions: South and South-East Asia, East Asia, West Africa, northern Australia.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • "Monsoon" means the wind regime, not just the rain.

los.lo: Explain how trade winds change character after a long track and become monsoon winds.
los.title: Trade winds changing into monsoon winds after a long track
los.html:
Theory & physics

When the ITCZ moves far into the summer hemisphere, the trades of the winter hemisphere cross the equator. Coriolis changes sign, so the SE trades are deflected to the right in the NH and become SW monsoon winds (India, West Africa); the NE trades crossing into the SH become NW monsoon (N Australia). The long sea track makes them very moist and unstable.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Explains why the Indian summer monsoon is south-westerly.

los.lo: Explain the weather and the flight hazards associated with a monsoon.
los.title: Monsoon weather and flight hazards
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wet (summer) monsoon: deep moist unstable air, extensive cloud (Cu, Cb, Ns), heavy and prolonged rain, TS, low ceilings and visibility, embedded Cb, flooding; onset often violent. Dry (winter) monsoon: dry offshore flow, fair, haze, dust, fog in some areas (N India).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Wet monsoon: contaminated runways, wind shear, heavy-rain engine ingestion, poor visibility. Dry monsoon: haze/fog reduce visibility (e.g. Delhi winter fog).

los.lo: Explain the formation of the SW/NE monsoon over West Africa and describe the weather, stressing the seasonal differences.
los.title: West African monsoon (SW/NE)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Summer (≈ June–September): ITCZ at ≈ 15–20°N; moist SW monsoon flow from the Gulf of Guinea; rainy season, line squalls moving westward, TS; south of the ITCZ low cloud and drizzle near the coast. Winter (≈ November–March): ITCZ near the Guinea coast; dry NE Harmattan from the Sahara: dust haze, visibility often < 1000 m, little cloud.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Visibility hazard in winter (Harmattan), convective hazard in summer (line squalls).

los.lo: Explain the formation of the SW/NE monsoon over India and describe the weather, stressing the seasonal differences.
los.title: Indian monsoon (SW/NE)
los.html:
Theory & physics

SW monsoon (June–September): the Asian thermal low and the northward ITCZ draw moist air from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal; onset early June in Kerala, covering India by mid-July; heavy rain on the west coast (Western Ghats) and in the north-east; Cb, TS, monsoon depressions; tropical cyclones in the Bay of Bengal before and after. NE monsoon (December–February): dry outflow from the Siberian high, fair weather, fog and haze in the north (Ganges plain); rain only on SE India and Sri Lanka (flow over the Bay of Bengal).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Delhi: TS in the SW monsoon (and pre-monsoon dust storms), dense fog in winter.

los.lo: Explain the formation of the monsoon over the Far East and northern Australia and describe the weather, stressing the seasonal differences.
los.title: Far East and northern Australia monsoons
los.html:
Theory & physics

East Asia: summer S/SE monsoon (wet, "Baiu/Meiyu" front rains in June–July over China/Japan), typhoons July–October; winter N/NW monsoon from the Siberian high: cold, dry over the mainland, snow on the Japan Sea coast after crossing the sea. Northern Australia: NW monsoon December–March (wet season, TS, cyclones), SE trades April–October (dry).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Strongest winter jet streams over Japan are linked to the strong continental winter monsoon contrast.

los.lo: Describe the formation and properties of sandstorms.
los.title: Sandstorms
los.html:
Theory & physics

Strong surface winds (> ≈ 15–20 kt) over dry, loose sand/dust lift particles in unstable, well-mixed air. Causes: Cb outflow (gust fronts: haboob), cold fronts, strong gradient winds, local winds (Harmattan, Khamsin, Shamal, Ghibli). Dust can rise to FL 100–150 and travel thousands of km.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • METAR: DS (dust storm), SS (sandstorm), BLSA/BLDU, +DS/+SS for visibility < 200 m.
  • Hazards: visibility < 1000 m, abrasion, engine erosion, pitot/static blockage, lightning-free "dust walls".

los.lo: Indicate when and where outbreaks of cold polar air can enter subtropical weather systems.
los.title: Cold polar air outbreaks into subtropical systems
los.html:
Theory & physics

In winter, cold air can surge far equatorward behind strong cold fronts, especially along the eastern sides of continents and across open plains: North America (to Gulf of Mexico/Central America: "northers"), South America (Pampas), East Asia (cold surges to the South China Sea), northern India. Brings sharp temperature falls, strong winds, sometimes snow at low latitudes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Gusty winds, low-level turbulence, icing and snow where not normally expected.

los.lo: Name well-known examples of polar-air outbreaks (Blizzard, Pampero).
los.title: Examples: Blizzard, Pampero
los.html:
Theory & physics

Blizzard: North American winter storm with strong winds (≥ 30–35 kt), heavy falling or blowing snow, very low visibility (≤ 400 m) and severe cold, behind deep lows/cold fronts. Pampero: cold, strong SW wind over the Argentine/Uruguayan pampas behind a cold front, often with a squall line, TS and a sharp temperature drop.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Pampero = South America; Blizzard = North America (exam matching).

los.lo: Explain the effect of easterly waves on tropical weather systems.
los.title: Easterly waves
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wave-shaped troughs in the trade-wind easterlies, moving westward at ≈ 10–15 kt, wavelength ≈ 2000–4000 km, period 3–4 days. Ahead (west) of the trough axis: divergence, fair weather. Behind (east) of the axis: convergence, deep Cb, showers and TS, the trade inversion lifts. Many N Atlantic hurricanes develop from African easterly waves.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Weather is worst behind (east of) the wave axis, opposite to a mid-latitude trough expectation.

subs.title: Typical weather situations in the mid-latitudes

los.lo: Identify on a weather chart the typical westerly situation with travelling polar front waves.
los.title: Westerly situation with travelling polar-front waves
los.html:
Theory & physics

Strong zonal westerly flow at mid-latitudes, with a family of frontal depressions forming on the polar front and moving rapidly east (≈ 25–40 kt), separated by transient ridges. On the surface chart: closely spaced, roughly W–E isobars, several lows in a row from the Atlantic to Scandinavia.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Weather changes every 1–2 days: frontal rain, then showers, then a brief ridge; strong winds and tailwinds eastbound.

los.lo: Describe the high-pressure zones with the associated weather.
los.title: High-pressure zones and associated weather
los.html:
Theory & physics

Subtropical highs (Azores) extending ridges over Europe, continental winter highs, blocking highs. Weather: subsidence, light winds, dry; summer: sunny, hot, haze, isolated TS at the edges; winter: fog, low St, frost, inversions trapping pollution.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • See 050.07.02.01.06 for warm/cold high weather.

los.lo: Identify on a weather chart the high-pressure regions.
los.title: Identify high-pressure regions on a chart
los.html:
Theory & physics

Closed isobars with pressure increasing towards the centre (H), widely spaced isobars, ridges as U-shaped extensions; clockwise circulation in the NH; often no fronts near the centre.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Combine with station data: small T/Td spread and calm wind under a winter high = fog forecast.

los.lo: Define ‘cold-air drop’.
los.title: Define cold-air drop (cut-off low)
los.html:
Theory & physics

A cold-air drop (cold pool, cut-off low; in Spain DANA, "depósito aislado en niveles altos") is an isolated pool of cold air in the middle and upper troposphere, with a closed cyclonic circulation aloft, cut off from the main westerly flow.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Often has little or no signature on the surface chart.

los.lo: Describe the formation of a cold-air drop.
los.title: Formation of a cold-air drop
los.html:
Theory & physics

An upper trough in a meandering (high-amplitude) westerly flow deepens and stretches equatorward; its southern part becomes separated (cut off) from the westerlies as the flow north of it reconnects. The cold-core low then drifts slowly and erratically, often for several days, until reabsorbed or filled.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Movement is slow and hard to forecast; may even move westward.

los.lo: Identify cold-air drops on weather charts.
los.title: Identify cold-air drops on charts
los.html:
Theory & physics

On upper-air charts (500/300 hPa): closed low contours with a cold centre (closed isotherms), separated from the main westerly belt. On the surface chart: a weak low, a trough or even slack pressure/high pressure. On satellite: a comma or spiral of convective cloud.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Always check upper charts: the surface chart alone can look harmless.

los.lo: Explain the problems and dangers of cold-air drops for aviation.
los.title: Problems and dangers of cold-air drops
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cold air aloft over a warm surface (or warm sea, e.g. the Mediterranean in autumn) gives strong instability: severe Cb, hail, heavy and persistent rain (flash floods, the Spanish Mediterranean coast in autumn), icing and turbulence; the area of bad weather moves slowly and unpredictably.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Forecasts are unreliable; carry extra fuel and choose alternates outside the cold-air drop area.
  • Severe weather can occur without fronts.

los.lo: Describe the mechanism for the development of Foehn winds (including Chinook).
los.title: Mechanism of Föhn winds (including Chinook)
los.html:
Theory & physics

See 050.03.03.01.08 and its diagram. Moist air ascends the windward side (DALR, then SALR in cloud with precipitation), descends dry on the lee side at DALR: warmer and drier than at the same level on the windward side. A second mechanism: the lee air may come from a higher, potentially warmer level (blocked low-level air on the windward side). Chinook = Föhn east of the Rocky Mountains; others: Zonda (Andes), Berg wind (South Africa).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Chinook can raise temperature by 20 °C in hours and melt snow rapidly ("snow eater").

los.lo: Describe the weather associated with Foehn winds.
los.title: Weather associated with Föhn
los.html:
Theory & physics

Windward: extensive cloud and precipitation, mountains obscured (Föhn wall). Lee: warm, dry, gusty wind, low RH, excellent visibility, clear Föhn gap in the cloud, lenticular clouds; mountain waves and rotors.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Lee aerodromes: strong gusty crosswinds, wind shear and severe turbulence despite clear skies.

los.lo: Describe the formation of, the characteristics of, and the weather associated with Mistral and Bora.
los.title: Mistral and Bora
los.html:
Theory & physics

Mistral: cold, dry, strong N/NW wind blowing down the Rhône valley into the Gulf of Lion, funnelled between the Alps and the Massif Central (Venturi) and partly katabatic. Occurs when a cold air outbreak follows a cold front, with high pressure over France/Biscay and low pressure over the Gulf of Genoa. Speeds often 30–50 kt, gusts 60–80+ kt; clear skies, excellent visibility; extends well out over the sea. Related: Tramontane (Languedoc/Catalonia). Bora: cold, dry, very gusty NE katabatic wind descending from the Dinaric Alps onto the Adriatic coast (Trieste, Croatia), when cold air pools over the Balkan plateau with low pressure over the Adriatic; gusts can exceed 100 kt; often cloudless or with a cloud cap on the mountains.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Hazards: severe low-level turbulence, strong crosswinds, wind shear, sea spray icing on ships; aerodromes such as Marseille, Montpellier, Split, Trieste affected.
  • Mistral = Rhône/France; Bora = Adriatic/Croatia (matching question).

los.lo: Describe the Harmattan wind and the associated visibility problems as an example of local winds affecting visibility.
los.title: Harmattan and visibility
los.html:
Theory & physics

The Harmattan is the dry, dusty NE (trade) wind blowing from the Sahara over West Africa in the dry season (≈ November–March), when the ITCZ lies near the Gulf of Guinea. It carries fine dust, sometimes to FL 100–150, producing extensive dust haze that can persist for days.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Visibility often 1000–3000 m and at times < 1000 m over large areas; very poor slant visibility on approach; METAR HZ/DU.
  • Little cloud: the hazard is visibility, not convection.

los.lo: Summarise the general conditions under which ice accretion occurs on aircraft (temperatures of outside air; temperature of the airframe; presence of supercooled water in clouds, fog, rain and drizzle; possibility of sublimation).
los.title: General conditions for ice accretion
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ice accretes when (1) the airframe surface is at or below 0 °C and (2) supercooled liquid water is present (cloud, fog, drizzle, rain) or water vapour can deposit directly as ice (sublimation/deposition, hoar frost). OAT range for airframe icing: practically 0 to −40 °C, most frequent and severe 0 to −15 °C. The airframe can be colder than the air (cold soak) or warmer (kinetic heating at high speed).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • OAT slightly above 0 °C can still give icing on a cold-soaked surface or on probes cooled by expansion.
  • Engine/airframe anti-ice activation per AFM: typically visible moisture and TAT/OAT ≤ +10 °C (jet) or ≤ +5 °C.

los.lo: Explain the general weather conditions under which ice accretion occurs in a venturi carburettor.
los.title: Carburettor icing
los.html:
Theory & physics

In a venturi carburettor, the pressure drop in the venturi (adiabatic cooling) and the evaporation of fuel (latent heat) cool the intake air by up to ≈ 20–30 °C. If the air is humid, water vapour condenses and freezes in the venturi and on the throttle valve. Possible from ≈ −10 °C to +30 °C OAT, most likely with high humidity (small spread) and OAT ≈ 0 to +20 °C, worst at low power (partly closed throttle) and in descent; can occur in clear air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "carburettor icing needs sub-zero OAT". It is most common well above 0 °C.
  • Use carb heat as per POH (expect RPM drop then rise when ice melts).

los.lo: Explain the general weather conditions under which ice accretion occurs on airframe.
los.title: Weather conditions for airframe icing
los.html:
Theory & physics

Flight in cloud or precipitation containing supercooled water: Cu/Cb, Ns, Sc, St, As at sub-zero temperatures; freezing rain/drizzle below warm-front inversions; freezing fog. Severity rises with liquid water content, drop size and temperature near 0 to −10 °C.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Worst icing situations: Cb, FZRA beneath warm fronts, SLD in St/Sc, orographic cloud.

los.lo: Explain the formation of supercooled water in clouds, rain and drizzle. (Refer to Subject 050 03 02 01)
los.title: Formation of supercooled water in clouds, rain and drizzle
los.html:
Theory & physics

Droplets cooled below 0 °C stay liquid because freezing nuclei are scarce (see 050.03.02.01.09). In cloud, rising air cools droplets below 0 °C. In freezing rain, rain from a warm layer falls into sub-zero air and supercools. Freezing drizzle often forms within supercooled St/Sc by coalescence.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Supercooled large drops (SLD) can exceed the certification envelope (CS-25 App. C vs App. O).

los.lo: Explain qualitatively the relationship between the air temperature and the amount of supercooled water.
los.title: Air temperature vs amount of supercooled water
los.html:
Theory & physics

The colder the air, the less water vapour it can hold and the more freezing nuclei become active, so the amount of supercooled water decreases with decreasing temperature: greatest from 0 to −10 °C, moderate to −20 °C, small below −20 °C (except in strong Cb updrafts), practically nil below −40 °C.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Escape strategy: climb to colder levels (< −20 °C) or descend into above-freezing air.

los.lo: Explain qualitatively the relationship between the type of cloud and the size and number of the droplets in cumuliform and stratiform clouds.
los.title: Cloud type vs droplet size and number
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cumuliform clouds: strong updrafts sustain large droplets and high liquid water content (up to several g/m³): rapid accretion over short horizontal extents. Stratiform clouds: weak updrafts, small droplets, lower water content (≈ 0.1–0.5 g/m³) but over large horizontal extents.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cumuliform → clear ice, intense but brief; stratiform → rime, lighter but prolonged.

los.lo: Indicate in which circumstances ice can form on an aircraft on the ground: air temperature, humidity, precipitation.
los.title: Ice on aircraft on the ground
los.html:
Theory & physics

Possible when surface temperature ≤ 0 °C (and up to ≈ +3/+5 °C OAT with cold-soaked wings) with: frost (clear night, high humidity, surface below frost point), freezing fog, snow, sleet, freezing drizzle/rain, rain or high humidity on cold-soaked surfaces, blown snow/slush from taxiing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Clean aircraft concept: no take-off with frost, ice or snow on critical surfaces; de-/anti-icing and holdover times.

los.lo: Explain in which circumstances ice can form on an aircraft in flight: inside clouds, in precipitation, and outside clouds and precipitation.
los.title: Ice in flight: in cloud, in precipitation, outside cloud
los.html:
Theory & physics

In cloud: supercooled droplets. In precipitation: freezing rain/drizzle (also below cloud), wet snow. Outside cloud and precipitation: hoar frost when an aircraft cold-soaked at altitude descends into warm, moist air (deposition), or after flying from a cold to a warm humid layer.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Icing can occur in clear air: hoar frost on descent and FZRA below cloud base.

los.lo: Explain the influence of fuel temperature, radiative cooling of the aircraft surface and temperature of the aircraft surface (e.g. from previous flight) on ice formation.
los.title: Fuel temperature, radiative cooling, previous flight
los.html:
Theory & physics

After long flights at cold altitude, fuel in the wing tanks stays very cold (≈ −20 °C or below); the wing skin over the tanks remains sub-zero on the ground, so rain, drizzle or humid air can freeze on it (cold-soak wing ice, clear and hard to see). Clear-sky radiative cooling can cool surfaces several degrees below air temperature (frost).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cold-soak ice can form on the upper wing at OAT up to ≈ +10/+15 °C; check by tactile inspection where required.

los.lo: Describe the different factors that influence the intensity of icing: air temperature, amount of supercooled water in a cloud or in precipitation, amount of ice crystals in the air, speed of the aircraft, shape (thickness) of the airframe parts (wings, antennas, etc.).
los.title: Factors influencing icing intensity
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Liquid water content (more water = faster accretion).
  • Drop size (larger drops impinge more and further aft).
  • Temperature (0 to −10 °C worst; colder = smaller amounts).
  • Ice crystals present: glaciated cloud reduces supercooled water (but ice crystals can still be ingested by engines).
  • Aircraft speed: higher speed sweeps more water (more accretion) but raises surface temperature by kinetic heating (≈ +1 °C at 100 kt TAS, ≈ +10 °C at 300 kt).
  • Shape: thin objects (antennas, probes, tailplane, thin wing leading edges) have high collection efficiency and ice faster than thick wings.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Tailplane collects ice before the wing → tailplane stall with flap extension.

los.lo: Explain the effects of topography on icing.
los.title: Effects of topography on icing
los.html:
Theory & physics

Orographic lifting produces strong, persistent upward motion on the windward side, condensing more water and keeping large drops supported; the freezing level may be lower over mountains (cold air pooling); escape options limited by MSA.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most severe icing on windward slopes and just above ridge level.

los.lo: Explain the higher concentration of water drops in stratiform orographic clouds.
los.title: High water concentration in stratiform orographic clouds
los.html:
Theory & physics

Continuous forced ascent over the mountain keeps supplying vapour, which condenses into a high concentration of droplets even in stable stratiform cloud; liquid water content can approach that of cumuliform cloud.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "stratiform cloud = always light icing". Orographic stratiform cloud can give moderate to severe icing.

los.lo: Define ‘clear ice’.
los.title: Define clear ice
los.html:
Theory & physics

Clear (glaze) ice: a smooth, transparent or translucent, dense, heavy layer of ice formed when large supercooled drops freeze slowly, spreading over the surface before freezing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most dangerous type: heavy, adheres strongly, hard to remove, may form horns.

los.lo: Describe the conditions for the formation of clear ice.
los.title: Conditions for clear ice
los.html:
Theory & physics

Large drops, high liquid water content, temperatures 0 to ≈ −10 °C (up to ≈ −15 °C in Cb); typical in Cu, Cb, Ns and in freezing rain.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • FZRA always gives clear ice (glaze).

los.lo: Explain the formation of the structure of clear ice with the release of latent heat during the freezing process.
los.title: Clear ice structure: latent heat release
los.html:
Theory & physics

A large drop striking the surface freezes only partly at first (≈ 1/80 of the drop per °C of supercooling); the released latent heat warms the rest towards 0 °C, so the unfrozen water flows back along the surface and then freezes, leaving no trapped air: dense, clear ice and runback behind protected areas.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Runback ice beyond the de-icing boots/heated zone disrupts the airflow over the wing.

los.lo: Describe the aspects of clear ice: appearance, weight, solidity.
los.title: Clear ice: appearance, weight, solidity
los.html:
Theory & physics

Transparent/glossy, smooth or lumpy with horns; heavy (density close to 0.9 g/cm³); very hard and strongly adhering.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Difficult to see on wings; often only detected by ice detectors or on wipers/probes.

los.lo: Define ‘rime ice’.
los.title: Define rime ice
los.html:
Theory & physics

Rime ice: white, opaque, rough, granular ice formed when small supercooled droplets freeze instantly on impact, trapping air between the frozen particles.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Builds forward into the airflow on leading edges and probes.

los.lo: Describe the conditions for the formation of rime ice.
los.title: Conditions for rime ice
los.html:
Theory & physics

Small droplets, low liquid water content, temperatures ≈ −10 to −20 °C (or colder); typical in St, Sc, As and freezing fog.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Rime in stratiform cloud can accumulate over long periods; blocks pitot/static ports and air intakes.

los.lo: Describe the aspects of rime ice: appearance, weight, solidity.
los.title: Rime ice: appearance, weight, solidity
los.html:
Theory & physics

White, opaque, rough/feathery; light (porous, air inclusions); brittle, relatively easy to remove by de-icing systems.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Less dangerous than clear ice for weight, but rough shape still degrades lift and increases drag.

los.lo: Define ‘mixed ice’.
los.title: Define mixed ice
los.html:
Theory & physics

Mixed ice: a mixture of clear and rime ice (layers or patches), often with snow or ice crystals embedded, formed when drop sizes vary or ice crystals and supercooled drops are present together.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Rough and solid: severe aerodynamic penalty.

los.lo: Describe the conditions for the formation of mixed ice.
los.title: Conditions for mixed ice
los.html:
Theory & physics

Temperatures typically ≈ −10 to −15 °C, varying droplet sizes, mixed-phase cloud (Cu, Ns, frontal cloud), snow mixed with supercooled drops.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Common in frontal Ns and in Cb flanks.

los.lo: Describe the aspects of mixed ice: appearance, weight, solidity.
los.title: Mixed ice: appearance, weight, solidity
los.html:
Theory & physics

Whitish/cloudy, rough, irregular shapes; fairly heavy; hard and adherent (between clear and rime).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Can form large irregular horns quickly.

los.lo: Describe the possible process of ice formation in snow conditions.
los.title: Ice formation in snow conditions
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dry snow at low temperatures usually does not stick. Wet snow (near 0 °C) and snow mixed with supercooled drops stick and freeze, building heavy deposits on leading edges, windscreens and in engine intakes; on the ground snow accumulates and may melt and refreeze on cold surfaces.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Wet snow can block intakes and pitot heads; de-icing fluid holdover times are short in snow.

los.lo: Define ‘hoar frost’.
los.title: Define hoar frost
los.html:
Theory & physics

Hoar frost: a white, crystalline (feathery) deposit of ice formed by deposition of water vapour directly onto a surface whose temperature is below the frost point.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No liquid phase: it forms in clear air.

los.lo: Describe the conditions for the formation of hoar frost.
los.title: Conditions for hoar frost
los.html:
Theory & physics

On the ground: clear, calm night, surface cooled by radiation below 0 °C and below the frost point. In flight: a cold-soaked aircraft descending rapidly from cold altitude into warmer, moist air; or climbing from a cold layer into a warmer moist layer (inversion).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Windscreen can frost over suddenly on descent; use windscreen heat early.

los.lo: Describe the aspects of hoar frost: appearance, solidity.
los.title: Hoar frost: appearance, solidity
los.html:
Theory & physics

White, feathery, crystalline; thin and light; loosely adhering, easily removed (though it must be removed before take-off).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Even a thin layer of frost on the upper wing (sandpaper roughness) can reduce max lift by up to ≈ 30 % and increase stall speed.

los.lo: State the ICAO qualifying terms for the intensity of icing.
los.title: ICAO intensity terms for icing
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Light: rate of accumulation may create a problem if flight is prolonged; occasional use of de-/anti-icing removes/prevents it.
  • Moderate: rate such that even short encounters become potentially hazardous; use of de-/anti-icing or diversion necessary.
  • Severe: rate such that de-/anti-icing equipment fails to reduce or control the hazard; immediate diversion/exit necessary.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • SIGMET is issued for SEV ICE (and SEV ICE (FZRA)); AIRMET/GAMET for MOD ICE.

los.lo: Describe, in general, the hazards of icing.
los.title: General hazards of icing
los.html:
Theory & physics

Loss of lift and higher stall speed (stall at a lower AoA), drag increase, weight increase, controllability problems (aileron/elevator hinge moments, tailplane stall), propeller and engine icing (power loss, damage from shed ice), blocked pitot/static and AoA sensors (unreliable instruments), windscreen obscuration, antenna damage, landing-gear and brake icing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stall warning may not protect an iced wing: add approach speed increments per AFM; avoid autopilot masking of control anomalies in severe icing.

los.lo: Assess the dangers of the different types of ice accretion.
los.title: Dangers of the different types of ice
los.html:
Theory & physics

Clear: most dangerous (heavy, adherent, runback beyond protection, horns). Mixed: severe roughness/shape penalty. Rime: blocks probes and intakes, lighter. Hoar frost: dangerous mainly on take-off (lift loss). SLD/FZRA: accretion aft of protected areas, beyond certification.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Priority: leave clear-icing/FZRA conditions immediately.

los.lo: Describe the position of the dangerous zones of icing in fronts, in stratiform and cumuliform clouds, and in the different precipitation types.
los.title: Dangerous icing zones in fronts, clouds and precipitation
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Warm front: FZRA/FZDZ in the cold air beneath the frontal inversion ahead of the surface front; moderate to severe icing in Ns/As near and above the freezing level.
  • Cold front / occlusion: severe clear icing in Cb and TCU along the front.
  • Cumuliform cloud: mid and upper part of the updraft region between 0 and −20 °C (highest water content).
  • Stratiform cloud: near the top of the cloud (largest drops) between 0 and −15 °C.
  • Precipitation: freezing rain and drizzle below the cloud; wet snow near 0 °C.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • See the warm and cold front cross-sections in 050.06.02.
  • In stratiform cloud, descending a short distance below the tops often reduces icing.

los.lo: Indicate the possibilities of avoiding dangerous zones of icing: in the flight planning: weather briefing, selection of track and altitude; during flight: recognition of the dangerous zones, selection of appropriate track and altitude.
los.title: Avoiding dangerous icing zones
los.html:
Theory & physics

Planning: weather briefing (freezing levels, SIGMET/AIRMET/GAMET, SWC icing areas, PIREPs), choose a route/FL with temperatures above 0 °C, below −20 °C, or out of cloud; consider aircraft certification for known icing; avoid FZRA areas. In flight: recognise accretion early (visual cues, ice detector, airspeed decay), activate anti-ice, change level (climb above tops, into a warm layer, or to colder air), change route, leave FZRA immediately (180° turn or climb into the warm layer if known).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Have an escape plan before entering icing conditions; non-certified aircraft must avoid known icing.

los.lo: Describe ice crystal icing.
los.title: Ice-crystal icing
los.html:
Theory & physics

At high altitudes in and near large convective systems, air may contain very high concentrations of small ice crystals with little supercooled water. Crystals entering a turbofan core partly melt on warm compressor surfaces; the wetted surface then captures more crystals and ice accretes inside the engine (ice accretion in the core), causing power loss, rollback, surge or flame-out and damage. Air-data probes (pitot, TAT) can also be affected.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Airframe usually shows little or no visible ice; airframe ice detectors may not trigger.

los.lo: Describe the atmospheric processes leading to high ice crystal concentration. Define the variable ice water content (IWC).
los.title: Processes leading to high ice-crystal concentration; IWC
los.html:
Theory & physics

Strong, deep convective updrafts carry large amounts of water to high levels where it freezes into many small crystals, which detrain into anvils and stratiform regions downwind. Ice water content (IWC) = mass of ice crystals per unit volume of air (g/m³); engine events are associated with high IWC (> ≈ 1 g/m³, up to ≈ 3+ g/m³).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • High IWC is not shown on weather radar as heavy returns (small crystals reflect weakly).

los.lo: Identify weather situations and their relevant areas where high concentrations of ice crystals are likely to occur.
los.title: Where high ice-crystal concentrations occur
los.html:
Theory & physics

Large tropical convective systems (MCS, ITCZ, monsoon, tropical cyclones), especially over warm oceans; above and downwind of Cb cores; in anvils; typically at altitudes above ≈ FL 200 and temperatures ≈ −10 to −50 °C, often near or above the freezing level in deep moist tropical air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most events occur in tropical and subtropical regions, at cruise altitudes.

los.lo: Name, in general, the flight hazards associated with high concentrations of ice crystals.
los.title: Flight hazards of high ice-crystal concentrations
los.html:
Theory & physics

Engine power loss/rollback/flame-out (often multiple engines), engine damage, air-data errors (pitot icing → unreliable airspeed, autopilot/autothrust disconnect), TAT anomaly (sticks near 0 °C), windscreen "rain" at sub-zero temperatures, light to moderate turbulence.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Recognition cues: appearance of precipitation on the windscreen at very low temperatures, St. Elmo's fire, ozone-like smell, TAT stuck near 0 °C.

los.lo: Explain how a pilot may possibly avoid areas with a high concentration of ice crystals.
los.title: Avoiding areas of high ice-crystal concentration
los.html:
Theory & physics

Avoid flying over and downwind of convective cores and through anvils; use weather radar tilt to look below the flight level (cores below) and increase gain; deviate upwind of Cb; treat areas of weak returns adjacent to strong cells with suspicion; follow manufacturer procedures (engine anti-ice, ignition).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Weak radar return in dense high-altitude IMC near Cb = possible high IWC zone.

los.lo: State the ICAO qualifying terms for the intensity of turbulence.
los.title: ICAO intensity terms for turbulence
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Light: slight, erratic changes in altitude/attitude; occupants may feel a slight strain against seat belts; loose objects remain at rest.
  • Moderate: changes in altitude/attitude but the aircraft remains in positive control; variations in indicated airspeed; occupants feel definite strains against belts; unsecured objects dislodged; walking difficult.
  • Severe: abrupt, large changes in altitude/attitude; large airspeed variations; aircraft may be momentarily out of control; occupants forced violently against belts.
  • (Extreme: aircraft violently tossed, practically impossible to control, possible structural damage.)

Exam traps & operational impact

  • SEV TURB triggers a SIGMET; MOD TURB appears in AIRMET/GAMET and SWC.

los.lo: Describe the effects of turbulence on an aircraft in flight.
los.title: Effects of turbulence on aircraft
los.html:
Theory & physics

Rapid variations in load factor (gust loads ∝ gust velocity × TAS × lift-curve slope), airspeed and altitude excursions, possible exceedance of structural limits or stall (high gust at low speed), crew/passenger injuries, loss of control, increased workload and instrument reading errors.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Fly the turbulence penetration speed (VRA/VB): balances stall margin against structural margin; maintain attitude, not altitude; autothrust off if recommended.

los.lo: Indicate the possibilities of avoiding turbulence: in the flight planning: weather briefing, selection of track and altitude; during flight: selection of appropriate track and altitude.
los.title: Avoiding turbulence
los.html:
Theory & physics

Planning: SWC turbulence/CAT/CB areas, jet stream positions, SIGMET/AIRMET, PIREPs, mountain-wave forecasts; choose route and FL away from jets, Cb, mountains in strong winds, low-level inversions with shear. In flight: change FL (often ≥ 2000–4000 ft) or track, use airborne radar for Cb, request ride reports from ATC, secure cabin early.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cb: avoid by ≥ 10 nm (≥ 20 nm for severe or at high levels), overfly by ≥ 5000 ft if possible.

los.lo: Describe atmospheric turbulence and distinguish between turbulence, gustiness and wind shear.
los.title: Turbulence vs gustiness vs wind shear
los.html:
Theory & physics

Turbulence: random, irregular three-dimensional eddies; mainly loads the structure and causes bumps. Gustiness: short-period fluctuations of the surface wind about its mean (turbulence near the ground as seen by an anemometer). Wind shear: a change of wind speed and/or direction over a distance (vertical or horizontal), including up/downdrafts; it changes the aircraft's airspeed and energy state and can produce turbulence.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Wind shear threatens performance (energy loss near the ground) more than structure.

los.lo: Describe that forecasts of turbulence are not very reliable and state that pilot reports of turbulence are very valuable as they help others to prepare for or avoid turbulence.
los.title: Turbulence forecasts are not very reliable; pilot reports are valuable
los.html:
Theory & physics

Turbulence occurs on small scales (hundreds of m to tens of km) and short time-scales, below the resolution of forecast models; forecasts are probabilistic. Pilot reports (AIREPs, special air-reports, automated EDR data) are the main observations and allow others to prepare or avoid.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Always report moderate or severe turbulence with position, FL, time and aircraft type.

topics.title: Clear-air turbulence (CAT): effects on flight, avoidance

los.lo: Describe the effects of CAT on flight. (Refer to Subject 050 02 06 03)
los.title: Effects of CAT on flight
los.html:
Theory & physics

Sudden onset without visual cue, usually light to moderate but occasionally severe; vertical accelerations can injure unbelted occupants; airspeed fluctuations at high altitude can approach buffet limits (low-speed and Mach buffet margins narrow at high FL); altitude excursions.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Seat belts fastened when seated at all times; reduce to turbulence speed while protecting buffet margins (consider descending).

los.lo: Indicate the possibilities of avoiding CAT in flight: in the flight planning: weather briefing, selection of track and altitude; during flight: selection of appropriate track and altitude.
los.title: Avoiding CAT
los.html:
Theory & physics

Planning: SWC CAT areas and jet streams, upper wind charts (strong vertical/horizontal shear, tight isotachs), tropopause breaks, upper troughs with sharp curvature, mountain-wave areas, PIREPs. In flight: change FL by 2000–4000 ft, move away from the jet core (often towards the warm/equatorward side), avoid areas of rapid temperature change, use ATC and company reports.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • If climbing/descending makes the temperature change rapidly, you are crossing a frontal/jet zone.

los.lo: Define ‘wind shear’ (vertical and horizontal).
los.title: Define wind shear (vertical and horizontal)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wind shear: a change in wind speed and/or direction over a short distance, including updrafts and downdrafts. Vertical shear: change with height (kt per 100 ft or per 1000 ft). Horizontal shear: change along a horizontal distance (kt per nm). For an aircraft the critical quantity is the rate of change of headwind/tailwind component and of vertical wind along its flight path.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Up/downdrafts are part of wind shear (e.g. microburst).

los.lo: Define ‘low-level wind shear’.
los.title: Define low-level wind shear
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wind shear along the final approach path or along the runway and the take-off/initial climb path, typically below ≈ 1600 ft (500 m) AGL, where aircraft are at low energy and low height.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Reported in METAR supplementary information: WS R24 or WS ALL RWY; also by ATIS, ATC and LLWAS/Doppler radar alerts.

los.lo: Describe the conditions, where and how wind shear can form (e.g. thunderstorms, squall lines, fronts, inversions, land and sea breeze, friction layer, relief).
los.title: Where and how wind shear forms
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Thunderstorms: downbursts/microbursts, gust fronts up to ≈ 10–20 nm from the cell.
  • Squall lines and active cold fronts: sharp wind shifts and gusts.
  • Fronts: change of wind across the frontal surface (most marked at fast cold fronts; at warm fronts below the inversion).
  • Low-level inversions: calm surface air beneath a strong wind above (night radiation inversion, low-level jet).
  • Land/sea breeze fronts.
  • Friction layer: strong winds over rough terrain.
  • Relief: mountain waves, rotors, lee eddies, buildings/hangars near the runway.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most dangerous: microbursts during approach and take-off.

los.lo: Describe the effects of wind shear on flight.
los.title: Effects of wind shear on flight
los.html:
Theory & physics

Because of inertia, the aircraft keeps its ground speed at first, so a change in headwind changes IAS immediately. Increasing headwind / decreasing tailwind: IAS increases, lift increases, aircraft goes above the path (performance-increasing shear). Decreasing headwind / increasing tailwind: IAS decreases, lift decreases, aircraft sinks below the path (performance-decreasing shear). Downdraft: direct loss of height and AoA change. A microburst combines all three in sequence.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: reducing thrust in the initial headwind gain (the classic accident sequence); the following tailwind and downdraft then cannot be recovered.
  • Performance-decreasing shear is the dangerous one near the ground.

los.lo: Indicate the possibilities of avoiding wind shear in flight: in the flight planning; during flight.
los.title: Avoiding wind shear
los.html:
Theory & physics

Planning: TAF/METAR (TS, CB, +SHRA, strong gusts, WS reports), SIGMET, aerodrome wind-shear warnings, PIREPs, LLWAS/Doppler radar alerts; delay departure or approach until the Cb/heavy shower has passed (≈ 15–20 min), choose another runway/aerodrome; use increased approach speed (gust/wind additive) and the longest runway. In flight: monitor IAS, ground speed and vertical speed vs expected values, predictive/reactive wind-shear warnings; at the first indication, wind-shear escape manoeuvre: TOGA thrust, pitch towards the pitch limit indicator/stick-shaker, no configuration changes until clear, do not chase airspeed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Signs on approach: sudden IAS gain > 15 kt, large thrust changes needed, groundspeed and IAS diverging, heavy rain shafts, virga, dust rings.

topics.title: Conditions for and process of development, forecast, location, type specification

los.lo: Name the cloud types which indicate the development of thunderstorms.
los.title: Cloud types indicating thunderstorm development
los.html:
Theory & physics

TCU (Cu congestus, rapidly growing, hard cauliflower tops), Ac castellanus and Ac floccus (mid-level instability, often in the morning before afternoon TS), Cb calvus (developing), Cb capillatus with anvil (mature).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Ac castellanus in the morning → TS in the afternoon/evening; signal for forecasting.

los.lo: Describe the different types of thunderstorms, their location, the conditions for and the process of development, and list their properties (air-mass thunderstorms, frontal thunderstorms, squall lines, supercell storms, orographic thunderstorms).
los.title: Types of thunderstorms: location, development, properties
los.html:
Theory & physics

Requirements: moisture, instability (conditional, deep), trigger (lifting).

  • Air-mass (single-cell) TS: surface heating of moist unstable air; isolated; summer afternoons over land (night over sea); 30–60 min per cell; weak wind shear.
  • Frontal TS: lifting at cold fronts (lines along the front) or embedded in warm fronts/occlusions (hidden in Ns/As); any time of day; can be widespread.
  • Squall line: organised line of multicell storms ahead of a cold front or in a convergence line; severe gusts, hail; long-lived (hours).
  • Supercell: single, very large, long-lived (hours) storm with a rotating updraft (mesocyclone); needs strong vertical wind shear and high instability; large hail, tornadoes, downbursts.
  • Orographic TS: forced ascent of unstable air over mountains; quasi-stationary over ridges; afternoon peak.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Embedded frontal TS are the most insidious: use radar.
  • Supercells need strong shear; air-mass storms form with weak shear (that is why they die quickly: the downdraft cuts off the updraft).

los.lo: Assess the average duration of thunderstorms and their different stages.
los.title: Average duration and stages of thunderstorms
los.html:
Theory & physics

Single cell ≈ 1–2 h in total. Cumulus stage (≈ 10–15 min): updrafts only (up to ≈ 3000 ft/min), cloud growing, no precipitation at the surface yet. Mature stage (≈ 15–30 min): starts when precipitation reaches the ground; updrafts and downdrafts side by side, lightning, hail, gust front, maximum intensity of all hazards; anvil forms. Dissipating stage (≈ 30 min+): downdrafts dominate, precipitation decreases, anvil detaches and may persist. Multicell storms renew themselves for hours; supercells last hours.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The start of the mature stage = rain at the surface (exam definition).
  • Lightning risk highest within ≈ ±5 °C of the freezing level.

los.lo: Describe a supercell storm: initial, supercell, tornado and dissipating stage.
los.title: Supercell storm: initial, supercell, tornado and dissipating stages
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Initial: strong updraft in an environment with strong, veering vertical wind shear; horizontal vorticity is tilted into the vertical.
  • Supercell: rotating updraft (mesocyclone, 3–10 km wide); separated updraft and downdraft allow long life; radar: hook echo, bounded weak echo region (vault); large hail; overshooting top; wall cloud below the base.
  • Tornado: the low-level mesocyclone tightens; the rear-flank downdraft wraps around; a tornado may descend from the wall cloud.
  • Dissipating: the downdraft cuts off the inflow; the mesocyclone weakens; the storm decays or a new cycle starts.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Avoid by ≥ 20 nm; hook echoes and large hail on radar = extreme danger.

los.lo: Summarise the flight hazards associated with a fully developed thunderstorm.
los.title: Flight hazards of a fully developed thunderstorm
los.html:
Theory & physics

Severe/extreme turbulence (updrafts/downdrafts up to 6000 ft/min), severe icing (clear) between 0 and −20 °C (higher in strong updrafts), hail (also from the anvil and in clear air nearby), lightning (strikes, temporary blindness), heavy rain (engine ingestion, visibility), microbursts and gust fronts (low-level wind shear), squalls, tornadoes, altimeter errors (rapid local pressure changes of several hPa), static/radio interference, ice-crystal icing aloft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Never take off or land with a TS over or approaching the aerodrome (within ≈ 5–10 nm).

los.lo: Indicate on a sketch the most dangerous zones in and around a single-cell and a multi-cell thunderstorm.
los.title: Most dangerous zones in and around single-cell and multicell thunderstorms
los.html:
Theory & physics

Single cell: the core (updraft/downdraft boundary), beneath the cloud (downbursts, heavy rain), below and downwind of the anvil (hail falling out), the region ahead of the storm along the gust front (wind shear up to 10–20 nm), above the top (turbulence, overshooting). Multicell: new cells develop on the flank (usually the right/forward flank in NH, often the south-west/south side); strongest turbulence between cells; mature cells in the middle, dissipating cells on the opposite flank.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • See the life-cycle diagram above (050.09.04.02.01) for updraft/downdraft structure.
  • Do not fly between closely spaced cells or under the anvil; pass upwind.

los.lo: Describe the basic outline of the electric field in the atmosphere.
los.title: Basic outline of the atmospheric electric field
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fair weather: the Earth's surface is negatively charged, the upper atmosphere (ionosphere) positively; field ≈ 100 V/m at the surface. In a Cb: charge separation by collisions of graupel and ice crystals in the presence of supercooled water: positive charge in the upper part (ice crystals in the anvil), main negative charge in the middle (around the −10 to −20 °C level), a small positive region near the base; the ground below becomes positively charged by induction.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most lightning strikes to aircraft occur near the freezing level (± 5 °C), often in or near precipitation.

los.lo: Describe types of lightning, i.e. ground stroke, intra-cloud lightning, cloud-to-cloud lightning, upward lightning.
los.title: Types of lightning
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cloud-to-ground (ground stroke), intra-cloud (most frequent, within the same cloud), cloud-to-cloud (between clouds), cloud-to-air, upward lightning (initiated from tall structures, or from aircraft acting as a conductor, travelling upwards).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Aircraft frequently trigger lightning themselves by bridging charge regions.

los.lo: Describe and assess the ‘St. Elmo’s fire’ weather phenomenon.
los.title: St. Elmo's fire
los.html:
Theory & physics

A visible bluish/violet corona discharge from sharp, pointed parts of the aircraft (windscreen frames, wiper blades, wingtips, static dischargers, nose) in a strong electric field, typically in or near Cb, in snow or ice crystals, or in volcanic ash.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Harmless itself but indicates a high electric field (lightning strike possible) and causes radio static (precipitation static).
  • Also a cue of ice-crystal or volcanic-ash environments.

los.lo: Describe the development of lightning discharges.
los.title: Development of lightning discharges
los.html:
Theory & physics

When the electric field exceeds the breakdown strength of air, a stepped leader propagates from the cloud in short steps, ionising a channel; an upward streamer from the ground (or object) meets it; a powerful return stroke flows (30 000 A typical, up to 200 000 A; temperature ≈ 30 000 K), followed by dart leaders and subsequent strokes. The rapid expansion of the heated channel produces thunder.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Distance of a storm ≈ time between flash and thunder (s) ÷ 3 = km.

los.lo: Describe the effect of lightning strike on aircraft and flight execution.
los.title: Effects of a lightning strike on aircraft
los.html:
Theory & physics

Usually entry and exit points (burn marks, small holes) on extremities (nose, wingtips, tail); possible damage to radome, antennas, composite structure, lights; electrical/avionics transients and failures; magnetic compass errors (structure magnetised); temporary flash blindness of the crew; rarely engine flame-out or fuel ignition (protected by design).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • At night in TS areas: cockpit storm lights on full to reduce flash blindness.
  • After a strike: check systems, compass deviation, and have an inspection carried out.

los.lo: Define the term ‘downburst’.
los.title: Define downburst
los.html:
Theory & physics

A downburst is a strong, localised downdraft from a convective cloud (Cb or even TCU, virga) that spreads out on or near the ground in a burst of damaging, divergent winds.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Divergent outflow: headwind on entry, tailwind on exit for an aircraft passing through.

los.lo: Distinguish between macroburst and microburst.
los.title: Macroburst vs microburst
los.html:
Theory & physics

Macroburst: outflow extent > 4 km (2.2 nm), damaging winds lasting 5–30 min, up to ≈ 120 kt. Microburst: outflow extent ≤ 4 km, peak winds lasting 2–5 min (whole event up to ≈ 15 min), outflow up to ≈ 150 kt, downdraft up to ≈ 6000 ft/min; headwind-to-tailwind change can exceed 50–80 kt across a few km.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The 4 km (2.2 nm) threshold and the 2–5 min duration are the classic exam numbers.

los.lo: State the weather situations leading to the formation of downbursts.
los.title: Weather situations leading to downbursts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cb and heavy showers, especially: high-based Cb or TCU over a deep, dry sub-cloud layer (dry microbursts with virga; evaporative cooling), heavy precipitation cores (wet microbursts, precipitation drag plus melting/evaporation), mature thunderstorms and squall lines. Also from TCU with little rain at the surface.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Virga beneath a high-based convective cloud in dry, hot conditions = dry microburst warning even without TS.

los.lo: Describe the process of development of a downburst.
los.title: Development of a downburst
los.html:
Theory & physics

Precipitation drags air downward; evaporation of rain (and melting/sublimation of hail and snow) in drier air below the cloud cools it, making it denser than its surroundings; the negatively buoyant air accelerates downward, strikes the ground and spreads out radially, often with a curling vortex ring at its leading edge.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Visual cues: rain shaft curling outward near the ground, ring of dust, virga.

los.lo: Give the typical duration of a downburst.
los.title: Typical duration of a downburst
los.html:
Theory & physics

Microburst: maximum intensity for 2–5 min, total life ≈ 10–15 min. Macroburst: 5–30 min.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Waiting ≈ 15–20 min after a heavy shower/TS has passed usually removes the hazard.

los.lo: Describe the effects of downbursts.
los.title: Effects of downbursts
los.html:
Theory & physics

For an aircraft on approach or take-off: (1) increasing headwind → IAS gain, climb above the path; (2) strong downdraft → sink; (3) increasing tailwind → IAS loss and loss of lift, sink below the path; total energy loss may exceed the aircraft's climb capability. On the ground: damaging winds, structural damage.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • See the microburst diagram (050.09.03.03.01). Escape early with maximum thrust and pitch up to the stick-shaker/PLI limit.

los.lo: Explain how the pilot can anticipate each type of thunderstorm: through pre-flight weather briefing, observation in flight, use of specific meteorological information, use of information given by ground weather radar and by airborne weather radar. (Refer to Subject 050 10 01 04), use of a lightning detector (stormscope). (Refer to Subject 050 10 01 04), use of the stormscope (lightning detector).
los.title: Anticipating thunderstorms
los.html:
Theory & physics

Pre-flight briefing: TAF/METAR (TS, CB, TCU, +SHRA), SIGMET (OBSC/EMBD/FRQ/SQL TS), SWC CB areas with tops, satellite (overshooting tops, cold IR tops), radar composites, lightning maps, stability forecasts. In flight: visual observation of Cu growth, anvils, mammatus; ATC radar information; airborne weather radar (tilt, gain, range; attenuation shadows); lightning detector (stormscope), which detects electrical discharges in all directions, including in areas without heavy rain, and complements radar.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Weather radar detects precipitation (liquid water), not turbulence or dry hail/ice crystals.
