  • Stormscope shows discharges but bearings/ranges are approximate.

los.lo: Describe practical examples of flight techniques used to avoid the hazards of thunderstorms.
los.title: Flight techniques to avoid thunderstorm hazards
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Avoid all Cb by ≥ 10 nm (≥ 20 nm for severe storms, at high altitude, or with strong echoes); deviate upwind where possible.
  • Do not fly under the anvil or overhang; do not fly between cells less than ≈ 20–30 nm apart.
  • If overflying, clear the top by ≥ 5000 ft (often impossible with tops at FL 400+).
  • Do not take off or land with a storm within ≈ 5–10 nm of the aerodrome or approach path.
  • If penetration is unavoidable: fly turbulence penetration speed, maintain attitude (not altitude), autothrust/autopilot per SOP, anti-ice on, cockpit lights full bright, do not turn back once inside, and choose the shortest path through the weakest part (lowest reflectivity) at an altitude per SOP that avoids the 0 to −20 °C band (worst icing and lightning) where possible.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trap: "pass on the downwind side" or "fly below the anvil to avoid hail". Both wrong.

los.lo: Define ‘tornado’.
los.title: Define tornado
los.html:
Theory & physics

A tornado is a violently rotating column of air, in contact with the ground, pendant from a cumuliform cloud (usually a supercell Cb), often visible as a funnel cloud (condensation) and/or a debris cloud. Over water: waterspout.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • A funnel cloud not reaching the ground is not yet a tornado. METAR: FC (funnel cloud: tornado or waterspout).

los.lo: Describe the formation of a tornado.
los.title: Formation of a tornado
los.html:
Theory & physics

Strong low-level vertical wind shear creates horizontal vorticity, which the supercell updraft tilts into the vertical, forming the mesocyclone; stretching of the rotating column (conservation of angular momentum) and interaction with the rear-flank downdraft concentrate the rotation into a narrow vortex reaching the ground. Pressure in the core can be tens of hPa lower than surroundings.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Requires a supercell (or strong squall line); not ordinary air-mass storms.

los.lo: Describe the typical features of a tornado such as appearance, season, time of day, stage of development, speed of movement, and wind speed.
los.title: Typical features of a tornado
los.html:
Theory & physics

Appearance: funnel or rope-like cloud from the cloud base (often from a wall cloud), with debris at the ground. Diameter ≈ 50–500 m (up to > 1 km). Season: spring and early summer (US: April–June). Time: late afternoon/early evening. Stage: mature supercell. Speed of movement: ≈ 10–40 kt, usually SW → NE in the US. Wind speed: ≈ 60 kt to > 250 kt (EF0–EF5); path length typically a few km, up to > 100 km.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Extreme winds and pressure drop: avoid the parent storm by ≥ 20 nm.

los.lo: Compare the occurrence of tornadoes in Europe with the occurrence in other locations, especially in the United States of America.
los.title: Tornadoes in Europe vs the USA
los.html:
Theory & physics

Far more frequent and violent in the US central plains ("Tornado Alley", ≈ 1000+ per year), where cold dry air from the Rockies, warm moist air from the Gulf of Mexico and strong shear meet. Europe: a few hundred per year, mostly weak (EF0–EF2), though strong ones occur occasionally; waterspouts over the Mediterranean in late summer/autumn.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Exam answer: tornadoes in Europe are less frequent and usually weaker than in the USA.

los.lo: Compare the dimensions and properties of tornadoes and dust devils.
los.title: Tornadoes vs dust devils
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dust devils: small whirlwinds (a few m to tens of m wide, up to a few hundred to ≈ 1000 m high) formed by intense surface heating in clear air, not attached to a cloud; short-lived (minutes); winds usually < ≈ 50 kt; may rotate either way. Tornadoes: attached to a Cb, much larger, stronger, longer-lived, mostly cyclonic.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Dust devils can upset light aircraft and helicopters near the ground on hot afternoons. METAR: PO (dust/sand whirls).

los.lo: Compare the flight hazards during take-off and approach associated with a strong inversion alone and with a strong inversion combined with marked wind shear.
los.title: Hazards of a strong inversion alone and with marked wind shear (take-off and approach)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Strong inversion alone: on take-off, climbing from cold air into the warm air above reduces air density, so thrust/power and lift fall and the climb gradient decreases (critical for heavy aircraft, obstacle clearance); poor visibility (haze, fog, smoke) below it. On approach, entering the cold layer increases performance slightly. Inversion with marked wind shear (calm cold surface layer under strong wind above, e.g. nocturnal low-level jet): crossing the inversion produces sudden IAS changes (gain or loss depending on wind direction relative to the flight path), possible sink near the ground and turbulence at the boundary.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Climbing out of a calm layer into a tailwind above → IAS loss at low height (most dangerous); descending from a strong headwind into calm air → IAS loss on short final.
  • Expect and brief the shear when the forecast shows strong winds at 1000–2000 ft over a calm surface.

los.lo: Summarise the advantages of stratospheric flights.
los.title: Advantages of stratospheric flight
los.html:
Theory & physics

Above almost all cloud and weather (except overshooting Cb tops); generally smooth air (except CAT near the tropopause/jets and breaking mountain waves); low density = lower drag and better specific range for jets; constant low temperatures (ISA −56.5 °C) favour engine efficiency; usually no icing; good visibility.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Optimum cruise levels for jets are near or just above the tropopause.

los.lo: List the influences of the phenomena associated with the lower stratosphere (wind, temperature, air density, turbulence).
los.title: Phenomena of the lower stratosphere: wind, temperature, density, turbulence
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Wind: maximum (jet core) just below the tropopause; decreasing with height above it.
  • Temperature: roughly isothermal or slightly increasing with height; but higher stratospheric temperatures than ISA reduce engine thrust and maximum altitude, and raise the speed of sound (Mach/TAS relationship).
  • Density: low, so narrow margin between low-speed and high-speed buffet (coffin corner), reduced manoeuvre margin.
  • Turbulence: CAT near tropopause breaks and above jet cores; breaking mountain waves; overshooting tops.
  • Also: ozone (cabin irritation) and cosmic radiation at high latitudes and altitudes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Turbulence at high FL near buffet limits: descend to increase margins.

topics.title: Influence of terrain on clouds and precipitation, frontal passage

los.lo: Describe the influence of mountainous area on a frontal passage.
los.title: Influence of mountains on a frontal passage
los.html:
Theory & physics

Mountains slow and deform fronts: the low-level cold air is blocked on the windward side (the front may become quasi-stationary and its passage delayed), enhanced lifting increases cloud and precipitation on the windward slopes (orographic enhancement, heavy rain or snow); in the lee the front may weaken (Föhn effect) and then re-form further downstream; lee lows may develop (e.g. Genoa).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Windward side of the Alps/Pyrenees: prolonged frontal weather; lee side: improvement, Föhn, turbulence.

topics.title: Vertical movements, mountain waves, wind shear, turbulence, ice accretion

los.lo: Describe the vertical movements, wind shear and turbulence that are typical of mountain areas.
los.title: Vertical movements, wind shear and turbulence in mountain areas
los.html:
Theory & physics

Upslope/downslope (anabatic/katabatic) and valley/mountain winds; forced ascent and strong descent across ridges; mountain waves with strong up/downdrafts; rotors; mechanical turbulence and lee eddies; channelling and Venturi acceleration in valleys and passes; marked wind shear near ridges and at valley inversions; convective turbulence over sunny slopes in summer.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cross ridges at a safe height and at 45°; approach the ridge from the upwind side where updrafts are found; avoid the lee at low level in strong wind.

los.lo: Indicate on a sketch of a chain of mountains the turbulent zones (mountain waves, rotors).
los.title: Turbulent zones on a mountain chain (waves, rotors)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Windward: mechanical turbulence close to the slope (moderate). Crest: accelerated flow, cap cloud, strong shear. Lee: strong downdraft along the slope; rotor zones beneath the wave crests, at or below ridge height (severe/extreme turbulence); laminar wave flow above with lenticulars; possible wave breaking at high levels (CAT).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • See the mountain-wave diagram in 050.02.05.01.03 (sketch questions place the rotor under the first wave crest in the lee).

los.lo: Explain the influence of relief on ice accretion.
los.title: Influence of relief on ice accretion
los.html:
Theory & physics

Orographic lift produces cloud with high liquid water content and large drops on the windward side and over the ridge, increasing icing intensity; the freezing level may be lower in valleys with cold-air pools; minimum safe altitudes may force flight in the icing layer with no escape downward.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Plan routes where MSA is below the freezing level, or above the cloud tops.

topics.title: Development and effect of valley inversions

los.lo: Describe the formation of a valley inversion due to katabatic winds.
los.title: Valley inversion due to katabatic winds
los.html:
Theory & physics

At night, air cooled on the slopes drains into the valley floor and accumulates as a cold-air pool below warmer air on the slopes above (thermal belt), forming a strong valley inversion; fog, frost and pollution are trapped.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Valley aerodromes: radiation fog and low St in the morning; mid-slope may be warmer and clearer.

los.lo: Describe the valley inversion formed by warm winds aloft.
los.title: Valley inversion formed by warm winds aloft
los.html:
Theory & physics

Warm air flowing over a valley (warm advection, Föhn) cannot displace a dense cold-air pool in the valley; the warm wind blows over the top, creating a sharp inversion with strong wind shear at its top and calm cold air below. The pool may persist for days in winter.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Strong shear when descending from the warm, windy layer into the calm cold pool on approach.

los.lo: Describe the effects of a valley inversion for an aircraft in flight.
los.title: Effects of a valley inversion on aircraft
los.html:
Theory & physics

Poor visibility (fog, haze, smoke) beneath the inversion; wind shear and turbulence at the inversion boundary; sudden IAS changes on climb/descent through it; reduced climb performance on climbing into the warmer air above; possible icing in fog/St if sub-zero.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Brief the shear and performance change for departures from valley aerodromes in winter.

topics.title: Reduction of visibility caused by precipitation and obscurations

los.lo: Describe the reduction of visibility caused by precipitation: drizzle, rain, snow.
los.title: Visibility reduction by precipitation: drizzle, rain, snow
los.html:
Theory & physics

Drizzle: numerous small drops, often with mist/fog: visibility often < 3000 m, sometimes < 1000 m. Rain: light rain little effect (> 5 km); moderate 3–10 km; heavy (especially showers) can reduce visibility to < 1000 m and also by water on the windscreen. Snow: most effective: light snow 1–5 km; moderate ≈ 500–1000 m; heavy < 500 m (down to ≈ 100 m).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • For the same intensity, snow > drizzle > rain in visibility reduction.

los.lo: Describe the reduction of visibility caused by obscurations: fog, mist, haze, smoke, volcanic ash.
los.title: Visibility reduction by obscurations: fog, mist, haze, smoke, volcanic ash
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fog < 1000 m; mist 1000–5000 m (wet); haze (dry particles), typically 1–5 km, worse into the sun; smoke (FU) from fires and industry, reduces visibility and slant visibility, often yellowish/brown; volcanic ash (VA): abrasive glass particles; visibility reduction plus severe engine damage, windscreen abrasion, pitot blockage, possible flame-out; often invisible at night or in cloud.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • VA: avoid completely; follow VAAC advisories and SIGMET (VA); signs include St. Elmo's fire, sulphur smell, dust in the cockpit, EGT rise.

los.lo: Describe the reduction of visibility caused by obscurations: sand (SA), dust (DU).
los.title: Visibility reduction by sand (SA) and dust (DU)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Widespread dust (DU) or sand (SA) suspended in the air (raised earlier by wind elsewhere) produces a dry haze; visibility can be reduced to a few km or less over large areas and for long periods (Harmattan, Saharan dust episodes reaching Europe).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • DU/SA persist after the wind has dropped; distinguish from BLDU/BLSA (raised by the local wind at the time of observation).

los.lo: Describe the differences between ground and flight visibility, and slant and vertical visibility when an aircraft is above or within a layer of haze or fog.
los.title: Ground vs flight visibility; slant and vertical visibility with haze or fog
los.html:
Theory & physics

Met visibility is measured horizontally at the surface. From above a shallow fog or haze layer, a pilot may see the ground vertically (short path through the layer) while the slant visibility along the approach path (long path through the layer) is much poorer. Inside the layer, flight visibility may differ from reported ground visibility; above a haze layer, horizontal visibility can be excellent but the ground is obscured at shallow angles.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • On approach into shallow fog, the runway lights can disappear as the aircraft enters the layer; rely on RVR and approach minima, not on what is seen from above.

topics.title: Reduction of visibility caused by other phenomena

los.lo: Describe the reduction of visibility caused by low drifting and blowing snow.
los.title: Low drifting and blowing snow
los.html:
Theory & physics

Drifting snow (DRSN): snow raised by the wind to a height below 2 m; visibility at eye level not significantly reduced, but surface features and runway markings hidden. Blowing snow (BLSN): raised to 2 m or more, reducing horizontal visibility (can be < 1000 m) even with no snow falling.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Loss of surface contrast (whiteout) and runway markings; reported even under clear skies.

los.lo: Describe the reduction of visibility caused by low drifting and blowing dust and sand.
los.title: Low drifting and blowing dust and sand
los.html:
Theory & physics

DRDU/DRSA: raised below 2 m; BLDU/BLSA: raised to 2 m or more by local wind, reducing visibility at eye level.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Engine ingestion and erosion on take-off; runway edges obscured.

los.lo: Describe the reduction of visibility caused by dust storm (DS) and sandstorm (SS).
los.title: Dust storm (DS) and sandstorm (SS)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Strong, turbulent winds raise large quantities of dust or sand to considerable heights (often several thousand ft, up to FL 100+); visibility generally < 1000 m, and < 200 m in heavy (+DS/+SS); often with a wall-like leading edge (haboob, from Cb outflow).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Avoid: aerodromes close; severe abrasion and engine damage; can arrive suddenly with a gust front.

los.lo: Describe the reduction of visibility caused by icing (windshield).
los.title: Visibility reduction by windscreen icing
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ice or frost on the windscreen (from supercooled drops, freezing rain, or hoar frost on descent into warm moist air) can reduce forward visibility to zero; rain on an unheated screen also reduces visibility.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use windscreen heat before entering icing conditions; hoar frost on descent can form suddenly.

los.lo: Describe the reduction of visibility caused by the position of the sun relative to the visual direction.
los.title: Position of the sun relative to the line of sight
los.html:
Theory & physics

Looking towards a low sun, light scattered by haze, dust or a dirty/scratched windscreen reduces contrast dramatically (glare): visibility into the sun is much worse than down-sun.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Landing into a low sun in haze: runway and traffic hard to see; consider timing and runway direction; use visors/sunglasses.

los.lo: Describe the reduction of visibility caused by the reflection of the sun’s rays from the top of the layers of haze, fog and clouds.
los.title: Sun reflection from the tops of haze, fog and cloud layers
los.html:
Theory & physics

Sunlight reflected from the tops of haze, fog or cloud layers produces a bright, uniform glare that reduces the contrast of objects below or within the layer and makes the horizon indistinct.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Difficult to see the ground, traffic and terrain; risk of spatial disorientation (false horizon) when flying just above such a layer.

los.lo: Define ‘gusts’, as given in METARs.
los.title: Gusts in METARs
los.html:
Theory & physics

A gust is a brief increase in wind speed. In METAR, gusts are reported (G after the mean speed) when the maximum wind speed during the last 10 minutes (3-s average) exceeds the mean speed by ≥ 10 kt. Example: 24018G32KT.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No G group if the gust is less than 10 kt above the mean.
  • Approach speed: add half the gust increment (typical SOP), within limits.

los.lo: Distinguish wind given in METARs and wind given by the control tower for take-off and landing.
los.title: METAR wind vs tower wind for take-off and landing
los.html:
Theory & physics

METAR/SPECI: 10-min mean, direction in degrees true, representative of the aerodrome (or the main runway). Tower (ATC/ATIS for take-off/landing): 2-min mean (gusts over 10 min), direction in degrees magnetic, from sensors at the relevant runway touchdown/departure zone.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • At aerodromes with large magnetic variation, METAR and tower directions differ noticeably.

los.lo: Define ‘visibility’.
los.title: Define visibility
los.html:
Theory & physics

Visibility for aeronautical purposes is the greater of: (a) the greatest distance at which a black object of suitable dimensions, near the ground, can be seen and recognised against a bright background; (b) the greatest distance at which lights of ≈ 1000 candelas can be seen and identified against an unlit background.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Night visibility uses lights; values differ from day for the same atmosphere.

los.lo: Describe the meteorological measurement of visibility.
los.title: Meteorological measurement of visibility
los.html:
Theory & physics

By an observer using visibility markers (objects/lights at known distances) around the aerodrome, or by instruments (forward-scatter meters, transmissometers) that measure the extinction coefficient (MOR, meteorological optical range) which is converted to visibility.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • AUTO METARs use sensors: visibility is representative of a small sample volume.

los.lo: Define ‘prevailing visibility’.
los.title: Define prevailing visibility
los.html:
Theory & physics

The visibility value that is reached or exceeded within at least half the horizon circle or within at least half of the surface of the aerodrome; these areas may be contiguous or not. Reported as the main visibility in METAR. If visibility in one direction is < 1500 m or < 50 % of the prevailing visibility, the lowest visibility and its direction are also reported (e.g. 4000 1200SW).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Prevailing visibility is not the minimum visibility.

los.lo: Define ‘ground visibility’.
los.title: Define ground visibility
los.html:
Theory & physics

The visibility at an aerodrome as reported by an accredited observer or by automatic systems.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Used for VFR take-off and landing (vs flight visibility, which is seen from the cockpit in flight).

los.lo: List the units used for visibility (m, km, statute mile).
los.title: Units of visibility
los.html:
Theory & physics

Metres (steps of 50 m below 800 m, 100 m up to 5000 m, 1000 m up to 9999); 9999 = 10 km or more; km in plain language; statute miles (SM) in the USA/Canada (e.g. 1/2SM, 10SM).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • CAVOK: visibility ≥ 10 km, no cloud below 5000 ft (or MSA if higher) and no CB/TCU, no significant weather.

los.lo: Define ‘runway visual range’.
los.title: Define runway visual range
los.html:
Theory & physics

RVR: the range over which the pilot of an aircraft on the centre line of a runway can see the runway surface markings or the lights delineating the runway or identifying its centre line.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • RVR is the controlling value for low-visibility approach minima and take-off minima.

los.lo: Describe the meteorological measurement of runway visual range.
los.title: Measurement of RVR
los.html:
Theory & physics

Instruments (transmissometers or forward-scatter meters) measure the atmospheric extinction; RVR is calculated by combining it with the runway light intensity setting and the background luminance (day/night). Reported when visibility or RVR is < 1500 m.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • RVR can be higher than met visibility at night (bright runway lights).

los.lo: Indicate where the transmissometers/forward-scatter meters are placed on the aerodrome.
los.title: Location of RVR sensors on the aerodrome
los.html:
Theory & physics

Alongside the runway, ≈ 120 m from the centre line (not more), at a height of ≈ 2.5 m (pilot's eye height), at the touchdown zone (TDZ) ≈ 300 m from the threshold, the mid-point (MID) and the stop-end (END) ≈ 300 m from the end.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Operator minima specify which RVRs are controlling (usually TDZ, plus MID/END for some operations).

los.lo: List the units used for runway visual range (m, ft).
los.title: Units of RVR
los.html:
Theory & physics

Metres in Europe (ft in the USA). METAR: R24/0550U: RVR runway 24 = 550 m, tendency up (U), down (D), no change (N); P1500 = more than 1500 m; M0050 = less than 50 m.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Variation: R24/0550V0800 indicates significant variations.

los.lo: List the different possibilities to transmit information to pilots about runway visual range.
los.title: Ways RVR is passed to pilots
los.html:
Theory & physics

METAR/SPECI (10-min mean, with tendency), local MET REPORT/SPECIAL (1-min values), ATIS, and ATC (tower/approach) by R/T with current instantaneous values (TDZ, MID, END).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • On approach, the latest ATC RVR is used for the approach ban.

los.lo: Compare ground visibility, prevailing visibility, and runway visual range.
los.title: Ground visibility vs prevailing visibility vs RVR
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ground visibility: general visibility at the aerodrome. Prevailing visibility: value reached in at least half the horizon/aerodrome. RVR: along a specific runway, from the pilot's eye position, accounting for runway lights; measured at specific points.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • If RVR is not available, a CMV (converted met visibility) may be used for some approaches per the operator's rules.

los.lo: Indicate the means of observation of present weather.
los.title: Observation of present weather
los.html:
Theory & physics

By human observers (precipitation type/intensity, TS, obscurations) and by automatic sensors: present-weather sensors (forward scatter + precipitation detection), precipitation gauges, lightning detection systems, ceilometers, visibility sensors.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • AUTO METARs may not detect some phenomena (e.g. TCU, small hail); unknown = "//".

los.lo: Indicate the means of observing clouds for the purpose of recording: type, amount, height of base (ceilometers), and top.
los.title: Observation of cloud type, amount, base and top
los.html:
Theory & physics

Type and amount: human observer; satellite. Base: ceilometer (laser/light pulse: time of return), cloud-base searchlight with alidade at night, pilot reports, balloons (ceiling balloon). Tops: pilot reports, satellite (IR temperature), radiosonde, radar.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • METAR heights of base are above aerodrome elevation; tops come from forecasts or PIREPs.

los.lo: State the clouds which are indicated in METAR, TAF and SIGMET.
los.title: Clouds named in METAR, TAF and SIGMET
los.html:
Theory & physics

Only CB and TCU are identified by type in METAR and TAF (e.g. SCT025CB). SIGMET refers to CB/TS (OBSC, EMBD, FRQ, SQL). Other clouds are described only by amount and base.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • NSC = no significant cloud; NCD = no cloud detected (AUTO).

los.lo: Define ‘oktas’.
los.title: Define oktas
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cloud amount in eighths of the sky covered. METAR: FEW 1–2 oktas, SCT 3–4, BKN 5–7, OVC 8.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • BKN begins at 5 oktas, i.e. more than half the sky.

los.lo: Define ‘cloud base’.
los.title: Define cloud base
los.html:
Theory & physics

The lowest zone in which the type of obscuration perceptibly changes from that corresponding to clear air or haze to that corresponding to water droplets or ice crystals; reported as the height above aerodrome elevation.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • In fog or heavy snow, cloud base is replaced by vertical visibility (VV).

los.lo: Define ‘ceiling’.
los.title: Define ceiling
los.html:
Theory & physics

The height above the ground or water of the base of the lowest layer of cloud below 20 000 ft covering more than half the sky (BKN or OVC).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • SCT layers never form a ceiling; VV is treated as a ceiling.

los.lo: Name the unit and the reference level used for information about cloud base (ft).
los.title: Unit and reference level for cloud base
los.html:
Theory & physics

Feet (hundreds of ft in METAR/TAF: BKN008 = 800 ft), above aerodrome elevation (threshold elevation for precision runways where specified; above MSL for offshore structures).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Compare with DH/MDH (above threshold/aerodrome), not with DA/MDA (above MSL).

los.lo: Define ‘vertical visibility’.
los.title: Define vertical visibility
los.html:
Theory & physics

Vertical visibility (VV): the maximum distance an observer can see vertically into an obscuring medium (fog, heavy snow, sand), reported when the sky is obscured and the cloud base cannot be determined.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • METAR: VV002 = 200 ft; VV/// = sky obscured, VV not available.

los.lo: Explain briefly how and when vertical visibility is measured.
los.title: How and when vertical visibility is measured
los.html:
Theory & physics

When the sky is obscured (fog, heavy precipitation); measured by the ceilometer (penetration depth of the laser into the obscuration) or estimated by the observer.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • VV appears instead of a cloud group, never together with one.

los.lo: Name the units used for vertical visibility (ft, m).
los.title: Units of vertical visibility
los.html:
Theory & physics

Hundreds of ft in METAR/TAF (VVhhh); metres in some local reports.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • VV001 = 100 ft.

los.lo: Indicate the means of observation of air temperature (thermometer).
los.title: Observation of air temperature
los.html:
Theory & physics

Thermometers (electrical resistance, mercury/alcohol, thermistors) in a ventilated, shaded screen at 1.25–2 m above the ground; maximum/minimum thermometers; aircraft measure SAT from TAT probes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • METAR temperature rounded to whole °C; M = minus (M02).

los.lo: Name the units of relative humidity ( per cent) and dew-point temperature (Celsius, Fahrenheit).
los.title: Units of RH and dew point
los.html:
Theory & physics

Relative humidity in %; dew point in °C (°F in the USA). Measured by hygrometers (capacitive sensors) or psychrometers (wet- and dry-bulb).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • METAR gives T/Td, not RH: estimate RH from the spread (050.03.01.03.06).

los.lo: Describe the principle of radiosondes.
los.title: Principle of radiosondes
los.html:
Theory & physics

A small instrument package carried by a hydrogen/helium balloon (ascent ≈ 5 m/s) measures pressure, temperature and humidity; wind is derived by tracking the balloon (GPS, radar: radiowind/rawinsonde). Data are transmitted by radio to the ground; the balloon bursts at ≈ 25–35 km. Standard launches at 00 and 12 UTC worldwide.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Radiosonde data feed upper-air charts, NWP models and stability diagrams.

los.lo: Describe and interpret the sounding by radiosonde given on a simplified temperature-pressure (T-P) diagram.
los.title: Interpret a radiosonde sounding on a simplified T–P diagram
los.html:
Theory & physics

Plot temperature and dew point against pressure (height). Read: ELR and stability (compare slope with DALR/SALR); inversions (temperature increasing with height) and isothermal layers; cloud layers where T and Td coincide or nearly so (spread ≤ ≈ 1–2 °C); dry layers where the spread is large; freezing level where the temperature curve crosses 0 °C; tropopause (lapse-rate change to near isothermal).

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Icing: look for cloud layers (T ≈ Td) between 0 and −20 °C.
  • An inversion with moist air below = St/fog/haze; with dry air below = clear but hazy.

los.lo: Describe the basic outlines of satellite observations.
los.title: Basic outline of satellite observations
los.html:
Theory & physics

Geostationary satellites (≈ 36 000 km above the equator, e.g. Meteosat, GOES, Himawari): fixed view of one hemisphere, images every 5–15 min, poor resolution near the poles (> ≈ 60–70°). Polar-orbiting satellites (≈ 800–850 km, e.g. NOAA, MetOp): high resolution, global coverage including poles, each area seen about twice a day.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Loops of geostationary images show the movement and development of systems.

los.lo: Name the main uses of satellite pictures in aviation meteorology.
los.title: Main uses of satellite pictures in aviation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Locating and tracking fronts, depressions, jet streams, Cb/MCS and tropical cyclones, fog/low stratus, volcanic ash and dust clouds, mountain waves (lee-wave cloud), icing-prone areas; estimating cloud-top heights (IR temperatures); input to NWP and nowcasting, especially over oceans and data-sparse regions.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Satellite cannot see CAT in clear air (050.02.06.03.04).

los.lo: Describe the different types of satellite imagery.
los.title: Types of satellite imagery
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Visible (VIS): reflected sunlight; daytime only; brightness = albedo (thick, high-water-content clouds, snow are bright); shows texture and shadows.
  • Infrared (IR): emitted thermal radiation; day and night; brightness = coldness (high, cold tops white; warm surfaces/low clouds grey/dark).
  • Water vapour (WV): emission from mid/upper-tropospheric moisture (≈ 6.2–7.3 µm); shows upper-level flow, dry intrusions, jet streams; cannot see the surface.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Fog/low St: bright on VIS, dark/grey (warm) on IR → use VIS by day or fog products at night.
  • Cb: bright on both VIS and IR.

los.lo: Interpret qualitatively the satellite pictures in order to get useful information for flights: location of clouds (distinguish between stratiform and cumuliform clouds).
los.title: Interpret satellite pictures: stratiform vs cumuliform clouds
los.html:
Theory & physics

Stratiform: smooth, uniform texture, sharp straight edges (often following coasts/terrain for fog/St), uniform grey in IR. Cumuliform: lumpy, cellular, mottled texture, shadows on VIS; Cb appear as bright, round, often with anvil plumes and overshooting tops; open cells (polar air over warm sea) and closed cells (Sc under an inversion).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Open cellular cumulus behind a cold front = cold unstable air, showers.

los.lo: Interpret qualitatively the satellite pictures in order to get useful information for flights: location of fronts.
los.title: Interpret satellite pictures: location of fronts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fronts appear as long, continuous cloud bands: cold front narrow band (sharp rear edge), warm front broad cloud shield with layered cloud ahead of the surface front, occlusion as a spiral/comma head around the low centre; the triple point at the junction.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The surface cold front usually lies along the rear (cold-air) edge of the cloud band.

los.lo: Interpret qualitatively the satellite pictures in order to get useful information for flights using atmospheric motion vector images to locate jet streams.
los.title: Atmospheric motion vectors to locate jet streams
los.html:
Theory & physics

Atmospheric motion vectors (AMV) are wind estimates derived by tracking cloud or water-vapour features between successive images, assigned to a height. Bands of high-speed vectors at upper levels show the jet axis; in imagery the jet is also marked by sharp moisture boundaries (WV) and cirrus edges/streaks parallel to the flow.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The jet often lies along the poleward edge of a frontal cirrus shield.

los.lo: Describe the basic principle and the type of information given by a ground weather radar.
los.title: Ground weather radar: principle and information
los.html:
Theory & physics

A ground radar transmits microwave pulses (S/C-band) and measures the energy reflected by precipitation particles; reflectivity (dBZ) relates to precipitation intensity (∝ D⁶ of drops); range from the echo delay. Doppler radars measure radial velocity (wind, wind shear, mesocyclones); dual-polarisation radars distinguish hail, rain, snow. Networks produce composite images.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Radar shows precipitation, not cloud: non-precipitating cloud and fog are invisible to it.

los.lo: Interpret ground weather radar images.
los.title: Interpret ground weather radar images
los.html:
Theory & physics

Colour scale of reflectivity/rain rate: weak (blue/green), moderate (yellow), heavy (orange/red), extreme (purple/magenta, hail). Convective cells = small intense cores with strong gradients; stratiform rain = wide uniform areas; lines = squall lines/cold fronts; bow echoes = damaging winds; animation shows movement.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Composite images may be several minutes old: do not use them for tactical close-in avoidance.

los.lo: Describe the basic principle and the type of information given by airborne weather radar.
los.title: Airborne weather radar: principle and information
los.html:
Theory & physics

Nose-mounted X-band (≈ 9.3 GHz, 3 cm) pulse radar with a pencil beam (≈ 3–5°), scanning ahead (± 60–90°); displays precipitation intensity in colour levels (green, yellow, red, magenta). Controls: range, tilt (beam elevation), gain; modes: WX, WX+T (turbulence, Doppler), MAP (ground mapping). Some systems give predictive wind-shear alerts.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use tilt to scan up and down: at high altitude tilt down to see the reflective lower parts of cells.

los.lo: Describe the limits and the errors of airborne weather radar information.
los.title: Limits and errors of airborne weather radar
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Detects liquid water best; dry hail, snow, ice crystals reflect weakly; CAT and dry turbulence invisible (except Doppler turbulence mode in rain).
  • Attenuation: heavy rain absorbs the beam, so cells behind appear weaker or not at all (radar shadow).
  • Beam spreading: at long range the beam is wide and may overshoot or undershoot cells; small cells under-represented.
  • Wrong tilt: overscanning the tops of cells (weak echoes at high altitude) or ground clutter.
  • Display delay and limited range.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No return behind a strong echo does not mean no weather (shadow).

los.lo: Interpret typical airborne weather radar images.
los.title: Interpret typical airborne radar images
los.html:
Theory & physics

Red/magenta = heavy rain/hail: avoid by ≥ 20 nm. Shapes indicating severe turbulence/hail: hooks, fingers (protrusions), scalloped edges, U-shapes/crescents, rapidly changing shapes, and steep reflectivity gradients. Uniform green = stratiform rain.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Deviate upwind and well clear of steep-gradient edges.

los.lo: Describe routine air-report and special air-report (ARS).
los.title: Routine and special air-reports
los.html:
Theory & physics

Routine air-report (AIREP): position, time, FL, wind, temperature (and other items), made at designated reporting points or intervals; today mostly automatic via datalink (ADS-C, AMDAR). Special air-report (ARS): made whenever specified hazardous phenomena are encountered or observed, by voice or datalink.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Special air-reports can trigger the issue of a SIGMET.

los.lo: State the obligation of a pilot to prepare air-reports.
los.title: Pilot's obligation to make air-reports
los.html:
Theory & physics

Pilots must make special air-reports when encountering or observing conditions specified (severe turbulence, severe icing, etc.) and routine reports where required by the air navigation services/operations.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Report as soon as practicable to the ATS unit; include position, time, level and phenomenon.

los.lo: Name the weather phenomena to be stated in an ARS.
los.title: Phenomena reported in a special air-report
los.html:
Theory & physics

Moderate or severe turbulence; moderate or severe icing; severe mountain wave; thunderstorms (without hail or with hail; obscured, embedded, widespread or in squall lines); heavy dust storm or sandstorm; volcanic ash cloud; pre-eruption volcanic activity or eruption. (Also, for supersonic flight, moderate turbulence and hail/Cb in transonic/supersonic phases.)

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Standard abbreviations: SEV TURB, MOD ICE, SEV MTW, TS, TSGR, HVY DS, VA CLD.

los.lo: Decode and interpret significant weather charts (low, medium and high level).
los.title: Decode and interpret significant weather charts (low, medium, high level)
los.html:
Theory & physics

SWC (SIGWX) charts are forecast charts valid at a fixed time (issued by WAFCs for high/medium level, by MET offices for low level), showing:

  • Jet streams (≥ 80 kt): axis arrow, wind barbs/flags, FL of the core, sometimes vertical extent (e.g. FL 270/390 = depth of the 80 kt isotach).
  • Tropopause heights: FL in boxes, with H/L centres.
  • CB areas (scalloped lines): ISOL (isolated), OCNL (occasional, well separated), FRQ (frequent, little or no separation), EMBD (embedded in layer cloud), with bases/tops (XXX = below the chart's lower limit). CB implies hail, moderate/severe icing and turbulence.
  • Turbulence / CAT areas (dashed lines) with intensity and vertical extent; icing areas; mountain waves.
  • Fronts and their speed/direction, tropical cyclones, volcanoes (eruption symbol), sandstorms, radioactive release site.
  • Low-level charts: cloud layers (amount, type, base/top), freezing level (0 °C : FL), visibility and weather.

Levels: high FL 250–630; medium FL 100–450 (regional); low SFC–FL 100 (FL 150 in mountainous areas, up to FL 245 for some products).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • XXX means the base or top is outside the chart layer (e.g. CB base below FL 250 on a high-level chart).
  • Exam figures: "where is turbulence absent at FL 340?", "cloud at FL 160 over Amsterdam?", "optimum FL Rome–Paris": read the areas, their vertical limits and the jet core FL.

los.lo: Describe from a significant weather chart the flight conditions at designated locations or along a defined flight route at a given FL.
los.title: Flight conditions from a SWC at locations or along a route at a given FL
los.html:
Theory & physics

Plot the route on the chart; for the planned FL check: inside a CB area (with tops above FL?); inside CAT/turbulence areas (FL range covers your FL?); jet core nearby (FL of core, shear zones on cold side); tropopause height (above or below you?); icing areas and freezing level (low-level charts); fronts crossed and their speed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • A CAT area labelled e.g. MOD 300/400 affects FL 300 to FL 400 only.
  • Choose FL to avoid CAT areas and to stay above or clear of CB tops where possible.

los.lo: Recognise the following weather systems on a surface weather chart (analysed and forecast): ridges, cols and troughs; fronts; frontal side, warm sector and rear side of mid-latitude frontal lows; high- and low-pressure areas.
los.title: Recognise weather systems on surface charts (analysed and forecast)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ridges (U-shaped isobars, high), cols (between two highs and two lows), troughs (V-shaped isobars, low), fronts (warm: red semicircles; cold: blue triangles; occluded: purple alternating; stationary: alternating red/blue on opposite sides; upper fronts: open symbols), frontal side (ahead of the warm front), warm sector, rear side (behind the cold front) of mid-latitude lows; highs and lows with central pressure; pressure tendencies on forecast charts (movement arrows).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Analysis = observed state at a time; prognostic (forecast) chart = expected state.

los.lo: Determine from surface weather charts the wind direction and speed.
los.title: Determine wind direction and speed from surface charts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Direction: tangent to the isobars, low pressure on the left (NH), giving the geostrophic/gradient wind at ≈ 2000 ft; surface wind backed ≈ 30° over land (≈ 10° over sea) towards low pressure. Speed: from isobar spacing using the geostrophic wind scale for the chart's latitude (closer = stronger), then ≈ 50 % (land) or 70 % (sea) at the surface. Curvature: lighter round lows, stronger round highs.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Compare spacings only at similar latitudes.

los.lo: Define ‘constant-pressure chart’.
los.title: Define constant-pressure chart
los.html:
Theory & physics

An upper-air chart showing conditions on a surface of constant pressure (e.g. 850, 700, 500, 300, 250, 200 hPa): contours (isohypses) of the height of that surface, isotherms, wind barbs, sometimes humidity. Height contours play the role of isobars: wind blows parallel to them.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Approximate FL equivalents: 850 hPa ≈ FL 050, 700 ≈ FL 100, 500 ≈ FL 180, 300 ≈ FL 300, 250 ≈ FL 340, 200 ≈ FL 390.

los.lo: Define ‘isohypse (contour line)’. (Refer to Subject 050 01 03 02)
los.title: Define isohypse (contour line)
los.html:
Theory & physics

A line joining points of equal geopotential height of a given pressure surface (e.g. 552 = 5520 gpm on the 500 hPa chart). Low heights = low pressure aloft = cold air in the column; high heights = warm air/high pressure.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Geostrophic wind on upper charts blows parallel to contours, low heights on the left (NH).

los.lo: Define ‘isotherm’.
los.title: Define isotherm
los.html:
Theory & physics

A line joining points of equal temperature (on a level or pressure surface).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Closely packed isotherms = frontal zone, strong thermal wind, jet stream above, CAT risk. The 0 °C isotherm marks the freezing level.

los.lo: Define ‘isotach’.
los.title: Define isotach
los.html:
Theory & physics

A line joining points of equal wind speed; used to show jet cores and wind-speed maxima.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Tight isotach gradients = strong horizontal shear = CAT.

los.lo: Describe forecast upper-wind and temperature charts.
los.title: Forecast upper-wind and temperature charts
los.html:
Theory & physics

WAFS charts for standard FLs (e.g. FL 050, 100, 180, 240, 300, 340, 390, 450) with wind arrows/barbs (direction true, speed in kt: half barb 5, full barb 10, pennant 50) and temperatures at grid points (numbers in °C, negative unless marked PS/+), valid at a fixed time (e.g. 00, 06, 12, 18 UTC).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Temperatures at high levels are printed without minus sign (all negative); a "+"/PS denotes positive.

los.lo: For designated locations or routes determine from forecast upper-wind and temperature charts, if necessary by interpolation, the spot/average values for outside-air temperature, temperature deviation from ISA, wind direction, and wind speed.
los.title: Spot and average OAT, ISA deviation, wind from upper-air charts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Read grid values near the route at the relevant FL; interpolate between charts for intermediate FLs (linear) and between points along the route; average wind as a vector (or component along track) and average temperature; ISA deviation = average OAT − ISA temp for that FL.

Worked: FL 300, temperatures along route −40, −44, −48 → mean −44; ISA at FL 300 = 15 − 60 = −45 → ISA +1.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Exam figure: "mean temperature deviation from ISA on route Frankfurt–Rome": always compute ISA for the FL, not for the altitude.
  • Wind averaging: average direction and speed separately only when directions are similar; otherwise use components.

los.lo: State that numerical weather prediction uses a 3D grid of weather data, consisting of horizontal data (latitude-longitude) and vertical data (height or pressure).
los.title: NWP uses a 3D grid
los.html:
Theory & physics

Numerical weather prediction represents the atmosphere on a three-dimensional grid: horizontal points (latitude–longitude, spacing from a few km to tens of km) and vertical levels (height or pressure/hybrid levels); the model solves the equations of motion, thermodynamics and moisture at each point in time steps.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Small-scale phenomena (single Cb, CAT patches) are below grid resolution and must be parameterised.

los.lo: Explain that world area forecast centres prepare global sets of gridded forecasts for flight planning purposes (upper wind, temperature, humidity).
los.title: WAFCs prepare global gridded forecasts for flight planning
los.html:
Theory & physics

The two World Area Forecast Centres (London and Washington) produce global gridded forecasts of upper wind, temperature and humidity at standard levels, used directly by flight-planning systems.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Flight plans computed from WAFS GRIB data; SWC charts also from WAFCs.

los.lo: State that the WAFCs also produce gridded datasets for Flight Level and temperature of the tropopause, direction and speed of maximum wind, cumulonimbus clouds, icing and turbulence.
los.title: WAFC datasets: tropopause, maximum wind, CB, icing, turbulence
los.html:
Theory & physics

Also gridded: FL and temperature of the tropopause; direction, speed and FL of the maximum wind; CB horizontal extent and base/top; icing potential; CAT and in-cloud turbulence potential (and geopotential altitude of FLs).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • These grids are the basis of the hazard layers in EFB/flight-planning tools.

los.lo: Explain that the data on CB and turbulence can be used in the visualization of flight hazards.
los.title: CB and turbulence data for visualising flight hazards
los.html:
Theory & physics

Gridded CB and turbulence data can be displayed as hazard areas on route maps and vertical cross-sections, allowing crews to see where along the route and at which FLs the hazards are forecast.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Used for strategic route and FL selection.

los.lo: Explain that the gridded forecasts can be merged in information processing systems with data relayed from aircraft or pilot reports, e.g. of turbulence, to provide improved situation awareness.
los.title: Merging gridded forecasts with aircraft and pilot reports
los.html:
Theory & physics

Information processing systems combine forecast grids with real-time aircraft data (automated EDR turbulence reports, AMDAR, PIREPs) and observations to give an updated, more accurate hazard picture (situational awareness) in dispatch and in the cockpit (EFB).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Real-time reports correct the forecast where it has erred.

los.lo: Describe, decode and interpret the following aviation weather messages (given in written or graphical format): METAR, aerodrome special meteorological report (SPECI), trend forecast (TREND), TAF, information concerning en-route weather phenomena which may affect the safety of aircraft operations (SIGMET), information concerning en-route weather phenomena which may affect the safety of low-level aircraft operations (AIRMET), area forecast for low-level flights (GAMET), ARS, volcanic ash advisory information.
los.title: Decode and interpret METAR, SPECI, TREND, TAF, SIGMET, AIRMET, GAMET, ARS, VA advisory
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • METAR: routine aerodrome observation, every 30 or 60 min. Order: type, ICAO, day/time Z, (AUTO), wind (dddffGfmfmKT, VRB, dddVddd), visibility (and minimum with direction), RVR, present weather (intensity/proximity, descriptor, phenomena), cloud (FEW/SCT/BKN/OVC hhh + CB/TCU, VV, NSC, NCD), T/Td, QNH (Q/A), supplementary (RE recent weather, WS wind shear), runway state, TREND. CAVOK replaces visibility, RVR, weather and cloud when conditions allow.
  • SPECI: special observation issued when specified changes occur between routine METARs.
  • TREND: 2-hour forecast appended to METAR: BECMG (becoming), TEMPO (temporary fluctuations, each < 1 h and in total < half the period), with FM/TL/AT times; NOSIG = no significant change.
  • TAF: aerodrome forecast, validity 9–30 h (e.g. 2412/2518); change groups FM (from, rapid change), BECMG (gradual change during the period), TEMPO, PROB30/PROB40 (probability, alone or with TEMPO); TX/TN max/min temperature; amendments AMD, corrections COR.
  • SIGMET: en-route hazardous phenomena for all aircraft (WS for weather, WV for volcanic ash, WC for tropical cyclone), valid ≤ 4 h (6 h for VA/TC).
  • AIRMET: hazards for low-level flights below FL 100 (FL 150 in mountains) not already in the GAMET.
  • GAMET: area forecast for low-level flights in abbreviated plain language (sections I hazards, II general).
  • ARS: special air-report.
  • VA advisory: VAAC message/graphic giving ash cloud position and FL now and at +6, +12, +18 h.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • TEMPO in a TAF is not the prevailing condition; BECMG change is complete by the end of its period.
  • PROB alone: 30 or 40 % only (no PROB10/20/50).
  • METAR visibility 9999 = ≥ 10 km; cloud heights in hundreds of ft above aerodrome.

los.lo: Describe, decode and interpret the tropical cyclone advisory information in written and graphical form.
los.title: Tropical cyclone advisory (text and graphic)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Issued by TCACs (e.g. Miami, Tokyo, New Delhi, Réunion, Darwin, Honolulu, Nadi): name, observed position and time, movement (direction/speed), central pressure, maximum surface wind, forecast positions and winds at +6, +12, +18, +24 h; remarks; next advisory. Graphical version shows track and CB area.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • SIGMET (WC) for the TC is issued by the MWO using the advisory.

los.lo: Describe the general meaning of MET REPORT and SPECIAL REPORT.
los.title: MET REPORT and SPECIAL REPORT
los.html:
Theory & physics

Local routine (MET REPORT) and special (SPECIAL) reports in abbreviated plain language for dissemination at the aerodrome (ATIS, tower, departing/arriving aircraft). They use the 2-min wind (magnetic for ATIS), runway-specific values (RVR by zone, wind by runway end) and are issued when changes occur.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • ATIS information comes from MET REPORT, not from METAR.

los.lo: List, in general, the cases when a SIGMET and an AIRMET are issued.
los.title: When SIGMET and AIRMET are issued
los.html:
Theory & physics

SIGMET (subsonic): TS (OBSC, EMBD, FRQ, SQL; with or without hail: TSGR), TC, SEV TURB, SEV ICE (incl. FZRA), SEV MTW, HVY DS, HVY SS, VA, RDOACT CLD.

AIRMET (below FL 100/150, not already in GAMET): surface wind > 30 kt (SFC WIND), widespread surface visibility < 5000 m (SFC VIS), ISOL/OCNL TS (with/without hail), MT OBSC (mountain obscuration), cloud: BKN/OVC base < 1000 ft AGL, ISOL/OCNL/FRQ CB or TCU, MOD ICE, MOD TURB, MOD MTW.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • ISOL/OCNL TS → AIRMET (not SIGMET); FRQ/EMBD/OBSC/SQL TS → SIGMET.

los.lo: Describe, decode (by using a code table) and interpret the following messages: runway state message (as written in a METAR). Remark: For runway state message, refer to ICAO Doc 7754 ‘Air Navigation Plan - European Region’.
los.title: Runway state message in a METAR
los.html:
Theory & physics

Format R + runway designator + / + deposit (1 digit) + extent (1 digit) + depth (2 digits) + friction/braking (2 digits). Deposit: 0 clear and dry, 1 damp, 2 wet, 3 rime/frost, 4 dry snow, 5 wet snow, 6 slush, 7 ice, 8 compacted snow, 9 frozen ruts. Extent: 1 (≤ 10 %), 2 (11–25 %), 5 (26–50 %), 9 (51–100 %). Depth: mm (00–90), 92–98 = 10–40 cm, 99 = runway not operational. Friction: 2-digit coefficient (e.g. 45 = 0.45) or braking action 95 good, 94 medium/good, 93 medium, 92 medium/poor, 91 poor, 99 unreliable. Specials: CLRD (contamination cleared), SNOCLO (aerodrome closed due to snow).

Worked: R27/290155 = RWY 27, wet snow (2), 51–100 % (9), depth 1 mm (01), friction 0.55 (55).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Since November 2021 Europe reports runway condition with the Global Reporting Format (RCR/SNOWTAM); the exam still tests the METAR code (ICAO Doc 7754 reference).

los.lo: Describe the meteorological content of broadcasts for aviation: meteorological information for aircraft in flight (VOLMET); automatic terminal information service (ATIS).
los.title: VOLMET and ATIS
los.html:
Theory & physics

VOLMET: continuous VHF (or datalink, D-VOLMET) broadcast of current METAR/SPECI and TREND (and sometimes TAF/SIGMET) for a group of aerodromes. ATIS: automatic, recorded broadcast for one aerodrome: identifier letter, time, runway in use, approach type, surface wind, visibility/RVR, weather, cloud, T/Td, QNH (QFE), TL, wind shear, NOTAM/operational information; updated with each new MET REPORT; also D-ATIS by datalink.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • ATIS winds are magnetic (local report); VOLMET relays METARs (true).

los.lo: Describe the meteorological content of broadcasts for aviation: HF-VOLMET.
los.title: HF-VOLMET
los.html:
Theory & physics

HF broadcast of METAR, TAF and SIGMET for major aerodromes, on fixed schedules (e.g. at set minutes past each hour) and frequencies, for long-range flights out of VHF range (oceanic, remote areas).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Used to update destination/alternate weather on oceanic crossings (now often replaced by datalink).

los.lo: Describe meteorological briefing and advice.
los.title: Meteorological briefing and advice
los.html:
Theory & physics

Briefing: oral explanation or consultation with a forecaster (personal or by telephone) or self-briefing via approved systems; flight documentation: written/printed/electronic charts and messages (METAR, TAF, SIGMET, SWC, wind/temperature charts, advisories) for the planned flight.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The commander must study the available meteorological information before flight (SERA/Air Ops).

los.lo: List the information that a flight crew can receive from meteorological services for pre-flight planning and apply the content of this information on a designated flight route.
los.title: Pre-flight information and its application to a route
los.html:
Theory & physics

MET services provide: METAR/SPECI and TAF for departure, destination and alternates; en-route SIGMET, AIRMET/GAMET; SWC charts; upper-wind and temperature charts; VA and TC advisories; satellite and radar images; aerodrome warnings. Application: choose route and FL (winds, CAT, CB, icing), fuel, alternates (TAF meets planning minima), take-off and landing performance (wind, temperature, contamination).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Alternate planning uses TAF including TEMPO/PROB per operator rules.

los.lo: List the meteorological information that a flight crew can receive from flight information services during flight and apply the content of this information for the continuation of the flight.
los.title: In-flight information and its application
los.html:
Theory & physics

From FIS/ATC: SIGMET and AIRMET relevant to the route, special air-reports from other aircraft, aerodrome weather (METAR/SPECI, TAF on request), ATIS/VOLMET/HF-VOLMET, D-ATIS and datalink weather (D-VOLMET, ACARS), radar weather information from ATC.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use updates to re-assess destination, alternates and fuel; continue, divert or hold accordingly.

los.lo: Describe and interpret aerodrome warnings and wind-shear warnings and alerts.
los.title: Aerodrome warnings and wind-shear warnings and alerts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Aerodrome warnings: concise plain-language information on conditions that could adversely affect aircraft on the ground (including parked aircraft) and aerodrome facilities: TC, TS, hail, snow (with accumulation), FZRA, FZDZ, rime/hoar frost, sandstorm/duststorm, rising sand/dust, strong surface wind and gusts, squall, frost, VA and deposition, toxic chemicals, tsunami. Wind-shear warnings: observed or expected wind shear (> 15 kt headwind/tailwind change or significant downdraft) between runway level and ≈ 1600 ft (500 m) along the approach or climb-out paths. Wind-shear alerts: automated, up-to-date alerts from ground-based detection systems (LLWAS, Doppler radar, lidar) passed by ATC, e.g. "WS ALERT, 30 KT LOSS, 2 MF" (2 nm final).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Aerodrome warnings concern the aircraft on the ground; wind-shear warnings concern approach/departure paths.

topics.title: World area forecast system and meteorological offices

los.lo: Name the world area forecast centres (WAFCs) as the provider for upper-air forecasts: WAFCs prepare upper-air gridded forecasts of upper winds; upper-air temperature and humidity; direction, speed and flight level of maximum wind; flight level and temperature of tropopause, areas of cumulonimbus clouds, icing, clear-air and in-cloud turbulence, and geopotential altitude of flight levels.
los.title: WAFCs as providers of upper-air forecasts
los.html:
Theory & physics

The World Area Forecast Centres (WAFC London and WAFC Washington, in the World Area Forecast System, WAFS) prepare global gridded forecasts of upper winds, upper-air temperature and humidity; direction, speed and FL of maximum wind; FL and temperature of the tropopause; areas of CB clouds, icing, clear-air and in-cloud turbulence; geopotential altitude of FLs; and SIGWX forecasts (high level), disseminated via SADIS and WIFS.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Two WAFCs only: London and Washington.

los.lo: Name the meteorological (MET) offices as the provider for aerodrome forecasts and briefing documents.
los.title: MET offices as providers of aerodrome forecasts and briefing documents
los.html:
Theory & physics

Aerodrome meteorological offices prepare TAFs, TRENDs, aerodrome warnings, wind-shear warnings, and provide briefing, consultation and flight documentation to crews and operators.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • TAF comes from the MET office, not the WAFC.

los.lo: Name the meteorological watch offices (MWOs) as the provider for SIGMET and AIRMET information.
los.title: MWOs as providers of SIGMET and AIRMET
los.html:
Theory & physics

Meteorological watch offices keep a continuous watch over the weather in their FIR(s) and issue SIGMET and AIRMET (and contribute to GAMET), passing them to ATS units and other MWOs.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The SIGMET header identifies the FIR and the issuing MWO.

los.lo: Name the aeronautical meteorological stations as the provider for METAR and MET reports.
los.title: Aeronautical meteorological stations as providers of METAR and MET REPORT
los.html:
Theory & physics

Aeronautical meteorological stations at aerodromes make the routine and special observations and issue METAR/SPECI and MET REPORT/SPECIAL.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Observations (station) vs forecasts (MET office) vs en-route warnings (MWO): classic matching question.

los.lo: Name the volcanic ash advisory centres (VAACs) as the provider for forecasts of volcanic ash clouds.
los.title: VAACs as providers of volcanic ash forecasts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Nine Volcanic Ash Advisory Centres (London, Toulouse, Anchorage, Washington, Montreal, Buenos Aires, Tokyo, Darwin, Wellington) issue VA advisories (text and graphic) with the observed and forecast extent and FLs of ash clouds.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Europe is covered by VAAC London and VAAC Toulouse.

los.lo: Name the tropical cyclone advisory centres (TCACs) as the provider for forecasts of tropical cyclones.
los.title: TCACs as providers of tropical cyclone forecasts
los.html:
Theory & physics

Tropical Cyclone Advisory Centres (Miami, Honolulu, Tokyo, New Delhi, La Réunion, Darwin, Nadi) issue TC advisories with position, movement, intensity and forecasts.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • MWOs base SIGMET (WC) on TCAC advisories.

los.lo: Describe briefly the following organisations and their chief activities in relation to weather for aviation: International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) (Refer to Subject 010 ‘Air Law’); World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
los.title: ICAO and WMO
los.html:
Theory & physics

ICAO: UN specialised agency for civil aviation; sets the standards and recommended practices for aeronautical meteorological service (Annex 3, PANS), regional air navigation plans and the WAFS/IAVW/TC frameworks. WMO (World Meteorological Organization): UN specialised agency for meteorology; sets technical regulations, codes (METAR/TAF formats jointly with ICAO), observing networks, data exchange, and training of meteorological personnel; works with ICAO through joint arrangements.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Annex 3 = Meteorological Service for International Air Navigation (ICAO); WMO publishes the corresponding technical regulations and the Manual on Codes.
